history.citation: The Wayne Sentinel (Palmyra, New York) (26 June 1829).
history.teaser:
An early newspaper article from Palmyra, New York, discussing the Book of Mormon before its publication, including skepticism from the public and a preview of its title page.

Key Points:

  • Speculation about a divine ancient record
  • Record referred to as the "Golden Bible"
  • Public views it as an imposition and superstition
  • Promise of publication upon completion of translation
  • Title page description provided
  • Book of Mormon intended for Lamanites, Jews, and Gentiles
  • Emphasizes the role of God in its interpretation and preservation
  • Mentions the book as an effort to convince of Christ's divinity

history.author: Chronicler
history.citation: Chronicler. “From the Golden Bible: Chronicles Chapter I.” Paul Pry's Weekly Bulletin (Rochester, New York) 1, no. 12 (25 July 1829): 1–2. CHRONICLER
history.teaser:
A satirical piece from a Rochester newspaper, mocking political and social figures through a parody of biblical style.

Key Points:

  • People became angry at Horace for favoring Israel, a deceitful man
  • Israel aspired to be a counsellor despite his abominations
  • Israel acknowledges his wrongdoings but seeks revenge
  • Israel seeks help from Joseph, Wanton, and Chad
  • Chad, described humorously as endowed like an ass, agrees to assist
  • Chad suggests crying persecution and improving Israel's image
  • Israel avoids Joseph and Wanton, feeling guilty
  • Israel is left in bitter contemplation

history.author: Castigator
history.citation: Castigator. “For Paul Pry’s Weekly Bulletin [From Palmyra].” Paul Pry’s Weekly Bulletin (Rochester, New York) 1, no. 14 (8 August 1829): 1.
history.teaser:
A satirical piece from a local newspaper mocking various individuals in Palmyra, including a veiled reference to the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Mockery of a merchant's pretense and lack of wealth
  • Questioning the appropriateness of someone's display of status
  • Calling out someone for acting above their station
  • Criticism of a young person's public behavior
  • Speculation about the failure of the "Twin Brothers"
  • Question about the Fire Warden's fortune ambitions with the Gold Bible
  • Comment on "Little Billy's" excessive spending on women
  • Skepticism about successfully tarnishing a political enemy's reputation

history.author: Chronicler
history.document: From the Golden Bible. Chronicles: Chapter III
history.citation: Chronicler. “From the Golden Bible: Chronicles Chapter III.” Paul Pry's Weekly Bulletin (Rochester, New York) 1, no. 14 (8 August 1829): 1.
history.teaser:
A satirical piece from a 1829 newspaper mocking the Book of Mormon and its narratives.

Key Points:

  • Horace the publican is depicted as meek and sober
  • Horace becomes an object of scorn for protecting Israel
  • Hiram the Jeromite is portrayed as deceitful and cunning
  • Community rejects Hiram despite his claims of friendship towards Egbert
  • Israel is supported by Chad, Joseph, and Wanton despite mockery
  • Chad the money lender experiences a frightening vision
  • George the laborer helps Chad out of a pit
  • Mockery of the Book of Mormon being a "Golden Book" in Joseph the prophet's custody

history.author: Chronicler
history.citation: “Chronicles: Chap. I.” Paul Pry's Weekly Bulletin (Rochester, New York) (29 August 1829).
history.teaser:
A satirical piece from a 1829 newspaper mocking religious fervor and leadership in the community.

Key Points:

  • Westleyets gather in the wilderness, doing evil in the Lord's sight
  • Roswel the mighty, a converted man with much money, joins them
  • Roswel lays grievous fines upon people brought before him
  • Samuel's lawful expositions ignored by the hard-hearted
  • Pious brothers seek to incriminate others for personal gain
  • Roswel, used by priests for their will, judges against the people
  • Scandalous behavior occurs, justified as "the work of the Lord"
  • Warning against following bad leaders or face torment by folly

history.citation: “Golden Bible.” Rochester Advertiser and Daily Telegraph (New York) (31 August 1829). Reprinted from Palmyra Freeman, 11 August 1829.
history.teaser:
An early skeptical report on Joseph Smith's discovery of the Book of Mormon, emphasizing disbelief and skepticism.

Key Points:

  • Described as the greatest piece of superstition by the Palmyra Freeman
  • Joseph Smith reported being visited in a dream by the spirit of the Almighty
  • Smith found the Golden Bible and a huge pair of spectacles
  • Under penalty of death, no one was allowed to examine them
  • Leaves of the bible were plates of gold with engraved characters
  • Smith claimed he could interpret the characters by looking into a hat
  • Martin Harris believed the story and sought external validation
  • Language and doctrine of the work said to be superior to the Bible

history.citation: The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 1, no. 1 (2 September 1829): 2.
history.teaser:
An early newspaper mention of the Book of Mormon, noting its imminent publication.

Key Points:

  • The Gold Bible by Joseph Smith Jr. is in press
  • It will be published shortly
  • Comment on priestcraft being short-lived

history.author: Ed. Gem
history.citation: “Golden Bible.” The Gem: A Semi-Monthly Literary and Miscellaneous Journal (Rochester,New York) (5 September 1829): 70.
history.teaser:
An early report on the efforts to print the Book of Mormon, referring to it as the “Golden Bible.”

Key Points:

  • Martin Harris sought to print a work called the Golden Bible
  • Joseph Smith claimed to find the Golden Bible in 1827
  • Found after being directed by a spirit in a dream
  • Contained on gold plates with hieroglyphics
  • Smith could interpret the hieroglyphics using spectacles
  • No one but Smith was intended to interpret the plates
  • The translation is now in press in Palmyra, Wayne Co.
  • The subject is attracting notice among a certain class

history.citation: The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 1, no. 3 (16 September 1829): 10.
history.teaser:
A newspaper announcement indicating the expected publication timeline for the Book of Mormon and predicting significant events upon its release.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon expected to be ready in one year
  • Predicts great and marvelous things will happen around that time

history.document: “We understand that the Anti-Masons have declared war”
history.citation: The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 1, no. 4 (23 September 1829): 14.
history.teaser:
A local newspaper editorial making fun of the Book of Mormon and its followers, and their ambitions to build a New Jerusalem.

Key Points:

  • Anti-Masons declared war against the Gold Bible
  • Gold Bible Apostles’ number is said to be complete
  • Jo Smith Jr. to assign missions to the heathen
  • Abraham Chaddock to build the first house in New-Jerusalem
  • A man in Mendon had a loud call to preach Gold Bible doctrines

history.citation: “An Extract.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 1, no. 5 (30 September 1829): 18.
history.teaser:
A sarcastic comparison between an early 16th-century religious movement and Joseph Smith’s revelations in The Reflector newspaper.

Key Points:

  • Mention of a 1511 denomination called “Men of Understanding”
  • Founded by Egidus Cantor and William of Henderison
  • Claimed to have celestial visions
  • Believed in divine illumination for understanding scriptures
  • Declared a new revelation more perfect than the Gospel of Christ
  • Implies similarity to Joseph Smith Jr.’s claims

history.citation: The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 1, no. 5 (30 September 1829): 18.
history.teaser:
A newspaper report that the Book of Mormon is gaining credibility, comparing its spread to that of Islam.

Key Points:

  • The Gold Bible is fast gaining credit
  • Its spread compared to the rapid spread of Islam

history.citation: “Our Own Affairs.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 1, no. 5 (30 September 1829): 17.
history.teaser:
An editorial piece from The Reflector criticizes the misuse of a quote attributed to George Washington by the Anti-Masons and discusses the dangers of secret associations.

Key Points:

  • Criticism of the Anti-Masons’ use of a misattributed quote
  • Discussion on the dangers of secret associations
  • Encourages scrutiny of the intentions behind political movements
  • Warns against the potential for cunning individuals to usurp power
  • Advocates for the truth and justice in political discourse
  • Emphasizes the importance of understanding historical documents
  • Rejects the notion that the piece is politically motivated
  • Seeks to illuminate truth in the face of deceit and manipulation

history.citation: The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 1, no. 6 (7 October 1829): 22.
history.teaser:
An early newspaper report on the Book of Mormon and Joseph Smith’s followers.

Key Points:

  • TEMPLE OF NEPHI building to start at the Millennium’s beginning
  • Thousands flocking to Joseph the Prophet’s standard
  • Book of Mormon expected to astonish the natives

history.citation: “Gold Bible.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 1, no. 15 (9 December 1829): 57.
history.teaser:
An announcement in a local newspaper about the upcoming publication of the Book of Mormon and plans to publish extracts from it.

Key Points:

  • A work called “Gold Bible” is now in press
  • Curiosity has been excited in the local area
  • Work will not be ready for delivery for some months
  • Plans to commence publishing extracts from it soon

history.citation: [Gold Bible.] The Reflector (Palmyra, New York), n.s., 1 (22 December 1829): 8.
history.teaser:
A brief announcement in a local newspaper regarding the upcoming publication of an article or series related to the Book of Mormon, referred to as the Gold Bible.

Key Points:

  • Announcement of “Gold Bible” feature next week
  • “Bard of Visions” rejected

history.document: The Biter bit–Or, Anti-Masonic Wit outwitted
history.citation: “The Biter bit—Or, Anti-Masonic Wit outwitted.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) newseries, no. 2 (2 January 1830): 13.
history.teaser:
A satirical piece in The Reflector mocking Joseph Smith and anti-Masonic sentiments through a biblical-style narrative.

Key Points:

  • Written in a biblical narrative style
  • Features characters with thinly veiled references to Joseph Smith
  • Addresses themes of greed and deceit
  • Portrays a moral lesson against avarice and wickedness
  • Uses a story of personal downfall as a cautionary tale
  • Mocks the tension between religious and secular ambitions
  • Illustrates divine intervention and judgment
  • Ends with the moral failure and flight of Adolphus

history.citation: “Gold Bible.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) new series, no. 2 (2 January 1830): 13.
history.teaser:
An editorial from “The Reflector” discussing the Book of Mormon without taking a definitive stance on its merits or faults, and emphasizing freedom of belief.

Key Points:

  • Editorial refuses to discuss merits or demerits of the Book of Mormon
  • Expresses surprise at neighbors’ uneasiness about the book
  • Book’s success dependent on reader’s whims and fancies
  • Uncertain how it will withstand rigorous criticism
  • Nothing treasonable or liberty-subverting in the first chapter
  • Religious character of the book not yet determined
  • Editorial avoids meddling with neighbors’ consciences

history.citation: “From the Book of Mormon. The First Book of Nephi. His Reign and Ministry. Chapter I.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) new series, no. 2 (2 January 1830): 1.
history.teaser:
A newspaper article from The Reflector presenting a summary of the first chapter of the First Book of Nephi from the Book of Mormon, focusing on Lehi’s visions and prophecies.

Key Points:

  • Nephi introduces his record and lineage
  • Lehi prays for his people and sees a vision of God
  • Lehi reads from a book given by a descending figure
  • The book prophesies the destruction of Jerusalem
  • Lehi rejoices in the Lord’s greatness after his visions
  • Lehi prophesies to the people, is mocked by them
  • Jews seek to take Lehi’s life for his testimonies
  • The Lord commands Lehi to flee into the wilderness with his family

history.citation: Gold Bible.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) new series, no. 3 (13 January 1830): 20.
history.teaser:
An article from “The Reflector” addressing the Book of Mormon, clarifying its name and origin.

Key Points:

  • “Gold Bible” is a derisive term used by unbelievers
  • The correct title is “The Book of Mormon”
  • The Book of Mormon is divided into chapters and books
  • First book mentioned is “First Book of Nephi”
  • Purports to be a compilation on gold-like plates
  • Compiled by Mormon, of the lost tribes

history.citation: “From the ‘Book of Mormon,’ erroneously called the ‘ Gold Bible. ’ The First Book ofNephi. His Reign and Ministry. Chapter I.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) new series,no. 3 (13 January 1830): 17.
history.teaser:
An excerpt from The Reflector newspaper featuring a portion of the First Book of Nephi from the Book of Mormon, which the newspaper refers to as the “Gold Bible.”

Key Points:

  • Departure into the wilderness with family and provisions
  • Travel near the Red Sea and settling beside a river
  • Building an altar and offering thanks to the Lord
  • Naming of the river and valley after Laman
  • Lehi’s wishes for his sons to be righteous
  • Laman and Lemuel’s murmuring against Lehi’s vision
  • Lehi’s powerful speech to his sons in the valley
  • Continuation of their journey in the wilderness

history.document: Extract from the Book of Alma
history.citation: “Book of Mormon. Extract from the Book of Alma. Chapter XX.” The Reflector (Palmyra,New York) new series, Extra (22 January 1830): 27–28.
history.teaser:
An early public dissemination of a Book of Mormon text, focusing on military strategy and divine guidance in Nephite-Lamanite conflicts.

Key Points:

  • Nephites use spies to gather intelligence on Lamanite movements
  • Alma receives divine guidance for Nephite military strategy
  • Moroni divides his forces to ambush the Lamanites
  • Nephites prepared to defend their lands, liberty, and church
  • Moroni employs stratagem to defend against Lamanites
  • Lehi leads a successful ambush against the Lamanites
  • Lamanites suffer heavy losses and flee
  • Nephites prevent Lamanite crossing of the river Sidon

history.author: Blatchley, C. C.
history.citation: Blatchley, C. C. “Caution Against the Golden Bible.” New-York Telescope 6, no. 38 (20 February 1830): 150.
history.teaser:
An early critique of the Book of Mormon, focusing on its authenticity, origin story, and literary style.

Key Points:

  • Published caution against the “Golden Bible” or Book of Mormon
  • Claims of supernatural revelation and golden plates questioned
  • Joseph Smith’s translation method described skeptically
  • Comparison of the Book of Mormon’s style to the Bible
  • Repetitive phrases used as evidence of Joseph Smith’s authorship
  • Speculation on the book’s financial motives and authenticity
  • Concerns over the book’s claim to surpass the Bible
  • Caution urged against spending money on what might be a hoax

history.citation: “Diabolical.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) new series, no. 8 (27 February 1830):66–67.
history.teaser:
A satirical piece in The Reflector mocking the translation of the Book of Mormon and comparing its challenges to deciphering a supposed diabolical correspondence.

Key Points:

  • Mocking the translation of the Book of Mormon
  • Comparison to the difficulty of translating “heathen Greek”
  • Editorial troubles exaggerated with humorous imagery
  • Claim of burning a scroll leading to supernatural phenomena
  • Mockery of the Book of Mormon’s language and translation process
  • Comparison of translating difficulties to diabolical challenges
  • Satirical commitment to exposing “deeds of darkness”
  • Humorous proposal to write about lost tribes of Israel instead

history.citation: Reply to Luther Howard. The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) new series, no. 11 (16 March 1830): 89.
history.teaser:
A letter to the editor of The Reflector expressing a subscriber’s desire to cancel his subscription, followed by a critical response from the editor.

Key Points:

  • Luther Howard requests cancellation of his subscription.
  • Editor expresses regret but criticizes Howard.
  • Howard described as a “little lump of anguish.”
  • Editor prefers support from enlightened, independent, liberal-minded people.
  • Howard accused of being a meddlesome, canting, whining hypocrite.
  • Howard ostentatiously belongs to a Calvinistic church.
  • Howard privately advocates the “Gold Bible.”
  • Editor plans to publish more communications about Howard.

history.citation: [We are requested to announce.] The Wayne Sentinel (Palmyra, New York) (19 March 1830).
history.teaser:
An announcement in a local newspaper about the upcoming availability of the Book of Mormon for sale.

Key Points:

  • Announcement of the Book of Mormon being ready for sale
  • Availability set for the next week from the announcement date

history.citation: Wayne Sentinel (Palmyra, New York) (26 March 1830).
history.teaser:
An advertisement for the sale of the Book of Mormon at a bookstore in Palmyra, NY.

Key Points:

  • The work contains about 600 pages, large Duodecimo
  • For sale, wholesale and retail, at the Palmyra Bookstore
  • Sold by Howard & Grandin
  • Date of advertisement: March 26, 1830

history.author: Newsmonger
history.citation: Newsmonger. Letter to the editor, March 1830. The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) newseries, no. 13 (30 March 1830): 106–7.
history.teaser:
A satirical letter to the editor of The Reflector, mocking the publication’s content and suggesting a recipe for creating a literary paper.

Key Points:

  • Satirical advice on creating a literary newspaper
  • Mentions a “soft head” for appealing to a certain audience
  • Emphasizes stating the paper’s devotion to “Literature and Science”
  • Advises using romances from the fifteenth century for content
  • Suggests altering names and details for originality, mocking the Book of Mormon’s translation
  • Recommends selecting flat articles for uniformity
  • Mentions appending nonsensical poetry for effect
  • Mockingly suggests boasting about new subscribers

history.document: A New Way of Raising the Wind
history.citation: “A new way of raising the wind.” Rochester Republican (New York) (30 March 1830).
history.teaser:
An early newspaper critique suggesting skepticism towards the Book of Mormon’s origins and intentions.

Key Points:

  • Any scheme will find dupes, according to a saying
  • The Book of Mormon’s promotion is being tested anew

history.citation: Morning Courier and New York Enquirer (31 March 1830).
history.teaser:
A newspaper announcement of the publication of the Book of Mormon, mentioning its alternative title “Gold Bible.”

Key Points:

  • The Book of Mormon has been published at Palmyra
  • Also known as the “Gold Bible”

history.document: Blasphemy—Book of Mormon, alias the Golden Bible
history.citation: “Blasphemy–‘Book of Mormon,’ alias The Golden Bible.” Rochester Daily Advertiser (NewYork) (2 April 1830).
history.teaser:
A scathing newspaper article criticizing the Book of Mormon, calling it fraudulent and blasphemous.

Key Points:

  • Article labels the Book of Mormon as a “viler imposition”
  • Describes the book as evidence of fraud, blasphemy, and credulity
  • Joseph Smith, Jr. is named as “author and proprietor”
  • Mentions financial backing from a Wayne county farmer
  • Farmer mortgaged his farm for $3000 for printing 5000 copies
  • Book of Mormon consists of about 600 pages
  • Divided into books of Nephi, Jacob, Mosiah, Alma, Mormon, Ether, and Helaman
  • Article questions the style and credibility of the work

history.citation: “Mr. Editor.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) n.s., 16 (19 April 1830): 130. ‘Gold-Bible’
history.teaser:
A letter to the editor expressing displeasure with the behavior of Hyrum Smith and associates regarding the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Hyrum Smith and associates are warned to be less impertinent
  • Decent folks denounce the ‘Gold-Bible’ as an imposition
  • Anathemas of the Book of Mormon followers are not feared
  • Apostles are advised to keep cool

history.document: The Book of Mormon, or Golden Bible
history.citation: “The Book of Mormon, or Golden Bible.” Village Chronicle (Dansville, New York) (27 April 1830).
history.teaser:
An early newspaper article summarizing the publication and contents of the Book of Mormon, with mention of witness testimonies to its origin.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon published in western New York
  • Author: Joseph Smith, Jr.
  • Contains about 600 pages, includes books of Mormon, Ether, and Helaman
  • Rochester Daily Advertiser published the preface and two letters
  • Eleven individuals testified to the book’s excellence and original plates
  • Book of Lehi was translated, stolen, and not re-translated
  • Testimony mentioned was viewed with hesitancy, noted as controversial
  • Plates had the appearance of gold and showed ancient workmanship

history.citation: “We are informed.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3d series, no. 1 (1 May 1830): 5. Jo Smith
history.teaser:
A newspaper report mocking the decision of an attorney to leave his profession to preach the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • An “honest Attorney” plans to quit his job
  • Intent to preach the “Gospel according to Jo Smith”

history.author: A.
history.citation: A. “‘When ignorance is bliss tis folly to be wise.’” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3dseries, no. 1 (1 May 1830): 6.
history.teaser:
An article from The Reflector discussing the misinterpretation of a story about “John Faust” and its mistaken connection to Joseph Smith and the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Article reflects on ignorance related to interpreting literature.
  • Discussion among men mistakenly connects “John Faust” to the Book of Mormon.
  • Surprise at the profound ignorance in the neighborhood.
  • Recommendation for an “march-of-intellect-society” for adult education.

history.citation: “Imposition and Blasphemy!!—Moneydiggers, Etc.” The Gem (Rochester, New York) (15 May 1830): 15.
history.teaser:
An early critical newspaper article from Rochester, New York, dismissing the Book of Mormon as a fraud and likening its discovery to local tales of treasure hunting.

Key Points:

  • Describes the Book of Mormon’s discovery as an imposition
  • Mentions the financial sacrifices made for its publication
  • Compares the Book of Mormon to Salem witchcraft and other local lore
  • Discusses Joseph Smith’s earlier involvement in treasure hunting
  • Describes a prior money-digging hoax involving Joseph Smith
  • Mentions skepticism around Joseph Smith’s claims to translate ancient plates
  • Highlights the public availability of the Book of Mormon for purchase
  • Compares the Book of Mormon story to an earlier local hoax

history.citation: “The Apostle to the Nephites . . .” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3d series, no. 4 (1 June 1830): 28. JoSmith
history.teaser:
An article mocking Oliver Cowdery’s mission to preach the Book of Mormon in the eastern United States.

Key Points:

  • Cowdery started for the East with a load of ‘Gold Bibles’
  • Under command to declare the truth in principal cities
  • Article compares Cowdery to Jemima Wilkinson, suggesting delusion
  • Warns Cowdery to be careful of the Old Saybrook Platform
  • Notes Cowdery left out his middle names in the Book of Mormon
  • Mocks Cowdery’s mission, suggesting he might end up in mines instead

history.document: “A fellow by the name of Joseph Smith”
history.citation: Cincinnati Advertiser and Ohio Phoenix (2 June 1830). Reprinted from Wayne County Inquirer, Pennsylvania, circa May 1830.
history.teaser:
An early newspaper account skeptical of Joseph Smith and the Book of Mormon, emphasizing skepticism and accusations of fraud.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith claimed to translate a new bible from a golden book
  • Smith used a white stone in a hat for translation
  • Claims to give an account of the “Ten Tribes”
  • Some people believe in Smith’s divine commission
  • Described as a “viler imposition” and “blasphemy”
  • Joseph Smith Jr. influenced a farmer to mortgage his farm for printing
  • Book of Mormon consists of about 600 pages
  • Divided into books of Nephi, Jacob, Mosiah, Alma, Mormon, Ether, and Helaman

history.citation: “The Book of Pukei.— Chap. I.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3d series, no. 5 (12 June 1830): 36–37.
history.teaser:
A satirical piece from The Reflector newspaper mocking Joseph Smith and the origins of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Wickedness abounds, leading to a search for Nephite treasure
  • Walters the Magician brought in to locate the treasure
  • Magician uses Cicero’s Orations to conjure stories of treasure
  • Magician and followers perform rituals to find treasure
  • Many nights spent digging for treasure, always disappointed
  • Followers become disillusioned with the magician’s promises
  • Magician retreats to mountains, continues communing with the Devil
  • Implication that Joseph Smith inherited the magician’s mantle

history.citation: “Our Citizens.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3d series, no. 6 (22 June 1830): 45–46.
history.teaser:
A satirical article from The Reflector mocking the early followers of Joseph Smith and the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Citizens agitated by a strange preacher’s appearance and actions
  • Comparison to Lorenzo Dow, a famous itinerant preacher
  • Preacher declared command to “preach the gospel to every creature”
  • Uncertainty whether the preacher follows Jemima Wilkinson, Jo Smith, or the devil
  • Report of a “Gold Bible” witness maltreating his wife to convert her
  • A “Gold Bible” apostle attempted to anathematize an infidel

history.citation: “A hungry lean-faced villain.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3d series, no. 7 (30 June 1830): 53–54. Jo SmithJo's Jo
history.teaser:
A critical article from The Reflector mocking Joseph Smith and his followers, particularly focusing on a supposed miracle of casting out a devil.

Key Points:

  • Describes Joseph Smith in derogatory terms
  • Claims the age of miracles has “again” arrived with the Gold Bible
  • Joseph Smith labeled as a “spindle shanked ignoramus”
  • Joseph Smith and followers accused of disturbing peace
  • Joseph Smith’s followers denounce damnation on skeptics
  • Joseph Smith’s latest miracle: casting out a large devil
  • Comparison to the spirits possessing Mary Magdalene
  • Describes the possessed man’s dire condition before the miracle

history.citation: Exemption from taxation. The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3d series, no. 8 (7 July 1830): 61.
history.teaser:
An article from The Reflector newspaper discussing a demand by a follower of the Book of Mormon for tax exemption.

Key Points:

  • A disciple of the Gold Bible demands tax exemption
  • Claims exemption as a Minister of the Gospel
  • Produces a certificate signed by Jo. Smith and Oliver Cowdery
  • The final decision on the matter was not reported

history.citation: The Book of Pukei.—Chap. 2.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3d series, no. 8 (7 July 1830): 60.
history.teaser:
A satirical piece from The Reflector mocking Joseph Smith and the origins of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Idle and slothful people revere Joseph as a prophet
  • Joseph claims the mantle of Walters the Magician
  • Joseph promises to show where Nephites hid their treasures
  • A spirit, claiming to keep all earth’s treasures, appears to Joseph
  • The spirit is described humorously with anachronistic details
  • Mormon, the apostle to the Nephites, allegedly contacted Joseph
  • The Nephites’ migration, wars, and transformation into Indians are mockingly recounted
  • Joseph is promised tools for translation and assistance by Oliver

history.author: Joppa
history.citation: Joppa. “Book of Daniel.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3d series, no. 10 (27 July 1830): 79. Joseph
history.teaser:
A satirical piece from The Reflector newspaper, likening Joseph Smith to a biblical prophet and mocking his influence.

Key Points:

  • Set in the years of American Independence
  • Compares Joseph Smith to a prophet
  • Mentions a character named Daniel with great self-respect
  • Daniel’s profession involves aiding the afflicted
  • He finds an audience among Jerseyans and Alleganians

history.author: Joppa
history.citation: Joppa. “Book of Daniel.—Chap. 2.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3d series, no. 11 (4 August 1830): 82–83.
history.teaser:
An editorial piece in a local newspaper using biblical language to mock the Book of Mormon and its revelations.

Key Points:

  • Uses biblical language for satirical purposes
  • Targets believers in the Book of Mormon
  • Implies believers claim to have “precious knowledge”
  • Suggests a disconnect between believers’ inquiries and their understanding
  • Foretells of “marvellous actions” yet to be understood
  • Indicates a future restraint on believers due to this knowledge

history.citation: “The First Book of John.” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3d series, no. 12 (14 August 1830): 94.
history.teaser:
A satirical piece from The Reflector newspaper, mocking the style of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Published in The Reflector in August 1830
  • Mimics Book of Mormon style
  • References Joseph the prophet
  • Introduces a character named John
  • John is described as a descendant of martyrs
  • John established himself near “veracity corner”

history.citation: “Every thing in this world . . .” The Reflector (Palmyra, New York) 3d series, no. 14 (28 August 1830): 108–9. JO SMITH’S
history.teaser:
An editorial piece from The Reflector that uses satire to comment on human nature and the perception of truth, making a jesting reference to Joseph Smith’s translation method.

Key Points:

  • Everything in the world contains jest and instruction

A skeptical article from The Reflector discussing discrepancies in the accounts of the Book of Mormon’s discovery and description by its witnesses.

A letter from Palmyra, New York, criticizing the Book of Mormon and its followers, published in the Painesville Telegraph.

history.citation: “Our neighbor-in-law . . . ” Painesville Telegraph (Painesville, Ohio) (22 March 1831).
history.teaser:
An editorial from the Painesville Telegraph criticizing the association between Mormonism and anti-Masonry.

Key Points:

  • Claims that all who embraced Mormonism are antimasons
  • Mentions zealot masons and republicans seeking more insight from Joseph Smith
  • The Book of Mormon printed in a masonic printing office

history.teaser:
An article from the Ohio Star discussing the antimasonic stance of the Book of Mormon and its followers.

Key Points:

  • The Mormon Bible is described as Antimasonic
  • Followers of the Book of Mormon are also antimasons
  • Discussion on the concept of “Church and State”
  • Masonry is humorously compared to the “Handmaid of Religion”

history.citation: “The Gold Bible fever . . .” Painesville Telegraph (Painesville, Ohio) (29 March 1831).
history.teaser:
A critical report from the Painesville Telegraph discussing skepticism and discrepancies in the narratives surrounding the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Gold Bible fever abating in the vicinity
  • Some followers breaking away, doubting the narrative
  • Discrepancy in the promised land’s location
  • Different accounts of the Book of Mormon by witnesses
  • Harris and Whitmar give conflicting descriptions of the plates
  • Accounts vary on how the Book of Mormon was translated
  • Descriptions of the plates’ appearance differ
  • Mormon apostles give varying accounts of the Book of Mormon

history.author: B., A. W.
history.citation: B., A.W. “Mormonites.” Evangelical Magazine and Gospel Advocate (Utica, New York) 2,no. 15 (9 April 1831): 120.

An article from 1831 criticizing Joseph Smith, Jr. and early Mormonism, depicting it as a scheme based on deception.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith was previously known as a “glass-looker”.
  • Smith was involved in money-digging schemes that failed.
  • He was arrested but escaped due to his youth.
  • Smith is accused of forging a new revelation for personal gain.
  • Meetings were held to proselytize “weak and silly” individuals.
  • The Book of Mormon was allegedly produced through magical means.
  • Testimonies during a trial questioned the truth of Smith’s claims.
  • Smith’s followers are described as children or ignorant adults.

history.citation: “Mormonites.” Working Man’s Advocate (New York) 2, no. 39 (14 May 1831).
history.teaser:
An article from the Working Man’s Advocate discussing the rise of Mormonism and the public’s reaction to it.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism is a new religion with hundreds of followers
  • Some editors seem alarmed by its growth
  • Comparison of the Golden Bible’s origin to other religions
  • Ridicule towards proving the inauthenticity of the Golden Bible
  • Painesville Gazette’s article on a Mormon sermon by Pratt
  • Pratt tried to establish the divine origin of the Mormon bible
  • Pratt’s sermon compared to promoting infidelity
  • Mormonites are journeying to the “far west” land of promise

history.citation: “The Mormonites.” The Village Chronicle (17 May 1831).
history.teaser:
A newspaper article critical of early Mormon community practices and incidents of misconduct among its members.

Key Points:

  • Unworthy members have joined the Mormon community in Painesville, Ohio
  • The community’s practices have attracted many, despite criticisms
  • Mormonites practice having “all things in common”
  • Community is criticized for attracting idlers and avoiding manual labor
  • Recent additions include individuals poor in spirit and dress
  • Some exploited the community, stealing clothes and leaving
  • Article questions the influence of the new golden bible
  • Suggests the sect should dissolve if conduct doesn’t improve

history.citation: “A new excitement: Mormonism versus Anti-masonry.” Morning Courier and New-York Enquirer (New York City, New York) 7, no. 1247 (21 May 1831).
history.teaser:
A newspaper report on the rise of Mormonism in an anti-masonic area of Ohio, noting its rapid spread and comparing its fervor to that of anti-masonry.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism rising in anti-masonic district of Ohio
  • Described as marching like a giant
  • Attacking citadels of anti-masonry
  • Mormonism making great progress in Ohio Reserve
  • Possesses more fanaticism than anti-masonry

history.citation: “Several families . . .” Wayne Sentinel (Palmyra, New York) (27 May 1831).
history.teaser:
A newspaper report on the departure of several families, including Martin Harris, from Palmyra to what they believed was the “promised land,” due to their belief in the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • 50 people left Palmyra for the “promised land”
  • Martin Harris, an early believer, was among them
  • Harris was known as honorable and upright
  • He had acquired a respectable fortune through honest industry
  • Left behind friends to pity his belief in the Book of Mormon

history.citation: “Mr. Alexa[n]der Campbell . . .” Painesville Telegraph (Painesville, Ohio) (21 June 1831).
history.teaser:
A report on Alexander Campbell’s criticism of the Book of Mormon and its origins, emphasizing his views on religious revelation and credibility.

Key Points:

  • Alexander Campbell delivered an eloquent discourse in Painesville, Ohio
  • He criticized delusions and religious impositions
  • Contended God wouldn’t make a new revelation after Christ
  • Revelations communicated by men of good repute, not money-diggers
  • Implied Joseph Smith lacked credibility for divine revelation
  • Had an interview with Sidney Rigdon about the Gold Bible
  • Interview revealed moral depravity associated with the Book of Mormon
  • Hope expressed for publicizing the substance of the interview

history.citation: “The Mormonites.” Geauga Gazette (Painesville, Ohio) (21 June 1831). Reprinted in Western Reserve Chronicle (Warren, Ohio) (30 June 1831): 3.
history.teaser:
A newspaper article describing the early movement of Mormon followers towards what they believed was their promised land.

Key Points:

  • Mormon followers are moving towards a spot on the Missouri River
  • About 30 have been ordained and are traveling in pairs
  • Travel routes are by western rivers and land
  • Those without property are moving immediately
  • Followers are selling property quickly, sometimes at a loss
  • Mormonites claim to work miracles, including healing and exorcism
  • Assertions of miracles made by previously rational men
  • Article suggests leaders are imposters but followers are sincere

history.citation: “Mormonism.” Niles’ Weekly Register (Baltimore, Maryland) 4 (16 July 1831): [853].
history.teaser:
A critical report from 1831 on the early Mormon movement, its leadership, and followers.

Key Points:

  • Report criticizes the origins of Mormonism in New York
  • Mormon leaders are accused of pretending to find holy writings
  • Mormonism has grown to 1,000 members
  • Joseph Smith has declared part of Geauga County, Ohio, as “the promised land”
  • People are moving to Ohio, attracted by communal wealth
  • Members include both honest believers and those deemed “lazy and worthless”
  • Claims of miraculous powers, including passage through ice and raising the dead
  • Leadership is accused of avoiding labor, suggesting ulterior motives

history.citation: “Mormonites.” Republican Advocate (Wooster, Ohio) (16 July 1831): 1.
history.teaser:
An article from the Republican Advocate describing the early Mormon settlement in Ohio and their beliefs.

Key Points:

  • Mormonites are rapidly increasing in numbers in Ohio
  • Many families from New York and other states have joined
  • The Book of Mormon described as a revelation from Heaven
  • Respectable and intelligent individuals, including ministers, have joined
  • Mormonites refuse medical aid, leading to deaths
  • Plan to perform miraculous feats, including raising the dead
  • Settlement located in Geauga County, Ohio
  • Over four hundred locals have become followers of Joseph Smith

history.author: Owen, Robert Dale, 1801-1877
history.document: Authenticity of the Golden Bible—References to the Book of Mormon

history.teaser:
An article by Robert Dale Owen in the Free Enquirer discussing the authenticity and rapid growth of the Mormon movement.

Key Points:

  • Mormonites believe in a Golden Book of Revelation from Heaven
  • Their numbers have grown to many hundreds
  • They are devoted to their new creed
  • They aim to inherit God’s promise to Abraham on the Missouri river
  • About 80 have been ordained and are moving to their new land
  • They claim the power to work miracles
  • Owen suggests humility and forbearance towards others’ beliefs
  • He questions the credibility of miraculous claims in religion

history.citation: “Mormonism.” Atkinson’s Saturday Evening Post (Philadelphia) 10, no. 521 (23 July 1831).
history.teaser:
An early 19th-century newspaper article expressing skepticism towards Mormonism and its founders.

Key Points:

  • Article refers to founders of Mormonism as “knaves”
  • Claims holy writings were found under a stone in New York
  • Leaders assert they can work miracles
  • Membership claimed to be 1,000 souls
  • Prophet Jo pronounced part of Geauga county, Ohio, as “promised land”
  • People flocking to Ohio, mainly from New York
  • Miracle claimed by clearing ice at Buffalo
  • Leaders exempt themselves from labor, suggesting ulterior motives

history.citation: Geauga Gazette (Painesville, Ohio) (26 July 1831): 2.
history.teaser:
An article in the Geauga Gazette addressing corrections to an earlier piece on Mormonism and the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Correction of typographical errors in a previous article on Mormonism
  • Errors were in quoting the Mormon Bible and other statements
  • Original article published during the editor’s absence
  • Correction includes changing “they have remained forever” to “they would have remained forever”
  • Correction of phrasing regarding a conversation with a lady
  • “Enabling them to work a miracle on me” corrected to “challenging them”
  • “But you in inquire the cause” corrected to “but you injure”

history.citation: Letter to the editor, 1 July 1831. Universalist Watchman, Repository and Chronicle (Woodstock, Vermont), n.s. 3, no. 16 (13 August 1831): 127.
history.teaser:
A letter expressing skepticism and concern over the early activities and claims of the Mormon movement in Ohio.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith claimed the Book of Mormon as a divine revelation
  • Moved followers to Ohio, claiming it was the new Jerusalem
  • Joseph Smith and others made proselytes in Hiram and Nelson, Ohio
  • Claims of new revelation pointing followers to Missouri
  • Belief in an imminent millennium and eternal life for followers
  • Claims of performing miracles and healing
  • John Johnson on a mission to Vermont to warn of “wrath to come”
  • Author expresses disgust at what he sees as religious deception

history.citation: “Mormonism is spreading faster . . .” Wayne Sentinel (Palmyra, New York) (23 August 1831).
history.teaser:
An 1831 newspaper article commenting on the rapid spread of Mormonism in comparison to anti-masonry, and the controversial claims of a preacher named Davidson.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism spreading faster than anti-masonry
  • Leaders of both groups accused of knowing the falsehoods
  • Both groups denounce non-joiners
  • Mormonites accused of seeking money, anti-masons seek office
  • Preacher Davidson gaining followers in Burlington, Vermont
  • Davidson claims his mentor Dilks has Almighty power
  • Davidson’s extreme teachings include Jesus being inferior to Dilks
  • Davidson’s followers expected a millennium event in 1832 in Philadelphia

history.citation: “Mormonism—Religious Fanaticism—Church And State Party,” Morning Courierand New-York Enquirer (New York City, New York) 7, no. 1333 (31 August 1831).
history.teaser:
An 1831 newspaper article expressing skepticism and criticism towards Mormonism, depicting it as a product of religious excitement and ignorance.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism viewed as a mix of roguery, ingenuity, and ignorance
  • Originated in Western New York
  • Founders were simple, unknown individuals before Mormonism
  • Joseph Smith described as indolent and aimless
  • Money-digging activities linked to early Mormon leaders
  • Mormonism’s early practices related to seeking hidden treasures
  • Introduction of a money dreamer from Ohio to the group
  • Skeptical view of Mormonism’s religious and moral claims

A critical account from a Presbyterian in Ohio detailing the early activities and beliefs of the Mormon community, drawing comparisons to an earlier religious movement.

  • Mormon community practices communal living, the “bag family”

  • Smith purportedly performs miracles and reads people’s hearts
  • Attendee observes unusual spiritual manifestations at a meeting
  • Methodists, Baptists, and Presbyterians have joined the Mormons
  • Comparisons made to the “Pilgrims” religious movement and its downfall
  • Editor suggests Mormonism may end similarly to the “Pilgrims”

history.citation: “Mormon Religion—Clerical Ambition—Western New York—The Mormonites Gone toOhio.” Morning Courier and New-York Enquirer (New York City, New York) 7, no. 1331 (1 September 1831).

An article from the Morning Courier and New-York Enquirer discussing the origins and criticisms of the Mormon religion, and its migration to Ohio.

Key Points:

  • Religious excitement and revival in New York
  • Efforts to blend religious and worldly concerns
  • Western New York as the headquarters of religious zealots
  • Religious fanaticism led to the infatuation of Mormonism
  • Joseph Smith claimed to find golden plates
  • Book of Mormon believed to be authored by an ex-preacher from Ohio
  • Martin Harris played a significant role in financing the Book of Mormon
  • Mormonites established a community system in Ohio

history.author: O., W. [Owen, William]
history.citation: O., W. [Owen, William]. “Mormon Bible.” Free Enquirer (New York) (3 September 1831):364.

  • Ten witnesses hefted the plates, three saw them with an angel

history.author: Owen, William

  • Notes both books’ historical and miraculous narratives
  • Compares figures and events in both books
  • Mentions the peaceful and moral nature of Mormons

  • Describes the historical narrative of the Nephites and Lamanites
  • Notes the Book of Mormon’s growing followers and their migration plans

An early critical newspaper article discussing the origins and expansion of Mormonism, focusing on Joseph Smith and the publication of the Book of Mormon.

  • Joseph Smith described as ignorant and indolent
  • Smiths engaged in digging for buried money
  • Joseph Smith claimed to find golden plates
  • Book of Mormon published with finances from Harris
  • Smith exhibited as a divinely inspired prophet
  • Mormons emigrated to Missouri seeking a promised land

history.author: Gimel

  • One convert’s property was estimated at $7,000
  • A Boston woman investigates Mormonism, becomes a convert

  • Report of a sick person miraculously restored to health

An early account of a Mormon preacher’s visit and lecture, detailing the origins of the Book of Mormon and the beliefs of its followers.

  • Young man found gold plates with Arabic characters

An article in the Ohio Star discussing the impact of Mr. Booth’s letters on exposing Mormonism to the public.

Key Points:

  • Mr. Booth’s letter is considered very interesting
  • Belief that the letters are influencing many deluded by Mormonism
  • Exposure of Mormonism seen as an important duty
  • Announcement that the letters will soon conclude

An account by Ezra Booth, a former Mormon, detailing his disillusionment with the Church and its leaders, particularly focusing on Joseph Smith’s actions and prophecies.

An early account of the origin of the Book of Mormon as presented by a follower, highlighting the supernatural aspects of its discovery.

history.author: Rigdon, Sidney, 1793-1876

history.author: Rigdon, Sidney, 1793-1876

Sidney Rigdon’s public challenge to Simons Rider to defend his accusations against the Book of Mormon in the Ohio Star.

Key Points:

  • Rigdon invited Simons Rider to discuss the Book of Mormon’s authenticity
  • Rigdon accuses Rider of avoiding the challenge
  • Claims Rider hides behind reproach and abuse instead of evidence
  • Rigdon uses biblical reference to highlight Rider’s evasion
  • Suggests Rider’s accusations are unfounded and cowardly
  • Emphasizes the importance of openly defending one’s accusations
  • Rigdon offers a standing challenge to investigate the Book of Mormon’s claims
  • Leaves the matter publicly, suggesting Rider reconsider his approach

history.citation: “Mormonism.” Cherokee Phoenix (New Echota, Georgia) 4 (21 January 1832). Reprinted from Boston Courier (Boston, Massachusetts) October 1831. [text illegible] [text illegible]
history.teaser:
An article from the Cherokee Phoenix discussing the spread and impact of Mormonism, including missionary efforts and communal living principles.

Key Points:

  • Writer formerly a respectable citizen of Boston
  • Mormonism causes great excitement
  • About 100 souls humbled themselves for baptism
  • Church structure includes elders, priests, teachers, and deacons
  • Missionaries preaching to Native Americans
  • Three hundred converts in Ohio, communal property contributions
  • Communal living as natural consequence of Apostolic doctrine
  • Visitation by angels and revelation through a seer

history.citation: “Mr. Booth . . .” Ohio Star (Ravenna, Ohio) (26 January 1832).
history.teaser:
A newspaper editorial discussing a dispute between Mr. Booth and Mr. Rigdon regarding the Book of Mormon and its authenticity.

Key Points:

  • Mr. Booth defends his character against attacks by Mr. Rigdon
  • Booth questions the wisdom of trusting those who assert the Book of Mormon’s authenticity
  • Implies those asserting authenticity could be capable of dishonesty
  • Newspaper declines to publish Booth’s vindication to avoid obligation for a reply

history.citation: “Mormonism.” Fredonia Censor (New York) (7 March 1832). Reprinted from the Franklin Democrat (Pennsylvania) circa March 1832.
history.teaser:
An early 1832 newspaper article detailing the beliefs and teachings of the Mormonites as they began to spread their religion in Pennsylvania.

Key Points:

  • Mormon missionaries visited Venango county, Pennsylvania
  • Joseph Smith received divine guidance to find gold plates
  • Gold plates contained an unknown language, translated by Smith
  • The Book of Mormon is another revelation to the house of Joseph
  • Lehi left Jerusalem, landing in South America, according to the Book of Mormon
  • Christianity flourished in the Americas for generations, then faded
  • Last prophet, Mormon, hid the plates to be found by a “gentile people”
  • Mormon missionaries predicted the imminent return of Jesus Christ

history.author: Skinner, Dolphus
history.citation: Skinner, Dolphus. “Changes of Mormonism.” Evangelical Magazine and Gospel Advocate (Utica, New York) 3, no. 11 (17 March 1832): 67.
history.teaser:
An article discussing a reported shift in Mormon theology towards universal salvation, prompting skepticism from the author.

Key Points:

  • New revelation reported among Mormonites about universal salvation
  • Revelation proclaimed by their seer, Jo Smith
  • Mormonites seeking forgiveness from those they previously cursed
  • Comparison made with Jews’ misunderstanding in the days of Jesus
  • Concern expressed about Mormonites aligning with Universalism
  • Previous Mormon teachings emphasized the doctrine of endless misery
  • Mormon Bible’s teachings on endless damnation highlighted
  • Assertion that embracing Universalism would require renouncing Mormonism

history.citation: “The Orators of Mormon.” Catholic Telegraph (Cincinnati, Ohio) 1 (14 April 1832): 204–5. Reprinted from Mercer Press (Pennsylvania), circa April 1832.
history.teaser:
A detailed account of early Mormon missionaries’ visit and teachings, as recounted in a secular newspaper.

Key Points:

  • Missionaries claimed to be sent by God to preach the gospel
  • Joseph Smith found plates after an angel’s visitation
  • Smith translated the plates with divine inspiration
  • Lehi’s journey to South America and division of his people
  • Final battle among these groups happened where the plates were found
  • Mormonite Bible connects and fulfills prophecies of Isaiah
  • Missionaries work without compensation, relying on faith
  • Joseph Smith, Cowdery, Whitmer, and Harris testify to seeing the plates

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “Selected.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 1 (June 1832): [3].
history.teaser:
An editorial in the first issue of The Evening and the Morning Star discussing the authenticity and origin of the New Testament in relation to the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Prophecy extract from the Book of Mormon shared
  • New Testament parts believed taken from Book of Mormon
  • Alleged tampering by the “Mother of Harlots”
  • Period of tampering estimated between A.D. 460 to 1400
  • Command given for a new translation of the Bible
  • King James’ translators did well but lacked revelation

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “[From the Book of Mormon].” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence,Missouri) 1, no. 1 (June 1832): 8.
history.teaser:
An early publication in the LDS church’s newspaper featuring a message from the Book of Mormon aimed at Gentiles to repent and be baptized.

Key Points:

  • Message directed to the Gentiles
  • Words commanded by Jesus Christ
  • Call to turn from wicked ways and repent
  • Mentions specific sins to repent from
  • Invitation to be baptized in Christ’s name
  • Promises remission of sins and the Holy Ghost
  • Opportunity to be numbered with the house of Israel

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Book of Mormon.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 1 (June 1832): [6].
history.teaser:
An article from the first issue of The Evening and the Morning Star encouraging inquiry into the truth of the Book of Mormon through biblical prophecy and archaeological evidence.

Key Points:

  • Encourages honest inquiry into the truth of the Book of Mormon
  • Links the Book of Mormon to the tribe of Joseph from Genesis
  • References Ezekiel 37’s “Stick of Ephraim” as possible evidence
  • Mentions Isaiah’s prophecy of a “marvelous work” linking to the Book
  • Points to archaeological remains as silent evidence of a civilized people
  • Advises seeking divine confirmation for truth seekers

history.citation: “Mormonism.” The Standard (Cincinnati, Ohio) (1 June 1832): 4.
history.teaser:
An early critical view of Mormonism from a local Ohio newspaper, highlighting concerns about its rapid growth and practices.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism seen as an ominous sign of change
  • Boasts hundreds of converts, threatening thousands
  • Deemed a cunningly formed plot covered by sanctimonious appearances
  • Converts include members from almost all denominations, especially Free Baptists
  • Success of Mormonism difficult to calculate
  • Many converts hadn’t read the Book of Mormon before joining
  • Smith’s word is seen as the word of God by followers
  • Mormons preparing to move to a promised land in Missouri Territory

history.citation: “Mormonism,” Painesville Telegraph (Painesville, Ohio) 4, no. 1 (21 June 1832). Reprinted from The Pioneer (Rock Springs, Illinois) circa June 1832.
history.teaser:
An article from the Painesville Telegraph discusses the impact of Mormon missionaries in Illinois, focusing on the conversion and subsequent mental breakdown of a local Methodist preacher and his wife.

Key Points:

  • Mormon preachers visited Illinois counties
  • Some families were ‘almost persuaded’ to convert
  • Mr. McMahan, a Methodist preacher, converted to Mormonism
  • McMahan attempted to work miracles and became deranged
  • McMahan and his wife attacked their house and furniture
  • There was a plan to ‘sacrifice’ one of their children
  • McMahan was confined in irons by a neighbor
  • This event halted further Mormon proselytizing in the area

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “Hosea Chapter III.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 2 (July 1832): [14].
history.teaser:
An analysis of Hosea Chapter III, emphasizing its literal interpretation and prophetic significance.

Key Points:

  • Hosea Chapter III contains figures of speech and prophecy.
  • The chapter alludes to sending the gospel to the Gentiles.
  • The woman represents the church, which will triumph over sin.
  • Salvation to the Gentiles was to continue for many days.
  • Children of Israel were to be scattered without sacred things.
  • The time of gathering and return of Israel is promised.
  • Israel is declared as the Elect of God.
  • David’s kingship in the latter days is prophesied.

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Book of Ether.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 3 (August 1832): [22].
history.teaser:
An article discussing the Book of Ether from the Book of Mormon, highlighting the history of the Jaredites and their significance.

Key Points:

  • Book of Ether details history of early people on the American continent
  • Period covered: From Babel to 600 years before Christ
  • Supported by the Bible’s account of scattering people from Babel
  • Jaredites named after one of the first families to migrate
  • Controlled America for nearly 1500 years
  • Relation to large bones found may indicate Jaredite skeletons
  • Man’s history not fully revealed until the Savior comes
  • Moroni provides a summary of the Book of Ether in the Book of Mormon

history.citation: “Mormonism.” Working Man’s Advocate (New York) 4, no. 1 ( 18 August 1832). Reprinted from Lynn Record (Massachusetts).
history.teaser:
An article describing a public meeting to discuss the origins and beliefs of Mormonism, highlighting the Book of Mormon and the call to gather in Missouri.

Key Points:

  • Meeting held to discuss the Book of Mormon
  • Highly respectable audience attended
  • Meeting began with prayer
  • Speaker discussed a revelation made by an angel
  • Revelation found on metallic plates
  • Related to the lost tribe of Israel
  • True believers called to gather in Missouri

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Book of Jacob.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 4 (September 1832): [26].
history.teaser:
An article from an early LDS publication discussing the significance of a parable and prophecy found in the Book of Jacob, part of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Focuses on a figure, a parable, and a prophecy in the Book of Jacob
  • Describes the language as both simple and sublime
  • Mentions an ancient prophet named Zenos
  • Compares Zenos’ and Isaiah’s representations of Israel
  • Zenos uses the tame and wild olive trees as symbols
  • References the Lord sending servants to prune the vineyard for the last time
  • Prophecies the return of Jacob’s captivity and unity of Israel and Judah
  • Encourages seeking a perpetual covenant with the Lord

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “Signs of the Times.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 5 (October 1832): [38].
history.teaser:
An article from an early LDS publication discussing the turbulent state of the world and its relation to biblical prophecy and Latter-day Saint beliefs.

Key Points:

  • Article emphasizes the importance of recognizing the “signs of the times”
  • References to global military tensions and political unrest
  • Critiques the moral and spiritual state of society
  • Discusses the role of various societies and their impact on religious practice
  • Mentions the Book of Mormon’s prophecy regarding the Gentiles and the promised land
  • Emphasizes the importance of repentance, faith, and baptism
  • Warns of the consequences of neglecting spiritual purity and engaging in worldly affairs
  • Encourages vigilance in observing heavenly and earthly signs of the times

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Far West.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 5 (October 1832): [37].
history.teaser:
An article from an early LDS publication contemplating the spiritual and prophetic significance of the American West.

Key Points:

  • The Far West is described as different and distant from the Atlantic States
  • Missouri River described as “waters of misery”
  • Region seen as ancient, tied to Jaredites and Nephites’ glory and downfall
  • Land currently inhabited by “Indians” seen as the land of Joseph
  • Missouri identified as the gathering place for saints for Jesus’ second coming
  • The land of Missouri and Zion linked to biblical prophecies of glory and redemption
  • Connection made between the division of the earth in Peleg’s time and the wickedness of Babel and idolatry
  • Encourages contemplation of God’s greatness and the prophetic destiny of the American West

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Book of Moroni,” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 5 (October 1832): [38].
history.teaser:
An article from an early Latter-day Saint publication advocating for the truth and relevance of Moroni’s writings in the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Advocates for the truth of Moroni’s last epistle to the Lamanites
  • Touches on the continuation of spiritual gifts
  • Addresses the cessation of gifts due to lack of faith
  • Presents Moroni’s writings as a guide for spiritual inquiry
  • Encourages readers to confirm the truthfulness through prayer

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Ten Tribes.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 5 (October 1832): [33–34].
history.teaser:
An article discussing the scattering and future gathering of the lost ten tribes of Israel, using biblical prophecies and references to the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Discussion on the scattering of Israel based on Deuteronomy
  • Ahijah’s prophecy on division of Israel during Solomon’s reign
  • Israel’s captivity and scattering by Assyria
  • Ezekiel’s prophecy on Israel’s restoration
  • Jesus’ ministry to the lost sheep of Israel
  • Book of Mormon’s account of Jesus’ words to the Nephites
  • Parable of the Lord’s vineyard relating to Israel’s future
  • Elijah’s future role in restoring the tribes of Jacob

history.citation: “Mormonism.” Boston Recorder (Boston, Massachusetts) 17, no. 41 (10 October 1832). Reprinted from Lockport Balance (New York), circa September 1832.
history.teaser:
A critical article from the Boston Recorder, reprinted from the Lockport Balance, discussing the origins and criticisms of Mormonism.

Key Points:

  • Article criticizes the rise and credibility of Mormonism
  • Mentions Joseph Smith, Oliver Cowdery, and Martin Harris as leaders
  • Describes the finding of the gold plates and spectacles
  • Book of Mormon criticized as a ridiculous imitation of the Bible
  • Mormonism has made over a thousand proselytes
  • Families and communities divided by belief in Mormonism
  • Reports of miraculous occurrences among believers
  • Claims of financial exploitation and communal living practices

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Tribe of Joseph.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 6 (November 1832): [41–43].
history.teaser:
An article discussing the significance of the tribe of Joseph, including prophecies and their implications for the Latter-day Saints and the gathering of Israel.

Key Points:

  • Joseph’s life seen as a type for future events regarding his descendants
  • Prophecies about Joseph’s seed crossing oceans and being gathered
  • The blessings of Joseph surpass those of ancestors, indicating a special role in the last days
  • Discusses the Book of Mormon as a fulfillment of prophecies about Joseph’s descendants
  • Mentions the joining of the records of Judah (Bible) and Joseph (Book of Mormon)
  • Highlights the role of Ephraim in gathering people to Zion in the last days
  • References to biblical prophecies regarding the restoration of Israel and the gathering of the tribes
  • The importance of the land blessed for Joseph’s descendants in the last days

history.citation: “Mormonism” Morning Star (Limerick, Maine) 7, no. 20 (16 November 1832). Reprinted from the Christian Herald (Boston), circa November 1832.
history.teaser:
A report from 1832 criticizing the practices and beliefs of early Mormonism, including Joseph Smith’s treasure seeking activities and early missionary efforts.

Key Points:

  • Mormonite preachers entered Maine, attempting to gain converts
  • Joseph Smith Jr. and others dug for money based on visions
  • Smith sold shares in the treasure, which allegedly “sunk” deeper
  • William Devenport’s disillusionment with Mormon leaders’ motives
  • Testimony taken on trial about Smith’s treasure seeking and divine revelations
  • Joseph Smith claimed to have translated the Book of Mormon through divine guidance
  • Smith’s practices of looking through stones for treasures
  • Joseph Smith was discharged due to statute of limitations

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Resurrection of the Just.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence,Missouri) 1, no. 7 (December 1832): [49–51].
history.teaser:
An exploration of the doctrine of the resurrection of the just as understood by early Latter-day Saints, emphasizing its uniqueness and importance within Christian theology.

Key Points:

  • The article emphasizes the resurrection of the just in the flesh.
  • It claims this belief is unique to the Church of Christ (Mormonites).
  • Enoch’s translation and preaching of the resurrection is highlighted.
  • Job expressed confidence in seeing God in the flesh after resurrection.
  • The resurrection includes the righteous rising to meet Christ.
  • Alma (Book of Mormon) elaborates on the resurrection and the state of souls after death.
  • Righteousness leads to resurrection and eternal happiness with God.
  • Wickedness results in eternal misery separate from God.

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Jews.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 7 (December 1832): [51–53].
history.teaser:
An article discussing the increasing population of Jews in Palestine and their hope for restoration, with scriptural commentary on gathering and redemption.

Key Points:

  • Jews have greatly increased in Palestine, particularly in Saphet and Jerusalem.
  • Despite long-term rejection and persecution, Jews maintain faith in divine promises.
  • Scriptural references to Zion and Jerusalem as places of gathering.
  • Prophecies about the restoration of Israel and the glory of Jerusalem.
  • Book of Mormon references to a New Jerusalem to be established in the Americas.
  • God’s command for restoration as a preparation for meeting Him.
  • The role of the Gentiles in the restoration and gathering of Israel.
  • Zechariah prophesies about Jerusalem’s future trials and ultimate protection by God.

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Indians.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 7 (December 1832): [54].
history.teaser:
A publication highlighting the gathering of Native Americans as a fulfillment of scriptural prophecy, linking it to the Book of Mormon teachings.

Key Points:

  • Witnessing the gathering of the Indians is seen as fulfilling scripture
  • Remnants of Joseph gather west of the Missouri and Arkansas
  • Link between government actions and biblical prophecy
  • Book of Mormon quoted regarding the gathering of Israel
  • Shawnees from Ohio moving west as part of this gathering
  • Gathering as a sign for the times of the last days
  • Emphasizes the role of the Gentiles in the fulfillment of prophecy
  • Speaks of a future work that will be marvelous and not believed by all

history.author: B., S.
history.citation: B., S. “Mormonism.” Morning Star (Limerick, Maine) 7, no. 34 (21 December 1832): 134.
history.teaser:
An article from the Morning Star newspaper expressing skepticism towards Mormonism and its practices, especially baptism and the establishment of a communal society in Zion (Missouri).

Key Points:

  • Article discusses the appearance of Mormon preachers in Maine
  • Comparison made between Mormonism and the movement led by Jacob Cochrane
  • Mormon preachers promote baptism and faith in the Book of Mormon
  • Children over eight years old eligible for baptism into Mormonism
  • Mormonism’s aim includes preparing for New Jerusalem in Missouri
  • Community advised to convert property into “common stock” for Zion
  • Warnings about potential financial distress from joining Mormon communal efforts
  • Article concludes with caution against being deceived by such movements

history.author: Priest, Josiah, 1788-1851
history.citation: Priest, Josiah. American Antiquities, 73. Albany: Hoffman and White, 1833.
history.teaser:
Josiah Priest’s critique of the idea that Native Americans are descendants of the Lost Ten Tribes of Israel, and his dismissal of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Priest opposes the doctrine of the Lost Ten Tribes in America
  • Claims Ten Tribes were never lost and remain in Asia
  • Ridicules authors linking Native American customs to Jewish traits
  • Describes the rise of a new religious sect, the Mormons
  • Mormons believe in a golden book detailing American Jews’ history
  • Criticizes the Book of Mormon as a poor imitation of the Bible
  • Asserts Book of Mormon language does not match Asiatic composition
  • Labels the Book of Mormon as folly and without coherent aim

history.author: Hamilton, Thomas, 1789-1842
history.citation: Hamilton, Thomas. Men and Manners in America, 364–65. Philadelphia: Carey, Lea & Blanchard, 1833.
history.teaser:
A skeptical British traveler’s account of encountering Mormon converts and the story of Joseph Smith’s discovery of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Encountered Mormonites going to Ohio
  • Joseph Smith, a bankrupt storekeeper, had a guiding dream
  • Smith found a book with golden clasps and special spectacles
  • The book appeared blank until viewed with the spectacles
  • Smith copied characters and sought interpreters
  • The book was titled the Book of Mormon, offering religious clarification
  • Smith’s fortunes improved with the Book of Mormon
  • Smith set up a religious establishment with believers

history.author: C. S. Francis and Co
history.citation: Mother Goose’s Melodies [title page]. Boston: C. S. Francis and Co., [ 1833].
history.teaser:
This title page humorously suggests that Mother Goose’s Melodies were discovered in the same stone box as the Golden Plates of the Book of Mormon, emphasizing the fantastical and legendary aspects of both.

Key Points:

  • Claims to be the “only Pure Edition” of Mother Goose’s Melodies
  • Includes all known writings of Mother Goose and those discovered in Herculaneum
  • Mentions new finds in the same stone box as the Golden Plates
  • Text revised and sanctioned by one of the annotators of the Goose family
  • Publication includes many new engravings
  • Published in 1833 by C. S. Francis and Co. in Boston
  • Entry according to the Act of Congress in 1833
  • Available in New York and Boston

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Book of Mormon.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 8 (January 1833): [57–59].
history.teaser:
An article from “The Evening and the Morning Star” highlighting the divine origins and purposes of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon emerged in a time of spiritual darkness
  • It contains the fullness of the gospel
  • Clarifies doctrines and prophecies that were unclear in the Bible
  • Explains the origin of the American Indians
  • Prophecies about the gathering of Israel and the building of Zion
  • Testimonies of three and eight witnesses support its truth
  • Encourages adherence to Christ’s teachings for salvation
  • Asserts the safety of the righteous in Zion at the Second Coming

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “Some of Mormon’s Teaching.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence,Missouri) 1, no. 8 (January 1833): [60].
history.teaser:
An article from an early LDS publication emphasizing the importance of the teachings in the Book of Mormon, specifically highlighting teachings from Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Encourages disciples to seek truth, goodness, and glory
  • Highlights the importance of remembering the words of the prophets
  • Stresses the need for continual engagement with the Book of Mormon
  • Warns against neglecting the Book of Mormon
  • Condemns hunting for mysteries in the prophecies as a distraction
  • Urges adherence to the new covenant and fulness of the gospel
  • Calls for repentance and living faithfully before God
  • Mentions the specific teachings of Moroni 7 from the 1830 edition

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.document: Discovery of Ancient Ruins in Central America
history.citation: “Discovery of Ancient Ruins in Central America.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 9 (February 1833): [71].
history.teaser:
An article discussing the discovery of ancient ruins in Central America, citing it as evidence supporting the historical claims of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Lieut. Col. Galindo discovered extensive ruins in Central America
  • The ruins suggest a highly civilized ancient society
  • Artifacts include a palace, religious worship place, and prison
  • Ruins buried in a thick forest, indicating ancient origin
  • Galindo’s findings suggest ancient Americans used signs for sounds
  • Article connects ruins to Book of Mormon accounts
  • Helaman and 3 Nephi passages from Book of Mormon cited as evidence
  • Discovery seen as confirmation of civilizations before the 14th century

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “New Hymns.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 9 (February 1833): [72].
history.teaser:
A collection of new hymns published in an early LDS periodical emphasizing themes of revelation, preparation for the Second Coming, and the importance of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • An angel revealed a record hidden in Cumorah
  • The record contains the fullness of Jesus’s gospel
  • It is a heavenly treasure that speaks from the dust
  • A call for Israel to prepare for the Lord’s return
  • Message to all nations about the awaiting great things
  • The kingdom of Jesus in Zion will flourish
  • A thankful acknowledgment to God for creation and redemption
  • A look forward to the blessings and rest promised in heaven

history.author: Smith, Joseph, 1805-1844
history.citation: “Mormonism.” Communication from Joseph Smith, Jr. American Revivalist and Rochester Observer (Rochester, New York) 7, no. 5 (2 February 1833).
history.teaser:
A letter from Joseph Smith, Jr., published in a newspaper, discussing the origins and prophecies related to Mormonism and the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • The letter is written with good feeling and urbanity
  • The Book of Mormon: record of the forefathers of American Indians
  • Western tribes of Indians are descendants of Joseph from Egypt
  • Land of America is a promised land to them and all Israel
  • The city of Zion will be built on American land
  • United States to experience unprecedented bloodshed and calamities
  • Call for repentance and to embrace the everlasting covenant
  • Exhortation to seek the Lord while he may be found

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Times.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 10 (March 1833): [76–77].
history.teaser:
An editorial from an early LDS publication reflecting on the troubled state of the United States and its implications for the future, drawing from religious prophecy.

Key Points:

  • Reflects on the troubled state of the United States in 1833
  • References biblical prophecies about nations at war and natural disasters
  • Views current events as signs of the approaching end times
  • Emphasizes the need for repentance and divine intervention
  • Asserts the kingdom of Jesus Christ will flourish despite worldly turmoil
  • Discusses God’s mercy and the call for all to repent
  • States America is a choice land, blessed or cursed based on righteousness
  • Urges preparation for the kingdom of glory through faith in Jesus Christ

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “Extract, &c.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 10 (March 1833): [79].
history.teaser:
An excerpt from The Evening and the Morning Star highlighting the value of the Book of Mormon’s teachings, especially in times of war and division.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon contains many good things
  • Extract from the writings of Nephi highlighted
  • Valuable to saints during times of war and commotion
  • Encouragement to look forward to peace

history.author: Marks, David
history.citation: Marks, David. [Untitled Remarks on Mormonism]. Morning Star (Limerick, Maine) 7, no. 45 (7 March 1833): 177.

David Marks’ skeptical observations on the early days of Mormonism, focusing on Joseph Smith’s character and the origins of the Book of Mormon.
