  • Joseph Smith discovered a golden Bible through divine guidance
  • Smith was described as obscure, illiterate, and into fortune telling
  • Concerns raised about Smith’s credibility due to his background
  • Twelve witnesses were allowed to see the plates, many related
  • Mrs. Harris hid the manuscript, leading to domestic violence
  • Witnesses claimed divine authenticity but lacked convincing evidence
  • Marks found the Book of Mormon to be uninspired and fraudulent

history.author: Western Traveller
history.citation: Western Traveller. “Mormonism.” Christian Advocate and Journal (New York) 7, no. 30 (22 March 1833): 1.
history.teaser:
An early critique of Mormonism, focusing on its founder, its scripture, and its practices as viewed by a contemporary observer.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith was described as illiterate and artful
  • Book of Mormon criticized for poor English and dull content
  • Mormonism’s rapid spread in Ohio noted
  • Claims of new revelations and immoral conduct by Mormons
  • Surprise at Mormonism’s growth in western New York
  • Belief in the Book of Mormon as divine revelation
  • Doctrine of a promised land and destruction of other states
  • Claims of miraculous gifts, including healing and prophecy

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “Baptism.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 11 (April 1833): [88].
history.teaser:
An article discussing the principles and importance of baptism as outlined in the Book of Mormon, with personal testimonies and reflections on religious conversion and the growth of the Church of Christ.

Key Points:

  • Article emphasizes the necessity of proper baptism knowledge
  • Baptism requires a broken heart, contrite spirit, and repentance
  • Those baptized are cleansed by the Holy Ghost
  • Baptized individuals are added to the church’s records
  • Church meetings focus on fasting, prayer, and communion
  • Comparison of civilized and savage societal norms
  • Personal testimony of conversion and baptism by Samuel Bent
  • Discussion on the opposition faced by the church in Michigan

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “From the Book of Ether.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence,Missouri) 1, no. 11 (April 1833): [87].
history.teaser:
An article from an early Latter-day Saint publication sharing excerpts from the Book of Mormon, specifically from the Book of Ether, to illustrate the narrative of Jared and his brother’s journey as commanded by the Lord.

Key Points:

  • Intention to share excerpts from the Book of Mormon for public benefit
  • Jared, his brother, and their families prepare for a journey
  • The Lord communicates and gives directions to them
  • They travel in the wilderness and build barges to cross waters
  • Land of promise preserved for a righteous people
  • Warning that those who possess the land must serve God
  • Brother of Jared repents and is forgiven by the Lord
  • Instructions given for building barges and for light within them

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.document: Rise and Progress of the Church of Christ
history.citation: “Rise and Progress of the Church of Christ.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 11 (April 1833): [84].
history.teaser:
An article detailing the early development and expansion of the Church of Christ (later known as the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) from its organization in 1830 through its growth and challenges up to 1833.

Key Points:

  • Church organized in April 1830 in Manchester
  • Branches established in Fayette and Colesville, New York
  • Persecution faced by early members and missionaries
  • Significant growth by October 1830, branches expanding to Ohio
  • Directed by revelation, members began moving to Ohio in 1831
  • Continued expansion and baptisms despite opposition
  • Arrival in western Missouri marks the beginning of the gathering
  • Article counters falsehoods and affirms church’s divine guidance

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Gospel.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 1, no. 11 (April 1833): [81–83].
history.teaser:
An article from The Evening and the Morning Star discussing the continuity and universality of the Gospel from Adam through various prophets to Jesus Christ and beyond.

Key Points:

  • The plan of salvation was revealed to Adam after the Fall.
  • Adam and Eve began to worship God and offer sacrifices.
  • The Gospel has been preached from Adam to Moses and beyond.
  • The Gospel includes repentance, baptism, and receiving the Holy Ghost.
  • Adam, Enoch, Noah, and other prophets taught their children the Gospel.
  • The Gospel was the same for Abraham, Moses, and all through history.
  • Jesus Christ’s coming was foretold as part of the Gospel.
  • The Gospel’s purpose is to bring salvation to all who believe.

history.author: B., P. H.
history.citation: B., P. H. “The Mormonites.” Ohio Eagle (Lancaster, Ohio) (20 April 1833). Reprinted from The Saturday Courier, circa April 1833.
history.teaser:
An article from the Ohio Eagle, reprinted from The Saturday Courier, providing an early outsider perspective on the Mormons in Missouri.

Key Points:

  • Mormon doctrines considered absurd but followers tenacious
  • Mormons described as peaceable, industrious, and honest citizens
  • Mormons believed in concurrent divine revelations across continents
  • Claimed ancient Americans received revelations similar to those in Asia
  • Joseph Smith found and translated gold plates by special inspiration
  • Mormons believed in lost books of the Old Testament, including the Book of Mormon
  • Mormons practiced communal property, akin to early Apostles
  • Some locals joined Mormons but later retracted and sought legal redress

history.citation: “Mormonites.” Gospel Luminary 6, no. 8 (May 1833): 263–65.
history.teaser:
An 1833 article in the Gospel Luminary offering a critical perspective on the early Mormon settlement, their beliefs, and practices.

Key Points:

  • Mormons arrived and settled near the Missouri State line
  • Mormons call their settlement Mount Zion or New Jerusalem
  • Believe in a gathering of Gentiles and Jews (Indians)
  • Prophecy of Christ’s coming within fifteen years to reign
  • Joseph Smith claimed unlearned but translated plates by divine gift
  • New converts immediately baptized and promised the Holy Spirit
  • Property given to the church’s store considered a permanent donation
  • Skepticism expressed about Mormons’ claims of miracles and healing

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “Good Proof.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 2, no. 13 (June 1833): 99.
history.teaser:
An article presenting archaeological findings as evidence supporting the historicity of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Jaredites and Nephites had advanced knowledge of arts and sciences
  • Stone house found in Rowan County, N.C., embedded in earth
  • House dimensions and construction showed advanced architecture
  • Relics of household furniture found, indicating civilized life
  • In Cincinnati, stone imitations of peach and pear found 27 feet underground
  • Artifacts are presented as evidence the Book of Mormon is true

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Book of Mormon.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 2, no. 13 (June 1833): 98.
history.teaser:
An announcement in a Latter-day Saint publication about the commencement of serializing the Book of Mormon for readers.

Key Points:

  • The church has received the gospel from the Book of Mormon
  • Members study it as a heavenly treasure
  • Very few outside the church are aware of its merits
  • Plans to publish the Book of Mormon in the Star
  • Publication aims to prepare readers for coming days
  • Encourages truth seekers to compare it with the Bible
  • Intends to highlight the Lord’s work in the last days
  • Includes excerpt from the 1830 edition (1 Nephi 1:1–3:14)

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.document: The Second Coming of the Savior, No. II
history.citation: “The Second Coming of the Savior, No. II” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 2, no. 13 (June 1833): 99.
history.teaser:
An article discussing the Second Coming of Christ, emphasizing its physical reality and criticizing both Jewish and Gentile misunderstandings.

Key Points:

  • Second Coming concerns all men, urging preparation
  • Christ will physically reign on earth for a thousand years
  • Many deny the physical return of Christ
  • Moses and Peter prophesied Christ’s return
  • Common misinterpretations of biblical prophecy addressed
  • Jews expected a single coming; Gentiles spiritualize the Second Coming
  • Before Christ’s return, the earth will face great tribulations
  • Zion, a New Jerusalem, will be established on earth

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “Great Events.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 2, no. 13 (June 1833): 102.
history.teaser:
An article from an early Latter-day Saint publication summarizing significant religious events across millennia.

Key Points:

  • Fall of man and Enoch’s city taken to heaven in first thousand years
  • World flooded, Tower of Babel, and continents formed in second thousand years
  • Pharaoh defeated, Israel led by God, Solomon’s Temple built in third thousand years
  • Ten tribes led away, Jaredites destroyed, Lehi arrives in America in fourth thousand years
  • Birth, crucifixion, and resurrection of Jesus in fifth thousand years
  • America settled, Book of Mormon comes forth in sixth thousand years

history.citation: “Mormoism [sic].” Painesville Telegraph (Painesville, Ohio) (21 June 1833).
history.teaser:
An early 1833 newspaper article expressing skepticism about the divinity of the Book of Mormon and the rationality of its followers.

Key Points:

  • Written communication challenges the divinity of the Book of Mormon
  • Joseph Smith, jun. described as “author and proprietor”
  • Mormon Bible considered an imposition by rational men
  • Skepticism towards arguments with Mormons who believe their inspiration is from God

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “A Bee Story.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 2, no. 14 (July 1833): 107. REMARKS
history.teaser:
An intriguing story about an exceptionally large and ancient bee colony in Virginia, with a reflection on its possible origins from a religious perspective.

Key Points:

  • Story of a massive bee colony in Virginia’s Alleghany Mountains
  • Fissure in the rock houses a vast number of bees
  • Bees form huge clusters and swarms around the fissure
  • Bees’ presence predates the oldest local traditions and settlers
  • No one dares to plunder or closely examine the colony
  • Linked to the Book of Ether’s mention of Jaredites bringing bees
  • Reflections on human detachment from divine knowledge
  • Speculation on bees’ global distribution pre- and post-flood

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The Book of Mormon.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Independence, Missouri) 2, no. 14 (July 1833): 109.
history.teaser:
An announcement about the halt of the Book of Mormon’s serialization in a newspaper, with plans for future publication alongside the New Testament.

Key Points:

  • Publication of the Book of Mormon in the newspaper stopped
  • Plans to print the Book of Mormon and New Testament together
  • Reason for stopping serialization deemed superfluous due to future plans

history.citation: “‘Regulating’ the Mormonites.” Niles’ Register (Baltimore, Maryland) 4th series, 3, no. 9 (14 September 1833): 47–48. Reprinted from Missouri Republican, 9 August 1833.
history.teaser:
A report on violent actions taken against Mormons in Jackson County, Missouri, including the destruction of their printing press.

Key Points:

  • Extraordinary proceedings against Mormons in Jackson County
  • Citizens’ meeting aimed to rid the area of Mormons
  • Mormons described as fanatics and a threat to public order
  • A committee was formed to enforce the expulsion of Mormons
  • The “Star” printing office was ordered to be closed
  • Mormon leaders were advised to prevent further emigration
  • Physical actions taken to destroy Mormon property
  • Report of a Mormon being tarred, feathered, and paraded

history.citation: “The Mormon Mystery Developed.” Wayne Sentinel (Palmyra, New York) (20 December 1833).
history.teaser:
An article from the Wayne Sentinel discussing Dr. P. Hurlburt’s investigation into the origins of the Book of Mormon, claiming it to be a fabricated document with origins in a fictional manuscript.

Key Points:

  • Dr. P. Hurlburt investigates the Book of Mormon’s origins
  • Claims of finding the original manuscript written as a romance
  • Manuscript allegedly written 30 years prior by a deceased clergyman
  • Author intended to publish it as a romance, but died
  • Religious character of the book added by a modern hand
  • Notorious Rigdon believed to have added the religious aspect
  • Information derived from the widow of the original author

history.author: Howe, Eber D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
A critical account by E. D. Howe challenging the origins, content, and claims of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • E.D. Howe critiques the origin story of the American Indians as described in the Book of Mormon.
  • Questions the priesthood and sacrifices mentioned, comparing to biblical standards.
  • Highlights inconsistencies with biblical teachings and historical timelines.
  • Challenges the use of the Egyptian language by ancient Jews as described.
  • Examines prophecies and teachings in the Book of Mormon related to Christ.
  • Discusses the impossibility of certain events and teachings pre-Christ.
  • Questions the translation process of the Book of Mormon plates.
  • Critiques the overall credibility and authenticity of the Book of Mormon.

history.author: Howe, Eber D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
A critical examination of the origins and claims of the Book of Mormon and the early days of the Latter Day Saint movement.

Key Points:

  • Rigdon’s angry response to comparisons of the Book of Mormon and the Koran
  • Rigdon’s claims about Joseph Smith’s supernatural gifts challenged
  • Rigdon contradicts the Book of Mormon on miracles as confirmation
  • Rigdon claims the Book of Mormon necessary for salvation
  • Rigdon’s fluctuating stance on defending the Book of Mormon
  • Smith and followers’ honesty questioned; no sacrifices made by them
  • Rapid spread of Mormonism through enthusiastic proselytizing
  • Prophecy about Native American conversion and reclaiming of lands

history.author: Howe, E. D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
An early critical examination of the Book of Mormon, its origins, and its claims, authored by E. D. Howe in 1834.

Key Points:

  • Claims Book of Mormon written by a single author in King James style.
  • Questions the historical accuracy and presence of steel in the narrative.
  • Discusses Nephi’s building of a ship and creation of metal plates as improbable.
  • Highlights inconsistencies and miracles as evidence against divine origin.
  • Criticizes the portrayal of God using murder and lying to fulfill plans.
  • Notes the absence of the plates of brass in contemporary times.
  • Argues the Christian religion was not revealed to Nephites before Christ.
  • Concludes the Book of Mormon contradicts and lacks evidence compared to the Bible.

history.author: Howe, E. D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
E.D. Howe’s critical examination of the Book of Mormon, its origins, and the claims of Joseph Smith and his followers.

Key Points:

  • Claims the Book of Mormon is a fabrication linked to Solomon Spalding
  • Describes the narrative and doctrines within the Book of Alma
  • Criticizes the historicity and authenticity of the Book of Mormon’s accounts
  • Questions the plausibility of the Nephites’ and Lamanites’ civilizations
  • Challenges the existence of Nephite coinage and military tactics
  • Expresses skepticism about the translation methods of the golden plates
  • Argues the Book of Mormon aims to establish a new religion
  • Condemns the Book of Mormon as an attack on Christianity and moral virtue

history.author: Howe, Eber D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
E. D. Howe’s book is a critical examination and denouncement of the origins, contents, and claims of the Book of Mormon, asserting it as a deliberate fraud.

Key Points:

  • Claims Joseph Smith’s accounts of finding the plates were inconsistent.
  • Describes the translation process as dubious, involving a “peep stone.”
  • Alleges the story of finding plates and translation was a pretext for profit.
  • Asserts the Book of Mormon is poorly written and devoid of interest.
  • Questions the divine origin of the Book of Mormon.
  • Discusses the controversy around the lost 116 pages.
  • Claims the Book of Mormon was an experiment on human credulity.
  • Criticizes Joseph Smith for presenting himself as the “author” for profit.

history.author: Howe, Eber D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
An early critical examination of the origins of the Book of Mormon, attributing its creation to Solomon Spalding and Sidney Rigdon.

Key Points:

  • E.D. Howe investigates the Book of Mormon’s origins.
  • Proposes Solomon Spalding as the original author.
  • Witnesses link Spalding’s manuscript to the Book of Mormon.
  • Spalding’s manuscript described similar historical narrative.
  • Alleges Sidney Rigdon embellished Spalding’s work.
  • Rigdon possibly used Spalding’s manuscript for the Book of Mormon.
  • Links between Rigdon, Spalding, and the Smith family suggested.
  • Rigdon posited as the “author and proprietor” of Mormonism.

history.author: Howe, E. D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
A critical and skeptical examination of the Book of Mormon, its origins, and its claims by E.D. Howe in 1834, which also posits the Spalding theory as a potential source for the text.

Key Points:

  • Claims the Book of Mormon to be a delusion and imposition.
  • Suggests Solomon Spalding may have written the historical part.
  • Describes the content and narrative structure of the Book of Mormon.
  • Critiques the Book of Mormon’s portrayal of ancient civilizations.
  • Questions the credibility of the Three Witnesses’ testimonies.
  • Highlights anachronisms and inconsistencies within the Book of Mormon.
  • Discusses the conflict between Nephites, Lamanites, and Jaredites.
  • Expresses skepticism towards Joseph Smith and the book’s origins.

history.author: Howe, Eber D. b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
E. D. Howe’s “Mormonism Unvailed” is an early critical examination of the origins and claims of the Latter Day Saint movement, particularly focusing on Joseph Smith and the Book of Mormon. It compiles affidavits and statements from residents of Palmyra, New York, and Harmony, Pennsylvania, to challenge the character of Smith and the divine origin of the Book of Mormon. The document suggests that Smith’s claims of finding golden plates and translating them into the Book of Mormon were part of a broader pattern of deceit and manipulation.

Key Points:

  • Howe questions the credibility of the Book of Mormon witnesses.
  • Claims Smith family known for digging for treasure and deceit.
  • Joseph Smith’s character repeatedly called into question.
  • Assertions of Smith’s treasure-seeking behavior linked to Book of Mormon.
  • Allegations of Smith using a seer stone for treasure hunting.
  • Critiques of Smith’s moral character and allegations of dishonesty.
  • Smith accused of changing his story about the golden plates.
  • Community members express skepticism about Smith’s claims.

history.author: Howe, Eber D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
An early critical examination of the Book of Mormon, questioning its origins and authenticity.

Key Points:

  • Claims of fabrication and delusion in the Book of Mormon
  • Human propensity for the marvelous exploited by its creators
  • Questions the divine authenticity of the Book of Mormon
  • Critiques the inclusion of Isaiah chapters as evidence of plagiarism
  • Highlights inconsistencies in the translation and narrative style
  • Discusses the supposed prophecies and their fulfillment
  • Examination of Nephi’s teachings and actions as implausible
  • Overall, presents the Book of Mormon as a work of fiction and deception

history.author: Howe, Eber D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
A critical examination and denouncement of the origins and claims of the Book of Mormon by E. D. Howe in his book “Mormonism Unvailed.”

Key Points:

  • Claims of “Reformed Egyptian” writings on the plates are debunked
  • Charles Anthon refutes claims he verified the writings
  • Anthon describes an encounter with Martin Harris and a hoax
  • Anthon warned Harris against a scheme to cheat him of money
  • Phelps letter recounts the story of the plates and spectacles
  • Phelps expresses doubts but leans towards belief in Mormonism
  • Howe critiques the changing stories about the discovery of the plates
  • Howe presents Mormonism’s origins as fraudulent and manipulative

history.author: Howe, Eber D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
An early critical examination of Mormonism and the Book of Mormon, arguing its foundation on falsehoods and delusions.

Key Points:

  • Book undertaken due to public request and concern over Mormonism
  • Claims difficulty in uncovering the whole truth about Mormonism
  • Asserts the foundation of Mormonism is built on falsehood
  • Discusses human susceptibility to religious delusions
  • Details previous religious impostors and delusions in history
  • Introduces the theory that the Book of Mormon was written by Solomon Spalding
  • Aims to warn those who might be susceptible to Mormonism
  • Expresses the challenge of convincing those already captivated by Mormonism

history.author: Howe, Eber D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. With Sketches of the Characters of Its Propagators, and a Full Detail of the Manner in which the Famous Golden Bible was Brought Before the World. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
An early critical account of the origins of Mormonism, focusing on the roles of Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Parley P. Pratt.

Key Points:

  • Parley P. Pratt converted after encountering Joseph Smith in Palmyra.
  • Sidney Rigdon, a preacher from Ohio, became a key figure in early Mormonism.
  • Expedition to convert the “Lamanites” led by Oliver Cowdery.
  • Joseph Smith provided revelations to guide the missionary efforts.
  • Emma Smith was commanded to be Joseph’s scribe and select hymns.
  • Smith and Rigdon claimed miraculous powers and performed baptisms.
  • Rigdon’s conversion marked a significant point in spreading Mormonism.
  • Mormonism’s early practices included speaking in tongues and prophesying.

history.author: Howe, Eber D., b. 1798
history.citation: Howe, E. D. Mormonism Unvailed: Or, A Faithful Account of That Singular Imposition and Delusion, From Its Rise to the Present Time. To Which Are Added, Inquiries Into the Probability that the Historical Part of the Said Bible Was Written By One Solomon Spalding, More than Twenty Years Ago, and By Him Intended to Have Been Published As A Romance. Painesville, Ohio:E. D. Howe, 1834.
history.teaser:
A critical account of the origins of Mormonism, focusing on Joseph Smith and his family, and the publication of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Describes the Smith family as lazy, indolent, and superstitious
  • Joseph Smith Jr. skilled in necromancy and divination
  • Joseph’s followers saw his ignorance as proof of divine mission
  • Martin Harris, a key financier, believed in Smith’s visions
  • Harris’s prophecies include drastic religious and political changes
  • Oliver Cowdery, another key figure, became an editor for Mormon publications
  • David Whitmer, a witness to the golden plates, described them in detail
  • Book questions the authenticity of the Book of Mormon’s origins

history.author: Whitman, Jason
history.document: Notices of Books: The Book of Mormon
history.citation: Whitman, Jason. “The Book of Mormon.” The Unitarian (Boston) 1 (January 1834): 40–50.
history.teaser:
An analytical review of the Book of Mormon by Jason Whitman, providing a critical perspective on its content, style, and the strategies used by Mormon missionaries to spread their faith.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon presented as a new sacred scripture by Joseph Smith
  • Historical account involves ancient peoples migrating to the Americas
  • Review critiques the book’s attempt to imitate biblical style
  • Mentions prophecies and visions about Christ
  • Observes lack of Jewish customs, reflecting modern Christian practices instead
  • Discusses the book’s appeal to prejudices against established religious and social structures
  • Notes the strategy of confirming the faith through claimed miracles and speaking in tongues
  • Whitman expresses concern over people’s susceptibility to the Mormon message due to lack of biblical and historical knowledge

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “Moroni’s Lamentation.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 16 (January 1834): 128.
history.teaser:
A lamentation poem attributed to Moroni, expressing grief over the destruction of the Nephite people.

Key Points:

  • Moroni is left without a home and mourns
  • He is pained by the sight of his people’s corpses
  • Moroni reflects on his father’s writings about the Nephites’ fear
  • Nephites were mercilessly killed by their enemies
  • Ten thousand led by Moroni died at the hill Cumorah
  • Moroni’s father despaired over the fallen Nephites’ beauty
  • Moroni yearns for death to join God and find peace
  • Moroni sang this lamentation observing the slain Nephites

history.citation: “Mormonism.” Protestant Episcopalian and Church Register (Philadelphia) 5, no. 1 (January 1834): 8. Reprinted from Maine Inquirer, circa January 1834.
history.teaser:
An article from 1834 commenting on the rapid spread of Mormonism as surprising given its origins and the doctrines of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Doctrine finding advocates despite being considered absurd
  • Surprise at the rapid spread of Mormonism
  • Mormon preacher from Ohio and New Hampshire making a stir
  • Whole of Freewill Baptist Church converted to Mormonism
  • Thirty persons and their pastor re-baptized
  • Troubles faced by preachers in Andover

history.citation: “To the Public.” Painesville Telegraph (Painesville, Ohio) (31 January 1834).
history.teaser:
A public statement by a committee in Kirtland, Ohio, aimed at discrediting Joseph Smith and the Book of Mormon, asserting it to be a work of fiction.

Key Points:

  • Committee formed in Kirtland, Ohio to investigate the Book of Mormon
  • Concerned about the societal impact of Joseph Smith’s followers
  • Committee employed D. P. Hurlbut for investigation
  • Aim to prove the Book of Mormon as fiction
  • Claims Book of Mormon written by Solomon Spalding
  • Seeks to discredit Joseph Smith’s honesty and prophetic claims

history.author: Briggs, J. A.
history.citation: Briggs, J. A. “Origin of the Mormons.” Christian Watchman (Boston) (31 January 1834).
history.teaser:
An article criticizing the origins and followers of Mormonism, including the Spaulding theory for the Book of Mormon’s creation.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism’s origin detailed by a former Mormon
  • Solomon Spaulding theorized as the original author
  • Spaulding’s manuscript supposedly copied by Mormons in Pittsburgh
  • Claims of similarities between Spaulding’s writings and the Book of Mormon
  • Mormons described as ignorant and deluded
  • Some Mormons have renounced their faith and returned to truth
  • Mormonism predicted to fail and scatter
  • Mormons arming themselves for conflict

history.author: Campbell, Alexander, 1788-1866
history.citation: Campbell, Alexander. “Signs of the Times.” Millennial Harbinger 5, no. 4 (April 1834):148,note.
history.teaser:
A critical review by Alexander Campbell, dismissing the Book of Mormon as absurd and a deception.

Key Points:

  • Describes the Book of Mormon as a disgrace to Christianity
  • Calls the book a “bundle of lies” written by an atheist
  • Claims it’s a trick to make money, with a poor style
  • Considers it carries its own condemnation in every page
  • God never demands faith without evidence
  • The book illegally anticipates Christian practices before Christ
  • Argues against two simultaneous systems of salvation
  • No one can practice the religion of a future dispensation beforehand

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.author: Editor of the Star
history.citation: “Considerable Excitement.” The Evening and the Morning Star (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 19 (April 1834): 150.
history.teaser:
An article discussing public reaction and legal proceedings against Doctor P. Hurlbut for threatening Joseph Smith Jr., and addressing misconceptions about Hurlbut’s intentions and qualifications.

Key Points:

  • Excitement among citizens regarding Doctor P. Hurlbut’s threats against Joseph Smith Jr.
  • Hurlbut held to bail for threatening Smith’s life
  • Public speculation and rumors spread about the legal case
  • Misconceptions about Hurlbut’s professional title and intentions clarified
  • Hurlbut’s claims to expose “Mormonism” debunked
  • Article criticizes those who support Hurlbut’s actions
  • Encourages lawful conduct and proper treatment of fellow men
  • Editor expresses confidence that truth will prevail despite Hurlbut’s efforts

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.citation: “The following is taken from . . .” The Evening and the Morning Star (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 19 (April 1834): 151.
history.teaser:
An article from The Evening and the Morning Star refuting a sensational story about a Mormon preacher’s alleged drowning during a failed miraculous act.

Key Points:

  • Story originated from the “Saturday Courier” of Philadelphia.
  • Claims of a Mormon preacher attempting to walk on water.
  • Alleged sabotage by “wicked Lamanites” who sawed his plank bridge.
  • Preacher supposedly drowned during a public demonstration.
  • Article criticizes the circulation of falsehoods against Mormons.
  • Challenges the claim that Mormonism is a delusion.
  • Questions the journalistic integrity of publishing such tales.
  • Editor sarcastically suggests the storyteller should write “religious lies.”

history.author: F., L. M.
history.citation: F., L. M. “Interview with the Mormon Prophet.” Evangelical Magazine and Gospel Advocate (Utica, New York) n.s., 5, no. 14 (5 April 1834): 107.
history.teaser:
An article detailing a skeptical and critical account of an encounter with Joseph Smith, the founder of the Latter Day Saint movement.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith made an ordinary appearance at a Mormon meeting
  • Smith acknowledged disbelief in his revelations
  • Described as having a physical appearance and manner that do not command attention
  • Smith’s approach to preaching and revelation is criticized
  • The interviewer attempted to question Smith directly about his mission
  • Smith avoided providing direct evidence of his divine mission
  • The conversation ended with Smith leaving abruptly
  • The writer remains skeptical of Smith’s claims

history.citation: “Mormon Trial.” Chardon Spectator and Geauga Gazette (12 April 1834).
history.teaser:
A newspaper article detailing a court case involving Joseph Smith, the founder of Mormonism, and Doctor P. Hurlburt, an ex-Mormon and critic of the faith.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith filed a complaint against Doctor P. Hurlburt
  • Hurlburt accused of threatening Smith’s safety
  • Case attracted great public interest and a crowded courtroom
  • Hurlburt was a former Mormon elder excommunicated for misconduct
  • After excommunication, Hurlburt criticized Mormonism and Joseph Smith
  • Hurlburt researched claims the Book of Mormon was plagiarized
  • Witnesses testified to Hurlburt’s threats against Smith
  • Court ordered Hurlburt to post a $200 bond to keep the peace

history.citation: “Mormonism.” Susquehanna Register (Montrose, Pennsylvania) 9, no. 21 (1 May 1834).
history.teaser:
An 1834 article from the Susquehanna Register featuring affidavits questioning the character and claims of Joseph Smith, the founder of Mormonism, and the authenticity of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Article responds to claims of forgery regarding Isaac Hale’s letter.
  • Isaac Hale provides a detailed account of Joseph Smith’s early activities.
  • Hale describes Smith’s involvement in “money-digging” and use of a “seer stone.”
  • Hale recounts Smith’s marriage to his daughter, Emma, and their move.
  • Smith claimed to have quit “glass-looking” but then found the Book of Plates.
  • Martin Harris and Oliver Cowdery played roles in translating the Book of Mormon.
  • Several affidavits declare Smith and his associates to be impostors and liars.
  • Community members affirm the good character of affidavit providers.

history.citation: “The Mormon Book.” Michigan Sentinel (3 May 1834).
history.teaser:
An article from the Michigan Sentinel discussing efforts to discredit the Book of Mormon and Joseph Smith’s prophetic claims.

Key Points:

  • Ohio paper reports a committee investigating the Book of Mormon’s origin
  • Committee aims to prove the Book of Mormon is fictional
  • Claims Solomon Spalding wrote the book over twenty years ago
  • Research seeks to undermine Joseph Smith’s claims to prophecy
  • Efforts to expose Joseph Smith’s “speculations” among Ohioans
  • Article suggests Ohioans are too knowledgeable to convert to Mormonism

history.author: M., F. E.
history.citation: “Mormonism.” Protestant Sentinel (Schenectady, New York) n.s. 5, no. 1 (4 June 1834): 4–5. Reprinted from New England Review, circa May 1834. Mormonism.
history.teaser:
An article from the Protestant Sentinel reprinted from the New England Review discussing the history, beliefs, and practices of early Mormonism.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith found golden plates and spectacles in 1828
  • Smith claimed exclusive ability to translate the plates
  • Martin Harris assisted Smith and funded the Book of Mormon’s publication
  • Smith and followers moved west seeking the “land of promise”
  • Claims of miracles and divine communications among followers
  • Mormonites eventually settled in Jackson County, Missouri
  • Mormon creed compared to Mahometanism with Smith as a prophet
  • Mormon influence spread beyond New York, reaching New England

history.source: The Evening and the Morning Star
history.author: Smith, Joseph, 1805-1844
history.citation: Joseph Smith to Oliver Cowdery. The Evening and the Morning Star (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 24 (September 1834): 192.
history.teaser:
A letter from Joseph Smith to Oliver Cowdery responding to criticism from Alexander Campbell, an influential religious leader.

Key Points:

  • Smith critiques Alexander Campbell’s negative stance on the Book of Mormon.
  • Joseph Smith has not personally met Alexander Campbell.
  • Campbell has shifted from direct criticism to more indirect remarks.
  • Smith suggests Campbell’s criticisms actually encourage investigation into the Book of Mormon.
  • Joseph Smith expresses satisfaction that opposition helps the truth of the Book of Mormon to be investigated.
  • Smith adheres to Christ’s teaching of turning the other cheek in response to Campbell’s attacks.
  • Joseph Smith remains committed to the testimony of the Book of Mormon.

history.author: Cowdery, Oliver
history.citation: Oliver Cowdery to W.W. Phelps, 7 September 1834. Latter-day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 1 (October 1834): 13–16.
history.teaser:
Oliver Cowdery’s letter to W.W. Phelps discussing early experiences and revelations in the formation of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

Key Points:

  • Cowdery reflects on the passage of time and eternity.
  • Shares experiences traveling and facing challenges with Joseph Smith.
  • Describes the process of translating the Book of Mormon.
  • Mentions the lack of authority in other religions.
  • Recounts receiving the priesthood from an angel.
  • Expresses joy and certainty in their religious experiences.
  • Describes the spiritual impact of their revelations.
  • Plans to provide a full history of the church’s rise.

history.author: Gilbert, Eli
history.citation: Eli Gilbert to Oliver Cowdery, 24 September 1834. Latter-day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 1 (October 1834): 9–10.
history.teaser:
A letter from Eli Gilbert to Oliver Cowdery discussing Gilbert’s personal loss, his interest in the Church, and his observations and opinions on religious matters in his community.

Key Points:

  • Gilbert’s sons were involved with the Church; one died from cholera.
  • Interest in the Book of Mormon and LDS teachings in Connecticut.
  • Gilbert read the Book of Mormon and found it corroborated the Bible.
  • Belief in the divine inspiration of the Book of Mormon.
  • Observations on local religious attitudes and prejudices.
  • Comments on the hardships faced by “Mormon” preachers and followers.
  • Discussion of local clergy and their compensation.
  • Queries about the lack of revelations in current publications.

history.author: Cowdery, Oliver
history.citation: Cowdery, Oliver. “Letter II.” Latter-day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1,no. 2 (November 1834): 27–32.
history.teaser:
Oliver Cowdery’s letter emphasizing the divine authority and continuity of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, paralleling its foundation to biblical precedents.

Key Points:

  • Cowdery promises a detailed history of the Latter Day Saints.
  • Emphasizes God’s works as clear, intelligible, and purposeful.
  • Draws parallels between the LDS Church and biblical narratives.
  • Argues the truth of the church is undeniable to honest seekers.
  • Claims pure religion withstands opposition and gains followers.
  • Notes the historical pattern of rejecting contemporary prophets.
  • Mentions the importance of judging by truth rather than rumor.
  • Intends to provide a narrative to inform and clarify the church’s history.

history.citation: “Mormonism Unvailed.” Painesville Telegraph (Painesville, Ohio) (28 November 1834).
history.teaser:
An advertisement for a book critical of Mormonism, providing a history and critique of the religion and its followers.

Key Points:

  • Book titled “Mormonism Unvailed” published in Painesville
  • Contains history of Mormonism from its rise to 1834
  • Includes peculiarities of the Mormon sect
  • 292 pages, 12 mo size
  • Available for sale at Painesville Telegraph office and book store
  • Merchants and booksellers can buy at reasonable terms

history.author: Smith, Joseph, 1805-1844
history.citation: Joseph Smith to Oliver Cowdery. Latter-day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland,Ohio) 1, no. 3 (December 1834): 40.
history.teaser:
A letter from Joseph Smith to Oliver Cowdery, discussing Smith’s early life and addressing accusations against his character.

Key Points:

  • Smith provides the time and place of his birth
  • Moved to Palmyra, N.Y. at the age of ten
  • Acknowledges youthful vices and follies
  • Denies gross violations of peace and good order
  • Regrets his former uncircumspect walk and unchaste conversation
  • Admits to acting against the precepts from God
  • Clarifies he is a man subject to passion
  • Requests the publication of his letter in the paper

history.citation: Oliver Cowdery to W. W. Phelps, letter no. 3. Latter-day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 3 (December 1834): 41–43.
history.teaser:
Oliver Cowdery’s letter to W. W. Phelps discussing early challenges and spiritual inquiries faced by the LDS Church and its members.

Key Points:

  • Cowdery addresses the persecution faced by the LDS Church.
  • Emphasizes the importance of a correct account of events.
  • Mentions Joseph Smith’s early life and spiritual inquiries.
  • Describes religious excitement and division in Palmyra.
  • Joseph’s family’s religious affiliations influenced his reflections.
  • Joseph struggled with the idea of joining any existing church.
  • Highlights the confusion over which church was true.
  • Joseph sought a more certain understanding of God’s will.

history.citation: “Mormonism.” Christian Register (Boston) (20 December 1834): 76. Reprinted from the Sacket’s Harbor Courier, circa December 1834.
history.teaser:
An 1834 article from the Christian Register, originally from the Sacket’s Harbor Courier, detailing accusations against Joseph Smith and early Mormonism.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith described as a former county pauper and money digger
  • Smith claimed to have found golden plates, later named the Book of Mormon
  • Martin Harris provided financial support for Smith’s endeavors
  • Harris and Smith described as using deception in their activities
  • Martin Harris accused of domestic violence and hypocrisy
  • Smith and Harris characterized as untrustworthy by local community
  • Harris’s failed prophecies led to his diminished credibility
  • All Mormonites reportedly left the state of New York

history.author: Griffiths, D., Jun.
history.document: Two Years' Residence in the New Settlements of Ohio
history.citation: Griffiths, D., Jun. Two Years’ Residence in the New Settlements of Ohio, North America: With Directions to Emigrants, 132–41. London: Westley and Davis, 1835.
history.teaser:
An 1835 account by D. Griffiths, Jr. of his observations and understanding of Mormonism during his residence in Ohio, including its origins, beliefs, and practices.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism highlighted as a notable example of American religious enthusiasm
  • Angel’s revelation to Joseph Smith in 1829 introducing the Book of Mormon
  • Griffiths’ personal encounter with Mormon Elder and examination of Mormon texts
  • Description of the Book of Mormon’s content and claim of ancient origin
  • Testimony of eleven witnesses regarding the golden plates
  • Mormon practices include baptism by immersion and communal support
  • Mormons claim supernatural powers like healing and prophecy
  • Griffiths criticizes Mormonism’s credibility, citing its origins as a novel

history.author: Abdy, E. S. (Edward Strutt), 1791-1846
history.document: Journal of a Residence and Tour in the United States of North America
history.citation: Abdy, E. S. Journal of a Residence and Tour in the United States of North America, from April, 1833, to October, 1834, 3:40–41, 54–59. London: John Murray, 1835.
history.teaser:
E. S. Abdy’s observations on Mormonism and its followers during his travels in the United States.

Key Points:

  • Mormons or Mormonites had settled in the west, numbering around 5-6,000.
  • Joseph Smith published his “seal,” with six more revelations pending.
  • Mormons live in common, emphasizing equality and harmony.
  • They believe in the eventual ascendancy of Indians and blacks over whites.
  • 20,000 converts and 800 ministers by the time of writing.
  • Mormons face persecution due to their inclusive beliefs.
  • Joseph Smith’s work includes historical, prophetic, and didactic parts.
  • Mormon doctrines emphasize natural equality and non-discrimination.

history.document: Hymn 63. P. M. “O stop and tell me, Red Man”
history.citation: “O Stop and Tell Me Red Man.” A Collection of Sacred Hymns, for the Church of the Latter Day Saints, 83–84. Kirtland, Ohio: F. G. Williams & Company, 1835.
history.teaser:
A hymn from the original LDS hymnbook contemplating the origin and destiny of Native Americans in the context of LDS theology.

Key Points:

  • Questions the identity and lifestyle of Native Americans
  • Native person identifies as Ephraim, once blessed by Jacob
  • Discusses the fall of their ancestors into darkness
  • Describes the transition to a hunting lifestyle
  • Mentions a dwindling of their race and arts
  • Expresses hope for redemption and an end to oppression
  • Foresees a gathering and transformation of Native peoples
  • Anticipates joy and blessings through pure religion

history.citation: “Mormonites.” J. Newton Brown, Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge, 844. Boston:Shattuck & Company, 1835. Reprinted from Cross and Baptist Journal, Fall 1834.
history.teaser:
An encyclopedia entry from 1835 providing a critical overview of the “Mormonites” and the origin of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Mormonites believe in the Book of Mormon, comparing it to the Bible or Koran.
  • Joseph Smith found brass plates in Palmyra, NY, in 1826.
  • Smith interpreted the plates using a stone in his hat.
  • Disagreement with Martin Harris led to Oliver Cowdery’s involvement.
  • Smith claimed the Book of Mormon was a revelation from heaven.
  • Followers were persuaded to move to a New Zion in Missouri.
  • A weekly periodical disseminates new revelations among the community.
  • The Book of Mormon described as puerile eastern romance with no connection to sober history.

history.author: Priest, Josiah, 1788-1851;
history.citation: Priest, Josiah. American Antiquities, 79. 5th ed. Albany: Hoffman and White, 1835.
history.teaser:
A critique of the Book of Mormon and its origins by Josiah Priest, questioning the connection between Native Americans and the lost tribes of Israel.

Key Points:

  • Priest opposes the idea that the Ten Tribes were lost
  • Claims Ten Tribes are still in the east, near ancient Syria
  • Ridicules authors linking Indians to Jews as ignorant
  • Mentions the rise of the Mormonites and their golden book
  • Describes the Book of Mormon as a poor Old Testament imitation
  • Asserts the Book of Mormon lacks connection, object, or aim
  • Criticizes the Book’s language as too modern for an ancient text
  • Points out the Book of Mormon was written in Ontario County, NY

history.document: Hymn 72. L. M. “Before this earth from chaos sprung”
history.citation: “Before This Earth From Chaos Sprung.” A Collection of Sacred Hymns, for the Church of the Latter Day Saints, 95–97. Kirtland, Ohio: F. G. Williams & Company, 1835.
history.teaser:
A hymn celebrating the creation, prophecies of ancient prophets, and the role of Joseph Smith in restoring the gospel in the latter days.

Key Points:

  • Jehovah foresaw all that would happen before creation
  • World created and man made its lord by God’s command
  • Ancient prophets foretold future events accurately
  • Joseph of Egypt prophesied about the latter days
  • God promised to restore gospel light and free Israel from bondage
  • A seer named Joseph to be raised to gather Israel
  • This seer, like Moses, would bring God’s word to man
  • The restoration of knowledge to fill the earth

history.document: Hymn 16. P. M. “An angel came down”
history.citation: “An Angel Came Down from the Mansions of Glory.” A Collection of Sacred Hymns, for the Church of the Latter Day Saints, 22–23. Kirtland, Ohio: F. G. Williams & Company, 1835.
history.teaser:
A hymn reflecting the early Latter Day Saint belief in the coming forth of the Book of Mormon and the gathering of Israel.

Key Points:

  • Verse 1: An angel announces the hidden record in Cumorah
  • Contains the fullness of Jesus’s gospel
  • Covenant to gather His people mentioned
  • Verse 2: Book speaks from the dust through the Spirit
  • A voice from the Savior to watch for Zion’s return
  • Verse 3: Calls to all nations to prepare for great things
  • The kingdom of Jesus in Zion will flourish
  • Righteous will gather, the wicked must perish

history.document: Hymn 26. P. M. “Now we'll sing with one accord”
history.citation: “Now We’ll Sing With One Accord.” A Collection of Sacred Hymns, for the Church of the Latter Day Saints, 33–34. Kirtland, Ohio: F. G. Williams & Company, 1835.
history.teaser:
A hymn celebrating Joseph Smith’s role in restoring the gospel and translating the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Verse 1: Celebrates the bringing forth of a prophet’s word
  • Verse 2: Joseph Smith sought a better way in darkness
  • Verse 3: An angel brought the priesthood back in purity
  • Verse 4: Joseph Smith inspired and fired with light for righteousness
  • Verse 5: The Book of Mormon translated for Gentile and Jew
  • Verse 6: Commandments came through Joseph Smith from Jesus Christ
  • Verse 7: Joseph Smith’s future contributions to the gathering for the Millennium
  • Verse 8: Triumph over foes and growth of Zion for eternity

history.author: Pratt, Parley P. (Parley Parker), 1807-1857
history.teaser:
An extensive collection of hymns, poems, and songs by Parley P. Pratt that reflects on various religious themes, including the Millennium, the gospel, and the destiny of different peoples according to Latter-day Saint beliefs.

Key Points:

  • Includes reflections on the Millennium and Latter-day Saint eschatology.
  • Discusses the restoration of the Ten Tribes and the Jews.
  • Contemplates the situation of the Nephites and Lamanites post-Columbus.
  • Considers the American Revolution’s impact and the current state of the United States.
  • Addresses the coming forth of the fullness of the Gospel.
  • Details the binding of Satan and the peace to come upon the earth.
  • Explores themes of redemption, gathering, and the building of Zion.
  • Emphasizes the missionary work of the Twelve Apostles and spreading the gospel globally.

history.source: References to the Book of Mormon
history.citation: “References to the Book of Mormon.” 1835.
history.teaser:
A comprehensive index of references to events, teachings, and notable occurrences within the Book of Mormon, categorized by book and chapter.

Key Points:

  • Index organized by book within the Book of Mormon
  • References include key events, prophecies, and teachings
  • Nephi’s journey to the promised land highlighted
  • Introduction of significant characters and their roles
  • Foretelling of Christ’s coming and teachings
  • Discourses on faith, hope, and charity in Moroni’s writings
  • Mormon’s role in hiding up the records
  • Prophecies regarding the destiny of the Gentiles and the House of Israel

history.author: Campbell, Alexander, 1788-1866
history.citation: Campbell, A. “Mormonism Unveiled.” Millennial Harbinger (Bethany, Virginia) 6, no. 1 (January 1835): 44–45.
history.teaser:
An editorial review of E.D. Howe’s “Mormonism Unveiled,” criticizing Mormonism and endorsing Howe’s findings.

Key Points:

  • Howe’s book is presented as a truthful account of Mormonism’s origins
  • Significant effort was made to uncover the facts of the Golden Bible
  • Joseph Smith and his colleagues are labeled as deceivers
  • Mormon followers are described as extreme fanatics
  • Fanaticism is considered a mental distemper more incurable than leprosy
  • The more absurd the belief, the more irreclaimable its followers
  • Mormonism’s influence is compared to the mythical powers of Lethe’s waters
  • The editor commends Howe for his efforts to expose Mormonism

history.author: Partidge, Edward
history.citation: Communication from Edward Partridge. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 4 (January 1835): 59–61.
history.teaser:
An early LDS leader, Edward Partridge, discusses the importance of the Book of Mormon and its alignment with the Bible’s teachings, urging acceptance of its truths.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon contains the fullness of the gospel of Christ
  • Testimony of credible individuals affirming the truth of the Book of Mormon
  • Emphasis on the necessity of receiving the Holy Ghost
  • Comparison of the Book of Mormon’s teachings with the Bible
  • The Book of Mormon and the Bible preach the same gospel
  • Signs following believers as evidence of the true gospel
  • Urges careful examination and comparison of the Book of Mormon with the Bible
  • Calls for embracing the gospel before divine judgments

history.author: Cowdery, Oliver
history.citation: “Letter IV.” Oliver Cowdery to W. W. Phelps. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 5 (February 1835): 77–80.
history.teaser:
A letter from Oliver Cowdery to W. W. Phelps discussing early events in Joseph Smith’s life and the discovery of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Oliver Cowdery apologizes for the brief nature of his historical recount.
  • Corrects an error: the religious excitement happened when Joseph Smith Jr. was 17, not 15.
  • Joseph Smith prayed for divine acceptance and assurance of a Supreme Being.
  • On September 21, 1823, a messenger appeared to Joseph Smith after fervent prayer.
  • The messenger was surrounded by a bright light and declared Smith’s sins forgiven.
  • The messenger announced a marvelous work that Smith would help bring about.
  • Smith was chosen to translate a history of the ancestors of the Native Americans.
  • The sealed part of the book contains revelations given to John on Patmos.

history.citation: “A Summary. ” Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 5 (February 1835):76–77.
history.teaser:
An editorial response to criticisms against the LDS Church, asserting the unstoppable growth and resilience of the church despite opposition.

Key Points:

  • Prospects for the church have never been more promising
  • Multitudes in all parts of the country are seeking truth
  • Critics like A. Campbell are described as howling in agony
  • Church’s growth seen as unstoppable, even by its fiercest critics
  • The “black speck” refers to criticism that won’t hinder the church
  • The gospel is unpreventable by men or devils
  • God will have the last laugh over opponents
  • A. Campbell’s refusal to engage in debate is mocked

history.author: Phelps, William Wines, 1792-1872
history.citation: “Letter No. 4.” W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery, Christmas 1834. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 5 (February 1835): 65–67.
history.teaser:
A letter from W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery discussing the early history and spiritual experiences tied to the foundation of the Latter Day Saint movement.

Key Points:

  • Phelps energized by idea of chronicling church’s rise
  • Encourages Cowdery to write plainly and truthfully
  • Recalls writing the Book of Mormon with Joseph Smith
  • Mentions an early rumor of a sacred record in gold
  • Belief in the scriptures led Phelps to embrace the Book of Mormon
  • Urges detailed history to illuminate church’s divine aspects
  • Shares a vision of an angelic visitation
  • Reflects on the joy of past and future divine interventions

history.citation: “The ‘Northern Times.’” Chardon Spectator and Geauga Gazette (Chardon, Ohio) (28 February 1835): 3.
history.teaser:
A critique of the “Northern Times” newspaper, edited by O. Cowdery, a Mormon preacher, which includes a strong attack on the United States Bank.

Key Points:

  • “Northern Times” issued from the seat of Mormonism
  • Edited by O. Cowdery, one of the Mormon preachers
  • Editor’s address suggests it might be his last
  • Six columns attacking the United States Bank
  • Comparison of Cowdery’s writing to Falstaff’s valor
  • Editor addresses Painesville friends about county seat removal
  • Editor expresses zeal for the “justice” of the objective
  • Selections may have been related to the golden plates

history.author: Cowdery, Oliver
history.citation: “Letter V.—TO W. W. PHELPS, ESQ.” Oliver Cowdery to W. W. Phelps. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 6 (March 1835): 95–96.
history.teaser:
Oliver Cowdery’s letter to W. W. Phelps discussing visions, the role of angels, and the gospel in the context of the Latter Day Saints’ beliefs and the gathering of Israel.

Key Points:

  • Discussion on the opposition to the truth and heavenly communications
  • Reflections on how God chose the “foolish things of the world”
  • Angels are considered former prophets and servants of God
  • Questions about the ministry of angels in the last days
  • Gospel’s unchangeability and the plan of redemption before the fall of man
  • Ministering of angels and the promise of redemption
  • Rejection of the gospel by the Messiah’s contemporaries and its consequences
  • The gathering of Israel as understood by ancient prophets

history.author: Cowdery, Oliver
history.citation: Cowdery, Oliver. “Delusion.” Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 6 (March 1835): 90–93.
history.teaser:
Oliver Cowdery defends the Book of Mormon against criticisms made by Mr. A. Campbell in 1831, focusing on the priesthood and promises to the tribes of Israel.

Key Points:

  • Campbell criticized the Book of Mormon’s credibility in 1831.
  • Cowdery argues the priesthood was conferred upon Aaron and his descendants.
  • Lehi and his sons had the Melchizedek priesthood, not Aaron’s.
  • Moses received the priesthood from Jethro and ordained Aaron.
  • God promised lands to Abraham and blessings to Joseph’s lineage.
  • Joseph’s descendants were promised lands beyond Canaan.
  • Campbell’s criticisms are seen as misunderstandings of scripture.
  • Cowdery suggests Campbell’s views are limited and incorrect.

history.author: Cowdery, Oliver
history.citation: Cowdery, Oliver. “Trouble in the West.” Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 7 (April 1835): 104–7.
history.teaser:
Oliver Cowdery defends the Book of Mormon and its teachings against criticisms in the Baptist publication “The Pioneer.”

Key Points:

  • Article responds to religious animosity toward LDS teachings.
  • Refutes claim of Joseph Smith being a book-peddler with false plates.
  • Addresses the Spaulding theory on the Book of Mormon’s origin.
  • Corrects misinterpretation of Christ’s birthplace in the Book of Mormon.
  • Defends pre-Mary knowledge of Jesus Christ’s name.
  • Clarifies the term “mother of God” as used in the Book of Mormon.
  • Disputes criticism of Christ’s post-resurrection visit to the Americas.
  • Asserts the book’s progress won’t be hindered by such criticisms.

history.author: Phelps, William Wines, 1792-1872
history.citation: “Letter No. 6.” W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery, 24 February 1835. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 7 (April 1835): 97.
history.teaser:
W. W. Phelps writes to Oliver Cowdery about the persecution faced by early Latter-day Saints and affirms his faith.

Key Points:

  • Phelps discusses the church’s persecution since its inception
  • Phelps’ heart was with the church since learning about the Book of Mormon
  • Phelps was imprisoned in 1830, allegedly to prevent him from joining the Mormons
  • Public sentiment was strongly against the Book of Mormon and its followers
  • Many could not believe a modern church would have a prophet
  • Phelps criticizes the world’s rejection of modern prophecy and revelation
  • Phelps asserts the persecution and martyrdom of Saints testifies to the truth of their religion
  • Phelps remains steadfast in his faith despite opposition

history.citation: “Letter VI.” Oliver Cowdery to W. W. Phelps. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 7 (April 1835): 108–12.
history.teaser:
Oliver Cowdery’s letter to W.W. Phelps discussing the history of the church, prophecies about the gathering of Israel, and the importance of visions and revelations in understanding God’s plan.

Key Points:

  • Cowdery emphasizes the deep bond among members through Ruth’s covenant.
  • Discusses the angelic message about the gospel and gathering of Israel.
  • References Psalms and Isaiah to illustrate the gathering and redemption of Israel.
  • Highlights the necessity of the gospel for both Israel and the Gentiles.
  • Mentions the glorious future awaiting the faithful and the importance of preparation.
  • Describes visions as a profound way of understanding God’s will.
  • Believes in the gradual revelation of God’s plan to His saints.
  • Expresses hope and blessings for Phelps and all faithful members.

history.author: G., A. B.
history.citation: “Statistics.—Mormonism.” Evangelical Magazine and Gospel Advocate (Utica, New York)6, no. 16 ( 18 April 1835): 126.
history.teaser:
An article from the Evangelical Magazine and Gospel Advocate discussing and dismissing Mormon interpretations of biblical prophecy.

Key Points:

  • Requests for statistical information on Universalist societies
  • Mormon preacher’s interpretation of Jeremiah and Genesis questioned
  • Prophetic names may mean something different in context
  • Jeremiah’s prophecy seen as historical, referring to Babylon’s fall
  • Genesis blessing of Jacob on Joseph debated in meaning
  • Christ referred to as “the Rock,” but interpretation disputed
  • Joshua, son of Nun, suggested as “the stone of Israel”
  • Dismisses idea of a “Jo. Smith dispensation” of Mormonism

history.citation: “Mormonism.” New York Weekly Messenger and Young Men’s Advocate (29 April 1835). Reprinted from The Pioneer (Rock Springs, Illinois), March 1835.
history.teaser:
An 1835 critique of Mormonism from a New York and Illinois newspaper, heavily criticizing its origins, teachings, and Joseph Smith.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism originated in Ontario County, New York, in 1830
  • Joseph Smith claimed to translate the Book of Mormon from golden plates
  • Martin Harris financially supported the printing after being convinced
  • The Book of Mormon’s authenticity is challenged
  • Claims of historical inaccuracies and contradictions within the text
  • Allegations that Smith used Spalding’s manuscript for the Book of Mormon
  • Criticism of Mormon doctrines as false and blasphemous
  • Warnings against the dangers of ignorance and superstition

history.author: Hyde, Orson, and McLellin, W. E.
history.citation: Orson Hyde and W. E. McLellin to Oliver Cowdery, 12 May 1835. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 8 (May 1835):115–16.
history.teaser:
An account of a conference in 1835 involving church leaders Orson Hyde and W. E. McLellin, discussing church affairs and addressing false teachings.

Key Points:

  • Conference concluded with discussions on church standings
  • Settled issues and erroneous teachings within the branches
  • Public meeting attracted nearly 500 people
  • Five individuals requested baptism after the meeting
  • Westfield Conference boundaries defined
  • Additional baptisms and confirmations performed
  • Instance of a man urgently seeking baptism noted
  • Mormonism Unveiled contrasted with the Book of Mormon’s value

history.author: Phelps, William Wines, 1792-1872
history.citation: “Letter No. 7.” W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery, 19 May 1835. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 8 (May 1835): 114–15.
history.teaser:
A letter from W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery discussing the significance of angelic visitations and the restoration of the gospel.

Key Points:

  • Phelps sees the angel’s visit as a sublime event in religious history
  • God’s consistency and mercy are emphasized
  • Angel’s visit marks the beginning of the restoration of the gospel
  • The Book of Mormon and the rise of the LDS Church are highlighted
  • Phelps encourages the gathering of souls for God
  • He reflects on the prospect of a glorious future as prophesied
  • Early challenges and opposition to the LDS Church are acknowledged
  • Phelps anticipates tribulation before full acceptance of the gospel

history.author: Phelps, William Wines, 1792-1872
history.citation: “Letter No. 8.” W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery, June 1835. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 9 (June 1835): 129–31.
history.teaser:
A letter from W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery discussing the role of prophecy, faith, and revelation in understanding and accepting the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • God chooses the weak to confound the wise.
  • Lack of faith and spirit in modern generation criticized.
  • Scriptural prophecy supports the coming of the Book of Mormon.
  • Isaiah’s prophecy seen as predicting the Book of Mormon.
  • God’s works continue regardless of human disbelief.
  • God’s books, beyond the Bible, are important for judgment.
  • Michael (Adam) is a figure of significant prophecy.
  • Phelps encourages Cowdery to continue documenting church history.

history.author: S.,D.
history.citation: “The Mormon Angel.” Evangelical Magazine and Gospel Advocate (Utica, New York) (6 June 1835): 192.
history.teaser:
A skeptical and mocking account of an alleged incident involving Joseph Smith and the appearance of an angel during a baptism.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith accused of being an imposter
  • Smith’s success in making proselytes in Ohio
  • Claim of an angel appearing during baptisms
  • Baptisms performed at night for the angel’s appearance
  • Three young men planned to capture the “angel”
  • The “angel” was chased and caught by the trio
  • The “angel” was discovered to be Joseph Smith with a lantern
  • Story provided by one of the trio involved

history.author: C.
history.citation: “Slanderous.” Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 10 (July 1835): 148–49. C.
history.teaser:
A defense against a slanderous story published about Joseph Smith, the founder of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

Key Points:

  • Story claims Joseph Smith pretended to be an angel during baptisms
  • Allegation originated from the New-York Mercury
  • Joseph Smith accused of deceiving followers in Ohio
  • Author refutes the story as a ridiculous falsehood
  • Assertion that Joseph Smith had not resided near Painesville since 1831
  • Denial that Smith ever baptized anyone near Painesville
  • Reports aim to forestall public opinion and slander the innocent
  • Questioning the credibility and motives of the story’s reporters

history.author: Phelps, William Wines, 1792-1872
history.citation: “Letter VII.” Oliver Cowdery to W. W. Phelps. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 10 (July 1835): 155–59.
history.teaser:
A letter from Oliver Cowdery to W.W. Phelps discussing the divine origin of the Book of Mormon and reflecting on its significance.

Key Points:

  • Oliver Cowdery emphasizes the importance of the Book of Mormon.
  • Reflections on the necessity of revelation and the consistency of God.
  • Discusses visions and divine guidance versus human interpretation.
  • Highlights the struggle between worldly desires and divine instructions.
  • Mentions Joseph Smith’s visitations and the instructions he received.
  • Describes the sacred place of the Book of Mormon’s origin, Hill Cumorah.
  • Reflects on the tragic history of the Nephites and Jaredites.
  • Concludes with thoughts on the resurrection and eternal judgment.

history.author: Phelps, William Wines, 1972-1872
history.citation: “Letter No. 9.” W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 10 (July 1835): 145–47.
history.teaser:
A letter discussing the significance of blessings and the historical continuity of God’s interaction with humanity, as seen through scriptural narratives and the restoration of the gospel according to LDS beliefs.

Key Points:

  • Moses’ command for nations to rejoice with God’s people highlighted
  • Reflection on the gathering of Israel and blessings for the faithful
  • Mention of the Book of Mormon as a messenger of truth
  • Discussion of the Urim and Thummim’s role in revealing divine will
  • Examination of blessings in biblical patriarchal stories
  • Emphasis on righteousness and obedience for obtaining blessings
  • Reiteration of the eternal gospel’s role in God’s plan for humanity
  • Encouragement to follow God’s way for blessings in time and eternity

history.citation: “Mormonism and Christianity.” Temple of Reason (Philadelphia) 1, no. 12 (25 July 1835):90–91.
history.teaser:
An article comparing the spread of Mormonism and Christianity, suggesting both began as delusions.

Key Points:

  • Article challenges the proof of divine origin through rapid spread
  • Mormonism’s quick expansion likened to early Christianity
  • Mormonism has wealthy converts, aiding its spread
  • Mormonism’s growth includes claims of miracles
  • Early Christians and Mormon apostles both faced skepticism and ridicule
  • Mormonism’s success highlighted despite lack of political power
  • Future deification of Joseph Smith speculated
  • Article calls for free inquiry into the foundations of faith

history.author: Phelps, William Wines, 1792-1872
history.citation: “Letter No. 10.” W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdrey. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 12 (September 1835): 177–79.
history.teaser:
A letter by W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery discussing the significance and impact of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Phelps views the Book of Mormon as a foundational document for the Church of Christ
  • Asserts that honest readers will feel grateful for the book’s knowledge
  • Phelps was struck with joy by the title page of the Book of Mormon
  • Describes the Book of Mormon as a history written by Mormon from Nephi’s plates
  • Phelps learned the right way to God through the Book of Mormon
  • The book is seen as a revelation from God, with its truth undeniable
  • Compares the Book of Mormon’s value and truth to the Bible
  • Views the revelation to the Three Witnesses as a crucial testimony of the book’s truth

history.author: S., D.
history.citation: “Complaints of a Mormonite.” Evangelical Magazine and Gospel Advocate (Utica, NewYork) ( 5 September 1835): 285.
history.teaser:
An article in which a Mormonite expresses grievances about how Mormons are being treated and a reply from the editors.

Key Points:

  • Mormonite questions the fairness of criticism towards Mormons
  • Compares the persecution of Universalists to that of Mormons
  • Questions if Universalists can maintain a clear conscience while criticizing Mormons
  • Editor acknowledges Universalists have faced persecution
  • Editor insists on the importance of calling things by their right names
  • Describes Joseph Smith as a “notorious impostor” and his followers as “deluded”
  • Editor recounts alleged fraudulent activities by Joseph Smith
  • Encourages the correspondent to follow Jesus Christ instead

history.author: Bradley, Joseph
history.citation: “Universalism in Ohio.” Evangelical Magazine and Gospel Advocate (Utica, New York) (12 September 1835): 291.
history.teaser:
An account of the spread of Universalism in Ohio, including interactions with and observations of the Mormons.

Key Points:

  • Universalism prospering in Ohio despite other religious movements
  • Liberal Christianity seen as a natural fit for the region
  • Mormons added Egyptian mummies to their beliefs
  • Joseph Smith claims to interpret ancient manuscripts
  • Methodist clergyman in Newburg converts to Universalism
  • Five Universalist preachers active within thirty-five miles of the city
  • Call for more laborers to spread pure and undefiled religion
  • Advocates for religion based on love for God and humanity

history.author: Cowdery, Oliver
history.citation: “Letter VIII.” Oliver Cowdery to W. W. Phelps. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 1 (October 1835): 195–202.
history.teaser:
A detailed letter from Oliver Cowdery to W. W. Phelps discussing the circumstances and divine experiences surrounding the discovery and translation of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Cowdery describes the location and deposit of the Book of Mormon plates.
  • Mentions divine instructions and reflections on holy grounds.
  • Details on how the plates were protected and preserved for centuries.
  • Joseph Smith’s initial failures to obtain the plates due to lack of obedience.
  • Divine manifestations and instruction on the importance of purity and obedience.
  • Joseph Smith’s character and the unjust slander he faced are defended.
  • References to divine guidance and prophecies concerning the Book of Mormon.
  • Emphasizes the sacredness and divine purpose of the Book of Mormon.

history.author: Phelps, William Wines, 1792-1872
history.citation: “Letter No. 11.” W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 1 (October 1835): 193–95.
history.teaser:
W. W. Phelps writes to Oliver Cowdery, discussing the Book of Mormon’s implications for Native Americans and their identification as descendants of Israelites.

Key Points:

  • Phelps connects the Book of Mormon to the history of Native Americans.
  • Describes Native Americans as remnants of Israel, deserving of the gospel.
  • Expresses joy over the prospect of Native Americans’ salvation.
  • Views the Book of Mormon as a key tool for Native American redemption.
  • Phelps is optimistic about Native Americans becoming a “white and delightsome people.”
