  • Considers the global population and hypothesizes about hidden tribes of Israel.
  • Criticizes contemporary Christianity for lacking faith and miracles.
  • Encourages the Latter Day Saints to keep faith for miracles and blessings.

history.author: Cowdery, Oliver
history.citation: Cowdery, Oliver. “The Record of the Nephites.” Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 1 (October 1835): 203–4.
history.teaser:
A letter by Oliver Cowdery reflecting on the journey and impact of the Book of Mormon since its revelation to Joseph Smith Jr. in 1827.

Key Points:

  • The angel of the Lord delivered the record of the Nephites in 1827
  • Thousands have heard its contents since its translation
  • The Book has been translated and printed despite opposition
  • Elders have been sent throughout the US and to Canada
  • The message has been proclaimed successfully against opposition
  • The church’s influence is reaching Europe
  • Call for saints to prepare for gathering and redemption
  • The church has grown significantly in eight years

history.author: Phelps, William Wines, 1792-1872
history.citation: “Letter No. 12.” W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 2 (November 1835): 221–23.
history.teaser:
A letter from W. W. Phelps to Oliver Cowdery discussing the significance of Cumorah and the message of the angel to Joseph Smith.

Key Points:

  • Phelps sees Cumorah as significant as Sinai to Latter Day Saints
  • Cumorah, a monument of marvelous works and a sacred depository
  • Discussion on the loss and wickedness of ancient peoples there
  • Angel’s message to Joseph Smith emphasized obedience to God
  • Pattern given by the angel as a guide to discern spirits
  • Book of Mormon seen as a cause of world commotion
  • Comparison to the finding of the book of the law by Hilkiah
  • Call for righteousness and rejection of false teachings

history.author: Scarritt, Isaac
history.citation: “Latter Day Saints.” Isaac Scarritt to Mr. H, 13 July 1835. Western Christian Advocate (Cincinnati, Ohio) 2, no. 30 (20 November 1835): 120.
history.teaser:
A letter by Isaac Scarritt, expressing his criticisms and doubts about the teachings and interpretations of the Latter Day Saints, published in the Western Christian Advocate.

Key Points:

  • Scarritt examined Latter Day Saints’ beliefs but remained unconvinced.
  • He criticizes the division of scriptural testimony between Judah and Joseph.
  • Questions the interpretation of Ezekiel’s sticks as scriptures.
  • Challenges the claim of Ephraimites in America and the historicity of the Book of Mormon.
  • Points out contradictions between the Book of Mormon and the Bible.
  • Criticizes the interpretation of Isaiah’s prophecy by Latter Day Saints.
  • Rejects the idea that translators of scriptures need to be divinely inspired.
  • Accuses the Latter Day Saints of detracting from the authenticity of the Bible.

history.author: Smith, Joseph, 1805-1844
history.document: To the Elders of the Church of the Latter Day Saints
history.citation: Smith, Joseph, Jr. “To the Elders of the Church of the Latter Day Saints.” Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 3 (December 1835): 227–28.
history.teaser:
A letter by Joseph Smith, Jr. to the elders of the Church, reflecting on the Book of Mormon’s significance and addressing opposition.

Key Points:

  • Comparison of the Book of Mormon to a mustard seed
  • Book of Mormon described as truth sprouting from the earth
  • God’s powers, gifts, and angels are lodging in its branches
  • Church likened to an impenetrable rock amidst opposition
  • Mentions opposition by referencing “Mormonism Unveiled”
  • Addresses critics and their tactics of falsehood
  • Mentions legal troubles of anti-Mormon author P. Hurlburt
  • Addresses disbelief and bias against Mormons

history.citation: “Thou Shalt Not Lie.” W. W. Phelps to John Whitmer. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 3 (December 1835): 230–33.
history.teaser:
An open letter from W. W. Phelps to John Whitmer discussing the persecution of the Latter Day Saints and defending their actions and beliefs against public slander.

Key Points:

  • W. W. Phelps addresses the public’s misunderstanding of the LDS Church
  • Phelps argues against the idea that the LDS members should not defend themselves
  • Discusses the misrepresentation and lies spread about the Church
  • Refutes false reports of a Mormon preacher’s tragical event
  • Criticizes the media for spreading falsehoods about the Church
  • Describes the persecution and challenges faced by the LDS Church
  • Phelps calls for repentance from those who have slandered the Church
  • Emphasizes the Church’s pursuit of truth and defense against falsehood

history.author: M., A. H.
history.citation: M., A. H. “Ancient and Modern Mormonism.” Western Examiner (St. Louis, Missouri) 2,no. 46 (10 December 1835): 366–67.
history.teaser:
An article from the Western Examiner comparing ancient and modern Mormonism, heavily critiquing the foundations and followers of the Latter Day Saint movement as an imposition on common sense.

Key Points:

  • Article criticizes the acceptance of Mormonism among people.
  • Leaders and followers of Mormonism described as societal dregs.
  • Comparison between ancient and modern revelations.
  • Claims both ancient and modern founders were impostors.
  • Mentions other religious texts as similar impositions.
  • Discusses human nature’s predisposition to believe in the marvelous.
  • Warns of the long-term impact of not refuting Mormon claims.
  • Calls for contemporary testimony to prevent future deceptions.

history.source: Memoir of the Rev. Samuel Green
history.author: Storrs, Richard S. (Richard Salter), 1787-1873
history.document: Memoir of the Rev. Samuel Green
history.citation: Storrs, Richard. Memoir of the Rev. Samuel Green, 129–39. Boston: Perkins & Marvin, 1836.
history.teaser:
A memoir containing a letter by Rev. Samuel Green expressing his concerns and warnings about the allure of Mormonism to a member of his congregation.

Key Points:

  • Rev. Green expresses vigilance and tenderness for his flock.
  • Warns against the delusions of Mormonism leading to perdition.
  • Emphasizes the importance of adhering to the teachings of the Bible.
  • Advises testing every spirit to see if it is from God.
  • Stresses that new revelations must be accompanied by clear miraculous proof.
  • Warns against accepting any teachings that go beyond the Bible.
  • Discusses the integrity and completeness of the Biblical canon.
  • Urges return to the “old paths” and good way of traditional Christian faith.

history.author: Hayward, John
history.citation: Hayward, John. The Religious Creeds and Statistics of Every Christian Denomination in the United States and British Provinces, with Some Account of the Religious Sentiments of the Jews, American Indians, Deists, Mahometans, &c. Alphabetically Arranged, 132–38. Boston:John Hayward, 1836.
history.teaser:
An 1836 analysis by John Hayward of the Book of Mormon, its content, structure, and the narrative it presents.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon contains 588 pages and several books.
  • Lehi’s journey from Jerusalem to the Americas is detailed.
  • Nephi retrieves records on plates of brass.
  • Lehi’s descendants split into Nephites and Lamanites.
  • Nephites practiced Christianity before Christ’s birth.
  • Jesus Christ visits the Americas after his resurrection.
  • Book of Ether recounts the Jaredites from the Tower of Babel.
  • Moroni concludes the record, promising spiritual gifts.

history.author: Phelps, W. W.
history.citation: Phelps, W. W. “The Indians.” Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio)2, no. 4 (January 1836): 245–48
history.teaser:
An article by W.W. Phelps discussing the LDS Church’s perspective on Native Americans and their role in the gathering of Israel, in light of U.S. government policies on Indian removal.

Key Points:

  • Gathering of Israel is a core belief of the LDS Church
  • Scripture guides the gathering of the elect from all nations
  • Book of Mormon identifies Native Americans as part of Israel
  • U.S. government relocating Indians to lands west of Mississippi
  • Removal plan aims to improve and protect Native Americans
  • Extensive territories allocated to various tribes
  • Arrangements include support for physical comfort and moral improvement
  • LDS view gathering of Native Americans as fulfilling prophecy

history.citation: “Beware of Delusion!” Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 4 (January 1836): 250–52.
history.teaser:
An article from the “Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate” defending the LDS faith against accusations of delusion and emphasizing the manifestation of spiritual gifts as evidence of its truth.

Key Points:

  • Article addresses concerns about being deluded by Mormonism
  • Questions the foundation of Protestant beliefs
  • Points to the absence of miraculous signs in other denominations
  • Highlights the presence of spiritual gifts among the Mormons
  • Warns against the materialistic values of the Protestant community
  • Mentions the Book of Mormon as a guide to happiness and truth
  • Emphasizes the importance of spiritual signs as evidence of faith
  • Discusses the slow progression of the Latter Day Saints in acquiring spiritual gifts

history.author: Ensley, Ephraim
history.citation: Ephraim Ensley to Brother Badger, 1835, Reading, New York. Christian Palladium (UnionMills, New York) 4, no. 18 (15 January 1836): 280.
history.teaser:
A letter expressing skepticism towards the authenticity of the Book of Mormon, contrasting its teachings with traditional Christian beliefs.

Key Points:

  • Mormon Preachers active in Reading, New York
  • Attempt to prove the Book of Mormon as the stick of Joseph
  • Ephraim Ensley borrowed and examined the Book of Mormon critically
  • Ensley found the book to be a farce
  • Critiques the Book of Mormon’s stance on infant baptism
  • Questions the historical and theological consistency of the Book of Mormon
  • Compares Mormon teachings unfavorably with traditional Christian views
  • Expresses hope that God saves the land from deception

history.author: Barr, Oliver
history.citation: Olion [Oliver] Barr to Ebenezer Barr, 22 September 1835. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 5 (February 1836): 257–58.
history.teaser:
A letter by Oliver Barr expressing skepticism towards the claims of Mormonism and emphasizing the completeness of the Gospel as delivered by Jesus Christ and the apostles.

Key Points:

  • Salvation plan devised in heaven and revealed through revelation
  • Revelation made to chosen individuals, not directly to everyone
  • Miracles are evidence of divine authorization of revelations
  • Moses, Jesus Christ, and Apostles confirmed their teachings with miracles
  • Once the Gospel was fully revealed, miracles ceased
  • Questioning the need for new revelations or miracles
  • Belief that the entire Gospel was delivered by the apostles
  • Open to being corrected if his objections to Mormonism can be answered

history.author: Barr, Oliver, d. 1853
history.citation: Oliver Barr to Sidney Rigdon, 29 February 1836. Latter-day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 6 (March 1836): 273.
history.teaser:
A letter from Oliver Barr to Sidney Rigdon expressing curiosity and skepticism about the teachings of the LDS Church.

Key Points:

  • Barr received Rigdon’s letter and examined it impartially.
  • Emphasizes the importance of understanding cardinal points of religion.
  • Acknowledges the kind spirit of Rigdon’s correspondence.
  • Expresses curiosity about Rigdon’s claim that the original Gospel has disappeared.
  • Asks specific questions about the nature and whereabouts of the Gospel.
  • Queries if the Mormons possess the complete Gospel.
  • Seeks candid responses to satisfy his inquiring mind.
  • Desires that their correspondence will glorify God and benefit them both.

history.author: Whitmer, John
history.citation: Whitmer, John. “Address.” Latter-day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2,no. 6 (March 1836): 286–88.
history.teaser:
John Whitmer expresses his reflections and testimonies concerning the early days of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and his role in its publication efforts.

Key Points:

  • Whitmer praises Oliver Cowdery’s character and leadership.
  • Highlights the responsibility and humility of an editor.
  • Emphasizes the power of preaching and God’s choice of simple means to confound the wise.
  • Reflects on living in a time when God is working for the good of His covenant people.
  • Testifies of the authenticity of the Book of Mormon and Joseph Smith’s prophetic role.
  • Emphasizes the importance of living by all of God’s revealed words.
  • Encourages elders to promote the Messenger and Advocate for the welfare of humanity.
  • Urges continued revelation and guidance by the Holy Spirit for truth.

history.author: Rigdon, Sidney, 1793-1876
history.citation: Sidney Rigdon to Oliver Barr, March 1836. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 6 (March 1836): 273–74.
history.teaser:
A letter from Sidney Rigdon explaining the gospel and its manifestations according to New Testament teachings, and asserting the restoration of these gifts in the Latter Day Saint movement.

Key Points:

  • Rigdon addresses questions about the nature of the gospel.
  • Defines the gospel as God’s power to save, made known in the New Testament.
  • Emphasizes the importance of receiving the Holy Spirit’s gifts.
  • Mentions specific spiritual gifts: speaking in tongues, prophecy, healing.
  • Asserts that the gospel includes a specific order of church offices.
  • Claims this gospel order had disappeared but has been restored.
  • Indicates that the power of God is received through ordained ministry.
  • Asserts the restoration of the gospel through divine revelation and messengers.

history.author: Hyde, Orson, 1805-1878
history.citation: Orson Hyde to the editor. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2,no. 7 (April 1836): 296.
history.teaser:
Orson Hyde reports on his missionary work and reflects on the opposition faced by the LDS Church.

Key Points:

  • Orson Hyde returns from a three-week mission in Portage, Ohio.
  • Preached in Hiram, where Joseph Smith Jr. and Sidney Rigdon were attacked.
  • Despite past violence, some in Hiram are embracing the truth.
  • Hyde baptized eight people in Mantua, Shalersville, and Middlebury.
  • Mentions the potential for further missionary work in the area.
  • Reflects on the resilience of the LDS Church against opposition.
  • Names A. Campbell, E. Booth, and E.D. Howe as notable opponents.
  • Asserts that opposition writings have failed to hinder the church’s progress.

history.author: Eells, James H.
history.citation: James H. Eells to Joshua Leavitt, 1 April 1836. New York Evangelist (New York) 7, no. 15 (9 April 1836): 59.
history.teaser:
A letter to the editor of the New York Evangelist by James H. Eells, discussing the rise of Mormonism and comparing it to Islam.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism compared to the rise of Islam
  • Mormons seen as a significant and growing religious sect
  • Description of the Kirtland Temple and its unique features
  • Mormons eager for education, including Hebrew studies
  • Mormons profess high levels of piety and devotion
  • Only Joseph Smith authorized to commit revelations to writing
  • Book of Mormon criticized for lacking literary quality
  • Mormons believed to be sincere but deluded by their faith

history.author: Pratt, Parley P. (Parley Parker), 1807-1857
history.citation: Parley P. Pratt to Oliver Cowdery, 26 May 1836. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 8 (May 1836): 3 18–20.
history.teaser:
A letter by Parley P. Pratt detailing his missionary experiences in Upper Canada, challenges faced, and his defense of the Book of Mormon against criticisms.

Key Points:

  • Pratt’s mission in Upper Canada with Elders O. Pratt and F. Nickerson
  • Difficulties in finding public spaces for preaching, leading to outdoor events
  • Encounters with clergy attempting to discredit the Book of Mormon
  • Rebuttal of criticisms regarding anachronisms and moral actions in the Book of Mormon
  • Comparison of criticisms of the Book of Mormon to the Bible
  • Public debate with Rev. Mr. Milkins and Pratt’s defense of Book of Mormon
  • Baptism of new believers following Pratt’s preaching and debates
  • Growth of the Church in Upper Canada as a result of missionary work

history.author: Rigdon, Sidney, 1793-1876
history.citation: Sidney Rigdon to Oliver Cowdery. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland,Ohio) 2, no. 9 (June 1836): 334–35.
history.teaser:
A letter from Sidney Rigdon to Oliver Cowdery discussing legal threats from Simons Rider and proposing a humorous solution.

Key Points:

  • Rigdon discusses being threatened with a lawsuit by Simons Rider
  • Rigdon pleads publicly with Rider not to sue him
  • Mentions the truth as a tight fit for Rider, causing discomfort
  • Proposes a humorous solution involving Rigdon’s wealthy uncle
  • Adamson Bentley suggested as a partner for Rider’s scheme
  • Bentley is accused of profiting from others’ property before
  • Rigdon suggests this scheme might prevent the lawsuit
  • Also mentions Darwin Atwater and Howe’s book in relation to Campbellism

history.author: Barr, Oliver, d. 1853
history.citation: Oliver Barr to Sidney Rigdon. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland,Ohio) 2, no. 9 (June 1836): 321–25.
history.teaser:
A letter from Oliver Barr to Sidney Rigdon discussing the nature of revelation, miracles, and the gospel according to the early Latter Day Saint movement.

Key Points:

  • Barr argues revelation and miracles were foundational to early Christian doctrine.
  • Disputes Rigdon’s views on the necessity of ongoing revelation and miracles.
  • Asserts that the New Testament contains the full plan of salvation.
  • Challenges the idea that modern revelation and miracles are needed.
  • Questions the LDS claim of a departed and restored gospel.
  • Argues for a return to the original gospel, not a new revelation.
  • Discusses the role of miracles in confirming the message of prophets.
  • Emphasizes the sufficiency of the New Testament for salvation.

history.author: Rigdon, Sidney, 1793-1876
history.citation: Sidney Rigdon to Oliver Barr, 15 November 1836. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 5 (February 1836): 258–63.
history.teaser:
A detailed letter from Sidney Rigdon discussing the nature of revelation, miracles, and the consistency of the gospel.

Key Points:

  • Revelation results from faith and presupposes belief in God.
  • Revelations are not solely based on the veracity of prophets.
  • Miracles are not the only proof of divine revelation.
  • Miracles were signs for believers, not exclusively for apostles.
  • Modern preaching lacks the power and authority of ancient gospel.
  • The absence of miracles in modern churches questions their authenticity.
  • The gospel’s effects differed greatly between ancient and modern times.
  • Restoration of the original gospel requires revelation from God.

history.author: Rigdon, Sidney, 1793-1876
history.citation: Sidney Rigdon to Oliver Barr, June 1836. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 2, no. 9 (June 1836): 326–29.
history.teaser:
A letter from Sidney Rigdon to Oliver Barr discussing the nature and necessity of revelation and miracles in the context of the Restoration movement.

Key Points:

  • Rigdon argues that faith precedes revelation.
  • Asserts that man cannot depend on others for knowledge of salvation.
  • Challenges the notion that miracles are the only proof of divine revelation.
  • Emphasizes that the Spirit can testify to the truth of revelations.
  • Questions the discontinuation of miracles in modern Christianity.
  • Highlights differences between ancient and modern gospel effects.
  • Argues for the restoration of the gospel through revelation.
  • Invites Barr to further discuss and explore these theological points.

history.citation: “The Mormons.” Wayne Sentinel (Palmyra, New York) (17 June 1836).
history.teaser:
A letter critiquing the Latter Day Saint movement’s claims about ongoing revelation and miracles.

Key Points:

  • Letter addresses the necessity of revelation and miracles.
  • Argues that revelation was necessary for initial faith in God.
  • Emphasizes that miracles confirmed the message of God’s messengers.
  • Claims the gospel is fully revealed and recorded in the New Testament.
  • Argues that no more revelation or miracles are needed today.
  • Asserts the gospel has not disappeared, refuting the need for restoration.
  • Urges the world to return to the gospel, not for the gospel to be restored.
  • Requests that the correspondence be published in full.

history.author: Campbell, Alexander, 1788-1866
history.citation: Campbell, Alexander. “Inspiration of the Scriptures.” Millennial Harbinger 7, no. 8 (August 1836): 347.
history.teaser:
A critique of religious movements, including Mormonism, by Alexander Campbell, highlighting perceived commonalities in their methods of attracting followers.

Key Points:

  • Campbell discusses how impostors manipulate desires for knowledge.
  • Mormonism is criticized for ministering to curiosity with the Book of Mormon.
  • Claims of miraculous power and mysterious visions are tactics used.
  • Comparison made with Islam and its promises of knowledge and paradise.
  • Mormonism’s appeal includes tales of the lost tribes of Israel and origins of Native Americans.
  • Mormonism’s methods likened to other religious movements’ use of novelties and visions.
  • Article implies the danger of forsaking duty for curiosity’s gratification.
  • Campbell aims to expose similarities between Mormonism and other deemed impostures.

history.citation: “Mormonism—Its History.” Philadelphia Mirror (22 August 1836).
history.teaser:
An article from the Philadelphia Mirror discussing the origins of Mormonism and the theory that it was derived from Solomon Spalding’s manuscript.

Key Points:

  • Article suggests Mormonism originated from Solomon Spalding’s work
  • Spalding was educated and ordained but left the ministry
  • Spalding wrote a historical novel, “Manuscript Found”
  • “Manuscript Found” is claimed to be the basis of the Book of Mormon
  • Describes a journey from Jerusalem to America, forming civilizations
  • Spalding’s manuscript explained as accounting for Native American ancestors
  • After Spalding’s death, Sidney Rigdon allegedly acquired the manuscript
  • Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon, claimed as divine revelation

history.author: Coe, Truman
history.citation: Coe, Truman. “Mormonism.” Cincinnati Journal and Western Luminary (25 August 1836). Reprinted from Ohio Observer, circa August 1836.
history.teaser:
An early critique of Mormonism by Truman Coe, expressing skepticism about its origins and practices.

Key Points:

  • Truman Coe located in Kirtland, criticizes Mormonism.
  • Joseph Smith’s history and the origin of Mormonism detailed.
  • Mormons have built a temple in Kirtland, costing $40,000.
  • Many Mormons are sincere, industrious, but possibly deceived.
  • Mormonism’s rapid spread and practices critiqued.
  • Contends that Mormons are the most priest-ridden of all men.
  • Mormons believe in continuous revelation and miracles.
  • Coe predicts Mormonism as a temporary fanaticism.

history.citation: “History of Mormanism.” The Ohio Repository (Canton, Ohio) (1 September 1836). Reprinted from New York Commercial Advertiser, circa August 1836.
history.teaser:
An article detailing the origin and spread of Mormonism, attributing the historical content of the Book of Mormon to Solomon Spalding’s manuscript.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism linked to Solomon Spalding’s “The Manuscript Found.”
  • Spalding intended his work as a historical novel, not religious text.
  • Manuscript suggests Native Americans descended from Jews.
  • Joseph Smith, Jr. presented as central figure in Mormonism’s founding.
  • Smith’s family described as superstitious and engaged in treasure hunting.
  • Golden plates translation claimed to be through divine assistance.
  • Book of Mormon claimed to be historical record of ancient Jews in America.
  • Initial converts drawn by Smith’s charisma and claims of divine revelations.

history.citation: “Origin of the Mormon Bible.” Trumpet and Universalist Magazine (Boston) (3 September 1836).
history.teaser:
An article from the Trumpet and Universalist Magazine presenting the Spaulding Theory as the origin of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Article claims Book of Mormon written by Solomon Spaulding
  • Spaulding wrote as a historical novel, not a religious delusion
  • Spaulding was a native of Connecticut, educated, and ordained minister
  • Financial failures led Spaulding to write “The Manuscript Found”
  • The novel was a fictional history linking Native Americans to the Ten Tribes of Israel
  • Unable to publish his work, Spaulding died in poverty
  • Manuscript allegedly fell into Joseph Smith’s hands and became the Golden Bible
  • Article dismisses Mormonism as a humbug followed by otherwise sensible people

history.citation: Goodson, J. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 3, no. 1 (October 1836): 397–99.
history.teaser:
A letter by J. Goodson addressing objections to the Book of Mormon, asserting its divine origin and translation.

Key Points:

  • Responds to criticism about uniform style despite different ages
  • Addresses the similarity of biblical quotations in the Book of Mormon
  • Refutes the claim that Book of Mormon scripture should not match modern translations
  • Argues against the notion that “reformed Egyptian” should not include familiar words
  • Questions why other ancient texts were omitted by Ezra but not questioned
  • Explains absence of Lehi’s prophecies in New Testament references
  • Asserts the necessity of revelation for the true church of Christ
  • Emphasizes the Book of Mormon’s simplicity and profound subjects as evidence of divine inspiration

history.author: Barr, Oliver
history.citation: Barr, Oliver. “‘What is Truth?’” [Mormonism—No. 1]. Christian Palladium (UnionMills, New York) 5, no. 15 (1 December 1836): 227–28
history.teaser:
An early critical examination of Mormonism by Oliver Barr, highlighting key theological disputes and personal interactions with Mormon leaders.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism unchristianizes the world, claiming exclusive truth since 1824
  • Mormons present the Book of Mormon as equal to the Bible
  • Oliver Barr engages Sidney Rigdon in theological debate
  • Debate topics include the design of revelation and miracles
  • Argues that the Gospel is the word of God, sufficient for salvation
  • Asserts no need for new revelations or miracles
  • Rigdon’s response deemed evasive, ending further discussion
  • Barr refutes claims of converting to Mormonism

history.author: Barr, Oliver
history.document: This wisdom descendeth not from above. “Mormonism–No. 2”
history.citation: Barr, Oliver. “‘This wisdom descendeth not from above’” [Mormonism—No. 2]. Christian Palladium (Union Mills, New York) 5, no. 16 (15 December 1836): 241–43.
history.teaser:
A critical examination by Oliver Barr, arguing against the divine origin of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon lacks divine testimonials compared to other revelations
  • Book of Mormon deemed unnecessary as the Gospel hasn’t lost its power
  • Claims made by Mormons seen as making them more intolerant and bigoted
  • Mormon book positioned as a counterpart to the Bible without valid evidence
  • Book of Mormon described as contradicting the Bible and containing vulgarisms
  • Claims of divine authorship of the Book of Mormon contested
  • Accusation of the Book of Mormon violating biblical laws and prophecies
  • Mormon practices of priesthood critiqued as blasphemous and unauthorized

history.author: H.
history.citation: H. “Joe Smith-ism, alias Mormonism.” Christian Palladium (Union Mills, New York) 5, no. 16 (15 December 1836): 243–44.
history.teaser:
An article criticizing Mormonism and its teachings, specifically focusing on Sidney Rigdon’s interpretation of Christian doctrine.

Key Points:

  • Article criticizes the spread of Mormonism in Boston
  • Sidney Rigdon accused of fabricating the Book of Mormon
  • Rigdon’s discourse questioned the necessity of miracles for belief
  • Claims Christianity and Mormonism founded on direct revelations
  • Rigdon’s interpretation challenges traditional Christian evidences
  • Author questions Rigdon’s claims with biblical references
  • Rigdon unable to satisfactorily answer the author’s questions
  • Article calls for Christian leaders to counter Mormon teachings

history.author: Clericus
history.citation: Clericus. “Mormonism.” Christian Register (Boston) 15, no. 52 (24 December 1836): 1. Reprinted from Hampshire Gazette, circa December 1836.
history.teaser:
An article from the Christian Register, reprinted from the Hampshire Gazette, critiquing the Book of Mormon and its origins.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism Unveiled critiques the Book of Mormon’s origins
  • Author doubts Joseph Smith authored the Book of Mormon
  • Book claims Solomon Spalding wrote the historical part
  • Religious additions to the manuscript possibly by Sidney Rigdon
  • Rigdon accused of inserting scripture and sectarian notions
  • Smith characterized as deceitful and Rigdon as a former preacher
  • Article suggests the Book of Mormon preys on the ignorant
  • Recommends reading both the Book of Mormon and Mormonism Unveiled

history.author: Peck, John Mason, 1789-1858
history.citation: Peck, John Mason. A Gazetteer of Illinois . . . , 36. Second edition, entirely revised,corrected and enlarged. Philadelphia: Grigg & Elliot, 1837.
history.teaser:
A sarcastic commentary on the Book of Mormon, comparing its battle narratives to historical wars and inviting scientific scrutiny.

Key Points:

  • Compares Book of Mormon battles to those of Alexander, Caesar, and Napoleon
  • Suggests Book of Mormon offers detailed descriptions of ancient military works
  • Claims it provides names and biographies of key figures
  • Calls for scientific examination of the Book of Mormon

history.source: Gazetteer of the State of Missouri
history.author: Wetmore, Alphonsos
history.document: Gazetteer of the State of Missouri
history.citation: Wetmore, Alphonoso. Gazetteer of the State of Missouri, 93–96. St. Louis: C. Keemle, 1837.
history.teaser:
An 1837 gazetteer entry criticizing the early Mormon settlement in Jackson County, Missouri, and recounting the expulsion of Mormons from the area.

Key Points:

  • Jackson County’s fertile land attracted Mormon settlers
  • Mormons’ “mock revelation city” criticized for taking advantage of local resources
  • Conflict arose from Mormons’ interference with slaves and feared alliance with Indians
  • Author portrays Joseph Smith as a lazy, unclean, and ignorant man
  • Smith’s claim of finding golden plates and translating them mocked
  • Mormon Bible described as nonsense and incomprehensible
  • Mormons expelled from Jackson County by “good citizens”
  • Mormons’ numbers and strength increased despite persecution

history.author: Pratt, Parley P. (Parley Parker), 1807-1857
history.document: A Voice of Warning and Instruction to All People
history.citation: Pratt, P. P. A Voice of Warning and Instruction to All People, Containing a Declaration of the Faith and Doctrine of the Church of the Latter-day Saints, Commonly Called Mormons. New York: W. Sandford, 1837. P. P. Pratt, A Voice of Warning and Instruction to All People, Containing a Declaration of the Faith and Doctrine of the Church of the Latter-day Saints (New York: W. Sandford, 1837).
history.teaser:
An early doctrinal exposition by P. P. Pratt, aiming to clarify the faith and beliefs of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints against widespread public misinformation and prejudice.

Key Points:

  • Aims to declare the faith and doctrine of Latter-day Saints
  • Responds to public agitation and misinformation about Mormonism
  • Highlights the role of the press in spreading misrepresentations
  • Seeks to defend the character of the LDS Church
  • Addresses the ignorance of critics regarding true LDS principles

history.author: West, William S.
history.citation: West, William S. A Few Interesting Facts, Respecting the Rise Progress and Pretensions of the Mormons, 15–16. 1837.
history.teaser:
A critical examination of the Book of Mormon’s authenticity, linking its origins to Solomon Spalding and challenging the claims made by its proponents.

Key Points:

  • Claims Book of Mormon’s historical part was written by Solomon Spalding
  • Alleges Sidney Rigdon obtained Spalding’s manuscript
  • Invites information to disprove the Book of Mormon
  • Three witnesses saw the plates only in their imagination
  • Book of Mormon’s Jaredites narrative questioned
  • Ancient American civilizations differ from Book of Mormon’s account
  • Mummies in Kentucky suggested to be of Egyptian origin
  • North American Indians possibly descended from ancient Scythians

history.author: Rigdon, Sidney, 1793-1876
history.citation: Rigdon, Sidney. “Persecution.” Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio)3, no. 4 (January 1837): 436–39.
history.teaser:
Sidney Rigdon’s article “Persecution” in the Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate, addressing the persecution faced by the Saints, particularly focusing on the actions of the Campbellites.

Key Points:

  • Rigdon criticizes the Campbellites for their hypocrisy and persecution.
  • Highlights a defamation and slander campaign against the Saints.
  • Mentions specific individuals involved in slandering the Saints.
  • Accuses Campbellites of false swearing and unjust actions.
  • Claims Campbellites violate their own principles of liberty and conscience.
  • Argues the Book of Mormon has exposed the true nature of Campbellism.
  • Believes Campbellism will eventually disappear due to its actions.
  • Intends for the article to be a historical record for future generations.

history.author: Smith, William
history.document: Evidences of the Book of Mormon
history.citation: Smith, William. “Evidences of the Book of Mormon.” Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 3, no. 4 (January 1837): 433–35.
history.teaser:
An article by William Smith defending the Book of Mormon as a legitimate and prophesied scripture.

Key Points:

  • Comparing unbelief in ancient and modern times
  • Prophecies cited as evidence for the Book of Mormon
  • Book of Mormon seen as fulfillment of Isaiah’s prophecies
  • Book of Mormon linked to the gathering of Israel
  • Scriptural arguments for the Book of Mormon’s authenticity
  • Book of Mormon as a record of Joseph’s descendants in America
  • Assertions that truth would spring out of the earth
  • Condemnation of opposition to the Book of Mormon

history.author: Clericus
history.citation: Clericus. “Mormonism.” Trumpet and Universalist Magazine 9, no. 29 (7 January 1837): 116.
history.teaser:
An early critical examination of the origins of the Book of Mormon, suggesting it was a fabricated document.

Key Points:

  • The book “Mormonism Unveiled” critiques the origins of the Book of Mormon
  • Joe Smith described as unlikely real author due to lack of education
  • Solomon Spalding proposed as the historical part’s writer
  • Spalding’s “Manuscript Found” suggested as base for Book of Mormon
  • Sidney Rigdon proposed to have added the religious content
  • Connection between Rigdon and Smith suggested as planned
  • Joe Smith characterized as dishonest and unreliable
  • Recommended to read both the Book of Mormon and “Mormonism Unveiled”

history.author: Barr, Oliver, d. 1853
history.citation: Barr, Oliver. “Mormonism No. iii.” Christian Palladium (Union Mills, New York) 5,no. 18 (16 January 1837): 273–75.
history.teaser:
An article by Elder Oliver Barr critiquing the doctrines of Mormonism, particularly its views on the nature of God and the fall of man.

Key Points:

  • Contrasts Mormon doctrine with traditional Christian beliefs
  • Questions the Mormon interpretation of the Fall of Man
  • Scrutinizes the Mormon concept of joy stemming from sin
  • Examines the Mormon portrayal of the Trinity and the divinity of Christ
  • Criticizes the claim of the Book of Mormon’s divine origin
  • Disputes Mormon teachings on the nature and birthplace of Jesus
  • Raises concerns about the coherence of Mormon theology
  • Invites readers to scrutinize the claims of Mormonism

history.author: F., E.
history.citation: F., E. “Sketches of a Traveller.—No. 25.” Missouri Republican (St. Louis, Missouri) 15, no. 1205 (29 April 1837): 109–12.
history.teaser:
An encounter with a Mormon emigrant traveling to Zion, filled with peculiar beliefs and intentions.

Key Points:

  • Encounter with a Mormon emigrant heading to Zion
  • Emigrant shares beliefs about the Book of Mormon and Zion
  • Claims about golden plates and lost kings of Israel
  • Christ was crucified where Adam was buried
  • Descendants of Cain under a curse
  • Millennium is dawning, and Christ to descend in Jackson County, Missouri
  • Only those baptized by Joe Smith or his peers will be saved
  • Emigrant was a pedagogue turned Mormonite with multiple wives

history.author: Z---a.
history.document: Mormonism: Scene in a Stage Coach
history.citation: Z—a. “Mormonism: Scene in a Stage Coach.” Christian Watchman (Boston) 18, no. 18 (5 May 1837): 1. Reprinted from Buffalo Spectator, circa April 1837.
history.teaser:
An account of a conversation in a stage coach challenging the credibility of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Mormon preacher unable to answer basic questions on evidence
  • Ignorance displayed in understanding internal and external evidence
  • Book of Mormon criticized for anachronisms like “gunpowder” and “mariner’s compass”
  • Passengers laugh at the claim Shakespeare borrowed from the Book of Mormon
  • Discussion highlights ignorance and simplicity of Mormon preacher
  • Preacher equates Joseph Smith with Moses, claiming Smith as superior

history.author: Newell, Grandison
history.citation: Grandison Newell to Sidney Rigdon. Painesville Telegraph (Painesville, Ohio) (26 May 1837).
history.teaser:
A letter published in the Painesville Telegraph accusing Sidney Rigdon and Joseph Smith of promoting violence against critics.

Key Points:

  • Newell accuses Smith of being an impostor and a swindler
  • Claims Smith incites followers to assassination
  • Alleges a plot to assassinate Newell under Smith’s direction
  • Assassination attempt foiled by the would-be assassins’ conscience
  • Newell criticizes Rigdon for preaching the infallibility of Smith
  • Accuses Rigdon of being complicit in the plot to kill him
  • Calls for public attention to the dangers of such impostors

history.citation: “The Golden Bible.” Painesville Telegraph (Painesville, Ohio) (26 May 1837). [text is indecipherable]
history.teaser:
A satirical poem published in the Painesville Telegraph mocking the discovery and content of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Mocks the discovery of the Book of Mormon
  • Compares its discovery unfavorably to biblical events
  • Suggests prominent religious figures never saw it
  • Joseph Smith found it with “a pair of white glasses”
  • Claims Smith had a “new revelation”
  • Describes Smith and Rigdon’s tar and feathering
  • Mormons built a tower for apostolic power
  • Overall, skeptical of the Book of Mormon’s authenticity

history.author: F., E.
history.citation: F., E. “Sketches of a Traveller.—No. 23.” Missouri Republican (St. Louis, Missouri) 15, no. 1231 (29 May 1837).
history.teaser:
An account of early encounters with and opinions on Mormonism and its practices, including a satirical portrayal of Joseph Smith’s supposed angelic visitations.

Key Points:

  • Encounter with a man discussing Mormon migration to Missouri
  • Mormons’ strict Sabbath observance and mission work
  • Claims of an angelic messenger appearing to Joseph Smith
  • Preparations for conflict and the building of Zion
  • Joseph Smith’s alleged angelic visitation debunked by locals
  • Widespread superstition and emergence of new religious movements
  • Critique of religious enthusiasm and fanaticism
  • Reflection on the absurdity and popularity of Mormon beliefs

history.citation: “Mormonites.” Christian Review 2 (June 1837): 203.
history.teaser:
An article from the Christian Review discussing the number of Mormons in the United States and expressing skepticism about the founders of Mormonism.

Key Points:

  • Twelve thousand Mormonites reported in the United States
  • Some Mormonites are respectable and wealthy
  • Founders believed to be crafty impostors
  • Expectation that the delusion will be dispelled

history.author: A Visitor.
history.citation: A Visitor. “Mormonia: Mormon Town. From the Miami of the Lake.” Daily National Intelligencer (Washington, D.C.) (4 July 1837).
history.teaser:
An 1837 visitor’s account of Kirtland, Ohio, detailing observations on Mormon community life, beliefs, and the construction of their temple.

Key Points:

  • Mormons congregated under Joseph Smith’s supervision in Kirtland, Ohio
  • Revelation dictated construction of a temple from stone, not brick
  • Banking institution established to accommodate domestic commerce
  • Sidney Rigdon became a significant figure alongside Joseph Smith
  • Visitor describes the temple’s architecture and interior design
  • Temple estimated to have cost around $60,000
  • Sidney Rigdon perceived as the intellectual force in Mormonism
  • Community praised for its industriousness and Christian charity

history.author: Barns, Lorenzo
history.citation: Lorenzo Barns to W. A. Cowdery, 3 August 1837. Latter Day Saints’ Messenger and Advocate (Kirtland, Ohio) 3, no. 11 (August 1837): 548–49.
history.teaser:
A letter from Lorenzo Barns to W. A. Cowdery detailing Barns’ missionary efforts and discussions in Ohio, including debates on the spiritual gifts and the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Lorenzo Barns details his missionary labors in Ohio
  • Encountered prejudice due to false reports about the church
  • Engaged in a public debate on spiritual gifts
  • Debate led to three baptisms; continued preaching led to more
  • Challenged to compare the Book of Mormon with the Bible
  • Debate opponent refused to continue discussing the Book of Mormon
  • Arguments against the Book of Mormon could also apply to the Bible
  • Held nearly forty meetings and baptized twelve individuals

history.author: Post, Stephen
history.citation: Post, Stephen. “Mormon Defence.” Christian Palladium (Union Mills, New York) 6,no. 7 (1 August 1837): 98–100.
history.teaser:
Stephen Post’s letter in defense of the Book of Mormon and its teachings, particularly addressing concerns about the birthplace of Jesus Christ.

Key Points:

  • Addresses Elder O. Barr’s criticisms of the Book of Mormon.
  • Clarifies the phrasing “at Jerusalem” regarding Jesus’s birthplace.
  • Explains “at Jerusalem” means near to, referencing Bethlehem.
  • Discusses the oneness of God and Jesus Christ from scriptures.
  • Emphasizes Jesus as both God and Savior.
  • Asserts Christ’s role as the creator of all things.
  • Reiterates Christ fulfilled scriptures about his life and mission.
  • Plans to discuss priesthood from a biblical perspective in future writings.

history.author: Barr, Oliver, d. 1853
history.citation: Barr, Oliver. “The Mormon Defence Refuted [Mormonism, no. 4].” Christian Palladium (Union Mills, New York) 6, no. 9 (1 September 1837): 138–39.
history.teaser:
Oliver Barr critiques the theological foundations of Mormonism, addressing perceived inconsistencies with biblical teachings.

Key Points:

  • Barr challenges the accuracy of Mormon claims about Jesus and God.
  • Questions about the birthplace of Jesus and the nature of God.
  • Disputes the idea that God could be born, die, or be seen.
  • Discusses biblical references to multiple “saviors” sent by God.
  • Argues that Jesus, being born and raised, cannot be the supreme God.
  • Explores the distinction between the Father and the Son.
  • Clarifies that Christ is not both Father and Son.
  • Criticizes the creation of new deities and doctrines in religion.

history.author: Pratt, Parley P. (Parley Parker), 1807-1857
history.citation: Parley P. Pratt to Don Carlos Smith, 3 October 1837. Elder’s Journal of the Church of Latter Day Saints (Kirtland, Ohio) 1, no. 1 (October 1837): 8–9.
history.teaser:
A letter from Parley P. Pratt detailing missionary efforts and spiritual experiences in New York, and interactions with Joseph Wolff, a Jewish scholar.

Key Points:

  • Pratt preached in various places in New York City.
  • Four people were baptized in the East River.
  • A vision confirming the truth of the gospel was shared.
  • Gift of healing beginning to manifest in New York.
  • Joseph Wolff’s lectures align with LDS beliefs on prophecy.
  • Pratt gave Wolff a Book of Mormon.
  • Wolff’s vision of Jerusalem’s future shared.
  • Pratt authored “A Voice of Warning and Instruction to All People.”

history.author: Post, Stephen
history.citation: Post, Stephen. “Mormon Defence.--No. II.” Christian Palladium (Union Mills, NewYork) 6, no. 15 (1 December 1837): 230–31.
history.teaser:
An early Latter-day Saint Elder’s defense of the divinity and unity of God the Father and Jesus Christ, against criticisms.

Key Points:

  • Elder Post criticizes Elder Barr’s separation of God and Christ.
  • Scriptures declare there is one God, not giving glory to another.
  • Father (spirit) and Son (in flesh) are one supreme power.
  • Scriptures support the unity and divinity of Christ and the Father.
  • Jesus Christ is eternal, foundational to creation.
  • God was manifest in the flesh through Jesus Christ.
  • Christ’s power unaffected by physical death, sustained the universe.
  • Invitation to repentance and baptism in Jesus Christ’s name.

history.document: Author of the Book of Mormon
history.citation: “Author of the Book of Mormon.” Zion’s Advocate (Portland, Maine) 10, no. 51 (20 December 1837). Reprinted in the Morning Star, 27 December 1837.
history.teaser:
An article examining the origins of the Book of Mormon, suggesting it was based on a manuscript by Solomon Spalding, and discussing early skepticism and criticism of the Mormon faith.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith deemed too ignorant to have written the Book of Mormon
  • Solomon Spalding suggested as the original author
  • Spalding’s manuscript, “The Manuscript Found,” linked to the Book of Mormon
  • Sidney Rigdon suspected of revising Spalding’s manuscript
  • Ezra Booth’s disillusionment and critique of Mormonism
  • Smith’s authority in the church as a Prophet and Translator
  • Claims of constant new commandments from the Lord
  • Scriptures alleged to be wrongly translated; Smith to correct them

history.author: Reese, David Meredith
history.citation: Reese, David Meredith. Humbugs of New York: Being a Remonstrance against Popular Delusion; Whether in Science, Philosophy, or Religion, 264–65. New York: John S. Taylor, 1838.
history.teaser:
David Meredith Reese criticizes the spread of Mormonism in New York, labeling it as a humbug and a form of popular delusion.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism added to New York’s “religious humbugs”
  • Lamentable spread of Mormonism in New York
  • Elder of Mormonism finds support in New York
  • Mormonism’s public propagation criticized
  • Mormonism attracts followers from various dubious beliefs
  • Community of infidels at Tammany Hall supports Mormonism
  • Scores of Christian church members re-baptized into Mormonism
  • Mormonism’s spread predicted to end in infamy and blood

history.author: Canning, Josiah D.
history.citation: Canning, Josiah D. Poems by Josiah D. Canning, 107–8. Greenfield, MA: Phelps & Ingersoll, 1838.
history.teaser:
A satirical poem by Josiah D. Canning critiquing Joseph Smith and the early Mormon movement.

Key Points:

  • Mormon claimed to have opened heaven’s gates with golden plates
  • Joseph Smith is depicted as an agent with school-boy tactics
  • Mormons moved west in search of a promised land
  • The poem describes Mormons as seeking command from heaven
  • Mormons believe in the exalted worth of a soul reborn
  • They esteem themselves as holy angels, unknown to sin
  • Mormons’ journey to the west led to fighting and bloodshed
  • The poem criticizes the presence of Mormonism under New England’s Christian influence

history.author: James, M'Chesney
history.citation: M’Chesney, James. An Antidote To Mormonism; A Warning Voice To The Church And Nation; The Purity Of Christian Principles Defended; And Truth Disentangled From Error And Delusion. Revised G. J. Bennet. New York, NY: Burnett & Pollard, 1838.
history.teaser:
A critical and extensive denouncement of Mormonism, framing it as a significant delusion with dangerous implications for society and Christian principles.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism labeled as a significant delusion and threat.
  • Belief in Mormonism equated to rebellion against God.
  • Mormonism accused of promoting war and bloodshed.
  • Claims of healing and miracles seen as deceitful.
  • Describes Mormonism as contradictory to Christian principles.
  • Mormon banking practices criticized as fraudulent.
  • Mormonism’s origins attributed to the manipulation of Solomon Spaulding’s manuscript.
  • Urges readers to adhere to traditional Christian values over Mormon teachings.

history.author: Bacheler, Origen
history.citation: Bacheler, Origen. Mormonism Exposed Internally and Externally. New York, 1838. _____ _____
history.teaser:
This document is a critical examination and summary of the Book of Mormon, its early reception, and the credibility of its witnesses, particularly focusing on the origins and claims made by Joseph Smith Jr. and others involved in its publication.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon presented as new revelation, contradicting scripture
  • Joseph Smith Jr. claimed to find golden plates with divine writings
  • Witnesses’ credibility questioned, including Smith’s and his family’s
  • Accusations of the Book of Mormon being a forgery
  • Claims of supernatural events (visions, angelic visitations) scrutinized
  • Challenges to linguistic and historical accuracy within the Book
  • Discussion on the impossibility of events described
  • Analysis of witnesses’ character, revealing inconsistencies and questionable behavior

history.author: Livesey, Richard
history.citation: Livesey, Richard. An Exposure of Mormonism, being a statement of facts relating to the self-styled “Latter day Saints,” and the Origin of the Book of Mormon, 2–12. Preston: J. Livesey, 1838.
history.teaser:
A critical examination of the origins of Mormonism and the credibility of its founders.

Key Points:

  • Claims to expose facts about Mormon leaders and the Book of Mormon
  • Questions the credibility of the Book of Mormon’s witnesses
  • Describes Joseph Smith and his family as known for fortune-telling and money-digging
  • Asserts Smith and witnesses were not credible due to their reputations
  • Alleges the Book of Mormon was plagiarized from Solomon Spalding’s manuscript
  • Details the supposed process of altering Spalding’s work into the Book of Mormon
  • Highlights the financial motivations behind the creation of the Book of Mormon
  • Includes testimonials disputing the truth of the Book of Mormon and its origins

history.author: Williams, S. [Samuel]
history.citation: Williams, S. Mormonism Exposed. 1838.
history.teaser:
An 1838 critique of Mormonism, arguing that it is based on falsehoods and implicating Sidney Rigdon as a key conspirator behind the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism criticized as absurd and growing rapidly
  • Sidney Rigdon suggested as the true mastermind behind Joseph Smith
  • Rigdon’s controversial religious positions and expulsion from the Baptist denomination
  • Allegations that Rigdon used Solomon Spaulding’s manuscript for the Book of Mormon
  • Critique of Mormon doctrines as contradicting traditional Christian teachings
  • Errors in grammar and spelling in the Book of Mormon highlighted
  • Claims of a conspiracy involving Rigdon, Smith, and others to create Mormonism
  • Testimonies and circumstantial evidence presented against the authenticity of the Book of Mormon

history.author: Pratt, Parley P. (Parley Parker, 1807-1857)
history.citation: Pratt, Parley P. Mormonism Unveiled: Zion’s Watchman Unmasked, and its Editor, Mr. L. R. Sunderland, Exposed: Truth Vindicated: the Devil Mad, and Priestcraft in Danger! New York: O. Pratt and E. Fordham, 1838.
history.teaser:
A defense of the Book of Mormon and the early Latter Day Saint movement by Parley P. Pratt against criticisms and accusations made by La Roy Sunderland in the “Zion’s Watchman.”

Key Points:

  • Pratt refutes Sunderland’s criticisms of the Book of Mormon.
  • Highlights Pratt’s personal involvement in early LDS history.
  • Pratt asserts the truth of the Book of Mormon through personal testimony.
  • Addresses accusations against Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon.
  • Denies the Spalding theory for the origin of the Book of Mormon.
  • Defends the character and intentions of early LDS leaders.
  • Challenges Sunderland to publish his response for fairness.
  • Invokes divine judgment on those who oppose or misrepresent the LDS faith.

history.citation: “Mormonism in America.” The Christian Witness (Plymouth, England) 5, no. 1 (January 1838): 1–38.
history.teaser:
Mormonism in America - The Christian Witness (1838)

This document is an extensive critique of Mormonism as presented in a Christian publication from Plymouth, England. It discusses the origins, beliefs, and perceived errors of the Mormon faith, comparing it unfavorably with traditional Christian teachings.

Key Points:
  • Mormonism claims a new apostolate and exclusive truth.
  • It emphasizes ordinances and diminishes scriptural liberty.
  • Both Mormonism and Irvingism emerged around the same time and share similar claims.
  • Mormon teachings on faith and salvation differ significantly from traditional Christianity.
  • Salvation in Mormonism is linked to works, contrary to the doctrine of salvation by faith.
  • Mormonism challenges the authenticity of traditional scriptures.
  • It promises a unique role for America in religious prophecy.
  • The critique warns of the dangers of departing from scriptural truths.

history.author: Sunderland, La Roy
history.citation: Sunderland, La Roy. “Mormonism.” Zion’s Watchman (New York) 3, no. 2 (13 January 1838): 6.
history.teaser:
An article by La Roy Sunderland in Zion’s Watchman critically examining the beliefs and practices of Mormonism.

Key Points:

  • Article aims to expose the foundations of Mormonism.
  • Joseph Smith claims to have 50,000 converts.
  • Mormons claim infallible inspiration and miracle-working powers.
  • Mormons profess to communicate with angels.
  • Mormons claim to be the only true Church.
  • New Jerusalem located in Missouri according to Mormons.
  • Mormon scriptures claimed to be translated by inspiration.
  • Mormon doctrine threatens eternal damnation to non-believers.

history.author: Barr, Oliver
history.citation: Barr, Oliver. “Mormonism--No. V.” The Christian Palladium (Union Mills, NewYork) 6, no. 18 (15 January 1838): 275. Mormonism—No. v.
history.teaser:
An article by Oliver Barr critiquing the Book of Mormon and its theological implications.

Key Points:

  • Claims the Book of Mormon lacks evidence of divine revelation
  • Asserts the Book of Mormon was not needed and contradicts the Bible
  • Points out discrepancies in prophecies between the Book of Mormon and the Bible
  • Discusses contradictions in the Mormon concept of the Trinity
  • Highlights the distinction between God the Father and Jesus Christ as separate personages
  • Questions the Mormon view of Jesus Christ’s nature
  • Criticizes the concept of a material aspect of God
  • Mocks the logic used to defend Mormon theological claims

history.author: Sunderland, La Roy
history.citation: Sunderland, La Roy. “Mormonism.” Zion’s Watchman (New York) 3, no. 3 (20 January 1838).
history.teaser:
An article by La Roy Sunderland in “Zion’s Watchman” critically comparing Mormonism to other religious movements and alleged impostures.

Key Points:

  • Every age has had its impostures, including Mormonism
  • Mormonism compared to Mohammedanism and the Koran
  • Similarities between the French Prophets and Mormons highlighted
  • Comparison with the Shakers and their founder’s claims
  • Swedenborg’s visions paralleled with Mormon claims
  • The Areekee’s claims of spiritual power likened to Mormon miracles
  • Historical impostors like Jemimie Wilkinson and Joanna Southcote mentioned
  • Mormonism criticized for its pretensions, details, and authorship

history.citation: Sunderland, La Roy. “Mormonism.” Zion’s Watchman (New York) 3, no. 4 (27 January 1838).
history.teaser:
An article by La Roy Sunderland in “Zion’s Watchman” critiquing the claims of Mormonism and comparing them unfavorably to biblical miracles and prophecies.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism claims inspiration similar to biblical apostles
  • Criteria to identify real miracles contrasted with Book of Mormon
  • Mormon miracles deemed trivial and not publicly verifiable
  • Book of Mormon translation done in secrecy, raising doubts
  • Real miracles are not the result of natural causes
  • Lack of public monuments or observances for Mormon miracles
  • Scriptural miracles supported by continuous observance and evidence
  • Prophecies in the Book of Mormon critiqued for lack of originality and accuracy

history.author: Sunderland, La Roy
history.citation: Sunderland, La Roy. “Mormonism.” Zion’s Watchman (New York) 3, no. 5 (3 February 1838).
history.teaser:
An article by La Roy Sunderland in “Zion’s Watchman” criticizing the Book of Mormon, Joseph Smith, and the practices of early Mormonism.

Key Points:

  • Claims Mormonism is aimed at making money.
  • Gifts to Mormon preachers required for membership.
  • Property given to the Mormon community cannot be reclaimed.
  • Uses God’s voice to enforce monetary contributions.
  • Backsliders from Mormonism treated harshly.
  • Mormon solicitude about money is emphasized.
  • Contradicts the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
  • Mormonism described as another gospel, directly opposed to Christianity.

history.author: Sunderland, La Roy
history.citation: Sunderland, La Roy. “Mormonism.” Zion’s Watchman (New York) 3, no. 6 (10 February 1838): 22.
history.teaser:
An article by La Roy Sunderland in “Zion’s Watchman” criticizing the Book of Mormon and its teachings as contrary to the Bible and filled with inconsistencies.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism receives no countenance from the Bible
  • Book of Mormon contradicts biblical teachings
  • Mormonism requires faith without evidence
  • Claims of Mormonism seen as cruel and duplicitous
  • Book of Mormon described as a history of wars and murders
  • Mormon writings filled with nonsensical and blasphemous content
  • Doctrine and Covenants seen as contradictory to the Bible
  • Book of Mormon criticized for grammatical and factual errors

history.author: Sunderland, La Roy
history.citation: Sunderland, La Roy. “Mormonism.” Zion's Watchman (New York) 3, no. 7 (17 February 1838).
history.teaser:
An article by La Roy Sunderland in “Zion’s Watchman” critiquing the Book of Mormon for its language, style, contradictions, and claimed plagiarisms.

Key Points:

  • Criticizes the language and style of the Book of Mormon
  • Points out repeated and peculiar use of certain phrases
  • Highlights supposed plagiarisms from other texts
  • Notes inconsistencies and anachronisms within the text
  • Questions the claim of the Book of Mormon being written in “plain English”
  • Lists contradictions between the Book of Mormon and the Bible
  • Challenges historical accuracy and linguistic claims
  • Argues that the Book of Mormon’s content and form offer evidence against its divine inspiration

history.author: Sunderland, La Roy
history.citation: Sunderland, La Roy. “Mormonism.” Zion’s Watchman (New York) 3, no. 8 (24 February 1838).
history.teaser:
An article by La Roy Sunderland in Zion’s Watchman critiquing the Book of Mormon and highlighting perceived inconsistencies and anachronisms.

Key Points:

  • Questioned the physical feasibility of brass plates’ weight
  • Doubts about writing on brass and the “reformed Egyptian” language
  • Questions regarding the whereabouts of the original plates
  • Use of modern terms like “synagogues” and “bountiful” critiqued
  • Claims of historical inaccuracies and anachronisms
  • Allegations of the book supporting murder, theft, and polygamy
  • Discussion on the sameness of language suggesting a single author
  • Points out peculiarities and errors as evidence against its authenticity

history.author: Sunderland, La Roy
history.citation: Sunderland, La Roy. “Mormonism.” Zion’s Watchman (New York) 3, no. 9 (3 March 1838): 34.
history.teaser:
An article by La Roy Sunderland in “Zion’s Watchman” discussing the origins of the Book of Mormon and criticizing its authenticity and the character of its founders.

Key Points:

  • Claims Book of Mormon was written by Solomon Spaulding
  • Testimonies in “Mormonism Unveiled” by E. D. Howe used as evidence
  • Witnesses recall similarities between Spaulding’s work and Book of Mormon
  • Spaulding’s widow mentions manuscript was taken to Pittsburgh
  • Testimony of eighty witnesses against the credibility of Joseph Smith and Book of Mormon
  • Joseph Smith and associates known as “fortune tellers” and “money diggers”
  • Martin Harris and Joseph Smith accused of seeing the venture as a way to make money
  • Claims of character flaws and dishonesty among Book of Mormon witnesses

history.author: S.
history.citation: “Mormonism Exposed and Refuted.” Universalist Union (New York) 3, no. 26 (5 May 1838): 205.
history.teaser:
An 1838 critique of Mormonism by La Roy Sunderland, highlighting perceived dangers and ethical concerns.

Key Points:

  • La Roy Sunderland critiques Mormonism in a pamphlet.
  • Mormonism found a receptive audience among Methodists.
  • Sunderland criticizes Mormonism’s use of damnation threats.
  • Claims Mormonism’s cruelty is unparalleled by any religion.
  • Joseph Smith is depicted as a dishonest individual.
  • Mormonism’s cruelty compared to common Christian threats.
  • Mormonism uses fear similar to other religious movements.
  • Sunderland argues Mormonism is not true Christianity.

history.citation: [Questions and Answers]. Elders’ Journal of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints (Far West, Missouri) 1, no. 3 (July 1838): 42–44.
history.teaser:
An article from the Elders’ Journal providing answers to various questions about the beliefs and practices of the early Latter Day Saint movement.

Key Points:

  • Belief in the Bible distinguishes them from other sects
  • Only the repentant will avoid damnation
  • Book of Mormon obtained through divine guidance
  • Joseph Smith Jr. is recognized as a prophet
  • Do not believe in communal ownership or polygamy at that time
  • Joseph Smith was a money digger but not profitable
  • Members support the church financially and help the poor
  • The fundamental principles include the testimony of Jesus Christ

history.author: Patten, David Wyman (1799-1838)
history.citation: Patten, David W. “To the Saints scattered abroad.” Elders’ Journal of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints (Far West, Missouri) 1, no. 3 (July 1838): 39–42. [?][?]
history.teaser:
David W. Patten’s letter to the Saints, discussing the significance of the dispensation received by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints.

Key Points:

  • Discusses the greatest of all dispensations revealed to the Church
  • References prophecies about Israel and the Gentiles
  • Explains the concept of the “dispensation of the fullness of times”
  • Describes the deliverer coming out of Zion
  • Highlights the recovery of the house of Jacob
  • Details the lineage of dispensations from Adam to the present
  • Emphasizes the authority and ordinances of this dispensation
  • Warns against sinning against the authority of this dispensation

history.document: Argument to argument where to find it
history.citation: “Argument to argument where to find it; Ridicule to ridicule, and scorn to scorn.” Elders’ Journal of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints (Far West, Missouri) 1, no. 4 (August 1838): 59–60.
history.teaser:
An editorial from the Elders’ Journal condemning the hypocrisy of religious leaders and their association with disreputable characters.

Key Points:

  • Modern priests compared to Satan’s making
  • Philastes Hurlburt’s hypocrisy highlighted
  • Hurlburt became favored by priests after being expelled for adultery
  • Hurlburt authored a book against the church, originally credited to E. D. Howe
  • Asahel Howe, related to E. D. Howe, had a criminal background
  • Priests publishing lies by disreputable people
  • Association with bad characters questions one’s integrity
  • Editorial concludes that such priests will be judged alongside the wicked

history.author: Parish, Warren
history.citation: “Mormonism.” Warren Parrish to E. Holmes, 11 August 1838. The Evangelist (Carthage,Ohio) 6, no. 10 (1 October 1838): 226–27.
history.teaser:
A letter from Warren Parrish, a former high-ranking member of the LDS Church, expressing his strong disillusionment with the movement and its leaders.

Key Points:

  • Parrish no longer believes in the divine origin of the Book of Mormon.
  • Martin Harris, a key witness, admitted he only saw the plates in vision.
  • Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon are moving to Missouri after failures in Kirtland.
  • Joseph Smith is accused of planning to propagate his religion by force.
  • Orson Pratt was last known to be preaching Mormonism in New York.
  • William McLellin, Oliver Cowdery, the Whitmers, and others have left the Church.
  • Lyman Johnson, an apostle, left and was allegedly targeted for assassination by Church members.

history.document: Review of Parley P. Pratt, A Voice of Warning
history.citation: Review of Parley P. Pratt, A Voice of Warning. Christian Examiner (November 1838): 270–72.
history.teaser:
A critical review of Parley P. Pratt’s A Voice of Warning, discussing its claims and the broader implications of Mormonism.

Key Points:

  • The review criticizes Mormonism as a mischievous imposture
  • Mormons are described as gathered in force and armed
  • Book of Mormon claimed to be translated by inspiration
  • Scriptural evidence is presented to support Book of Mormon claims
  • Book of Mormon supposedly reveals important unknown history
  • Claims to explain the origin of American Indians
  • Contains prophecies concerning the present generation
  • Mentions a political end goal of gathering to build a New Jerusalem

history.citation: “Mormonism.” Supplement to the Connecticut Courant (Hartford, Connecticut) 5, no. 22 (15 December 1838): 175–76.
history.teaser:
A critical and satirical account of the origins of Mormonism as reported in the Connecticut Courant, presenting Joseph Smith in a disparaging light.

Key Points:

  • Portrays Joseph Smith as an “idiot” visited by an angel
  • Describes the discovery of golden plates and a pair of spectacles
  • Mockingly recounts the translation and publication process of the Book of Mormon
  • Claims the original manuscript was lost and had to be rewritten
  • Alleges differences between the original and rewritten pages
  • Describes disbelief and skepticism surrounding the golden plates
  • Details the formation of the Mormon community and their practices
  • Criticizes the Book of Mormon’s language and content

history.author: M'Chesney, James
history.document: Supplement to an Antidote to Mormonism, &c
history.citation: M’Chesney, James. Supplement to an Antidote to Mormonism, &c. , 1–4. Brooklyn, 1839.
history.teaser:
A critique of Mormonism and its practices, focusing on the perceived dangers and the author’s skepticism towards its teachings and fundraising efforts.

Key Points:

  • James M’Chesney stands by his previous publication against Mormonism
  • Compares Mormonism to other delusions, emphasizing its foundation on hatred to virtue
  • Criticizes Mormon fundraising for widows and orphans of Missouri conflict
  • Questions the legitimacy and morality of Mormon practices
  • Describes the Book of Mormon as a humbug and a modern speculation
  • Details Joseph Smith’s method of translation as dubious
  • Comments on Mormon attempts to establish Zion and their conflicts in Missouri
  • Warns of the broader societal dangers posed by Mormon influence

history.author: Stevenson, H.
history.citation: Stevenson, H. A Lecture on Mormonism, 3-32. Newcastle: J. Blackwell and Co., 1839.
history.teaser:
A lecture criticizing Mormonism, delivered in Alston in 1838, focusing on the Book of Mormon’s authenticity and Mormon practices.

Key Points:

  • Lecture aimed to prove the Book of Mormon a forgery.
  • Claims no historical evidence supports the Book of Mormon.
  • Argues the Book of Mormon contradicts known American history.
  • Mormonism described as a system of absurdities.
  • Claims Mormonism does not worship Jesus Christ directly.
  • Notes direct quotations from the New Testament in the Book of Mormon.
  • Describes Mormonism as a threat to all Christian denominations.
  • Encourages unity among Christian sects against Mormonism.

history.author: Caswall, Henry, 1810-1870
history.citation: Caswall, Henry. America, and the American Church, 322–23. London: J.G. & F. Rivington, 1839.
history.teaser:
A critical account by Henry Caswall on the origins and beliefs of the Mormon faith as described in his book “America, and the American Church”.

Key Points:

  • Describes Mormonism as a gross imposture
  • Mormon belief in American Indians’ descent from Israel’s lost tribes
  • Claims of ancient Israelite crossing to America and hiding golden plates
  • Angel allegedly reveals location of golden plates in 1829
  • Joseph Smith found and translated the plates into the Book of Mormon
  • Original golden plates never produced
  • Mormonites claim America (beyond Mississippi) as the Land of Promise
  • Mormons engaged a Hebrew teacher, emphasizing study of Hebrew

history.author: Corrill, John, b. 1794
history.document: A Brief History of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
history.citation: Corrill, John. A Brief History of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, 1–14, 16. St. Louis: for the author, 1839.
history.teaser:
An early account of the LDS Church’s history and doctrines, written by a former member seeking to explain his involvement.

Key Points:

  • Corrill was frequently asked about his involvement with the Mormons
  • He aims to explain his motives and observations in joining the LDS Church
  • Encounters with early missionaries sparked his interest in the Church
  • Initial skepticism turned into curiosity after Sidney Rigden’s conversion
  • Investigations led Corrill to believe in the need for modern prophets
  • The Book of Mormon’s origin and witnesses were critically examined
  • Scriptural comparisons influenced Corrill’s belief in additional revelation
  • Moral teachings of the LDS Church aligned with biblical principles

history.document: “How a Mormon Preacher tried to walk”
history.citation: “How a Mormon Preacher Tried to Walk on Water.” Livingston Register (Geneseo, NewYork) 16, no. 784 (15 January 1839).
history.teaser:
A newspaper article recounting an event where a Mormon preacher attempted to walk on water and tragically drowned.

Key Points:

  • Mormon preacher planned to walk on water to preach
  • Event attracted both believers and skeptics
  • Opponents sabotaged a hidden plank bridge
  • Preacher fell into a swampy part of the pond and drowned
  • Spectators were shocked and horrified by the outcome
  • Incident led to the decline of Mormonism in that area

history.author: Storrs, John
history.citation: Storrs, John. “Mormonism.” Boston Recorder (Boston, Massachusetts) 24 (19 April 1839).
history.teaser:
An article by John Storrs in the Boston Recorder discussing Mormonism and presenting a narrative claiming the Book of Mormon was derived from Solomon Spaulding’s manuscript.

Key Points:

  • John Storrs views Mormonism as a delusion
  • Storrs aims to expose the origins of the Book of Mormon
  • Solomon Spaulding’s widow claims he authored the original manuscript
  • Spaulding’s manuscript, “Manuscript Found,” is suggested as the source
  • Spaulding’s narrative was meant to be a historical romance
  • Spaulding’s manuscript was known to his community
  • Connection between Spaulding’s manuscript and Sidney Rigdon suggested
  • Document aims to prevent delusion and expose deceit

history.citation: “The Mormon Bible.” Christian Register and Boston Observer (Boston,Massachusetts) 18, no. 970 (4 May 1839).
history.teaser:
An article from a Boston newspaper discussing the origins of the Book of Mormon, suggesting it’s a product of both a cultivated mind and gross superstition.

Key Points:

  • Article from the Boston Recorder discusses the Mormon Bible’s origin
  • Book seen as a mix of cultivated production and gross superstition
  • Narrative procured by Rev. Mr. Stow, who encountered Mormonism
  • Stow’s experiences suggest he’s witnessed Mormonism’s “grossest forms”

history.author: C.
history.citation: C. “For the Register and Observer.” Christian Register and Boston Observer (Boston) 18, no. 971 (11 May 1839).
history.teaser:
An 1839 article questioning the origins of the Book of Mormon and the legitimacy of the claims made by Matilda Davison regarding its connection to her late husband Solomon Spaulding’s manuscript.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism described as speculative and rapidly adopted
  • Mormons portrayed as victims of persecution
  • Question raised about the origin of the Mormon Bible
  • Matilda Davison’s letter suggests a connection to Spaulding’s manuscript
  • Article questions the proof of Davison’s claims
  • Public unaware if the Spaulding manuscript was compared to the Book of Mormon
  • Questions why Mormons continue to grow despite controversy
  • Author seeks answers for personal and public clarification
