  • Asserts Jesus and other figures are portrayed using inexplicable language
  • Questions the logical consistency of the narrative in the Book of Mormon
  • Concludes by likening the Book of Mormon to the Koran as an imposture

history.author: White, Joseph
history.citation: White, Joseph. “The Latter-day Saints. To the Editor of the Cheltenham Free Press.” Latter-day Saints’ Millennial Star (Manchester, England) 2, no. 6 (October 1841): 88–89.
history.teaser:
A letter defending the Latter-day Saints against accusations published in the Cheltenham Journal.

Key Points:

  • Nauvoo misrepresented in Cheltenham Journal
  • Clarifies geographical distance between Nauvoo and Missouri
  • Interview with Mrs. Margretts about her Nauvoo experience
  • Nauvoo described as a city with future potential
  • Margretts did not ask Joseph Smith about the Book of Mormon plates
  • Mr. and Mrs. Embry support Latter-day Saint doctrines
  • Claims against the Saints called lies and slander
  • Letter aims to correct public misconceptions

history.author: Snow, E., and Benjamin Winchester
history.document: An Address to the Citizens of Salem (Mass.) and Vicinity
history.citation: Snow, E. and Winchester, Benjamin. “An Address to the Citizens of Salem (Mass.)And Vicinity.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 2, no. 24 (1 October 1841): 574–76.
history.teaser:
An address aimed at clarifying misconceptions and defending the practices and beliefs of the Latter Day Saint movement.

Key Points:

  • Intended to uphold Christian principles and encourage open-mindedness
  • Emphasizes liberty of conscience and respectful religious expression
  • Rejects the use of slander and persecution in religious debate
  • Calls for scriptural investigation of religious matters
  • Addresses and refutes negative rumors and accusations against the LDS Church
  • Denies communal living and polygamy among early church practices
  • Asserts lawfulness and patriotism within the LDS community
  • Clarifies adherence to and reverence for the Scriptures

history.author: Pratt, Parley P. (Parley Parker), 1807-1857
history.document: A Letter to the Queen of England
history.citation: Pratt, Parley P. “A Letter to the Queen of England.” Times & Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3,no. 2 (15 November 1841): 591–96.
history.teaser:
Parley P. Pratt’s letter to Queen Victoria, discussing the impending global revolution foretold by scripture, and the significance of the Book of Mormon in understanding these prophecies.

Key Points:

  • Pratt addresses Queen Victoria, highlighting the momentous era she lives in.
  • Discusses a global revolution, more significant than any before.
  • References Daniel’s prophecies to explain the political and religious changes to come.
  • Claims England and its government are part of biblical prophecy.
  • Introduces the Book of Mormon as a key to understanding these events.
  • Links the discovery of the Book of Mormon to a larger divine plan for the world.
  • Urges repentance and acceptance of the Book of Mormon’s teachings.
  • Warns of the consequences of ignoring these divine messages.

history.author: Snow, E., and Benjamin Winchester.
history.document: An Address to the Citizens of Salem (Mass.) and Vicinity
history.citation: Snow, E. and Winchester, Benjamin. “An Address to the Citizens of Salem (Mass.)And Vicinity.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 1 (15 November 1841):578–84.
history.teaser:
An extensive address by E. Snow and B. Winchester to the citizens of Salem, Massachusetts, detailing the beliefs and doctrines of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

Key Points:

  • Belief in God the Father and Jesus Christ as co-eternal and Savior
  • Emphasis on faith, repentance, and baptism by immersion
  • Doctrine of receiving the Holy Ghost through the laying on of hands
  • Church organization according to the New Testament pattern
  • Expectation of spiritual gifts and miracles as in ancient times
  • Preaching of the gospel to all nations as a sign of Christ’s second coming
  • Belief in ongoing revelation and the Book of Mormon as another testament of Jesus Christ
  • Call for examination and acceptance of their testimony and doctrines

history.author: Pratt, Parley P. (Parley Parker), 1807-1857
history.document: Wholesale Conversion of Methodists to Infidelity
history.citation: Pratt, Parley P. “Wholesale Conversion of Methodists to Infidelity.” Latter-day Saints Millennial Star (Manchester, England) 2, no. 8 (December 1841): 114–15.
history.teaser:
An account by Parley P. Pratt discussing a debate on the legitimacy of the Book of Mormon and its broader implications on faith.

Key Points:

  • Discussion held in Manchester between Rev. Mr. Sleep and Elder Wm. Hardman.
  • Rev. Mr. Sleep denounced the Book of Mormon, calling it devil’s work.
  • Comparison made with Biblical figures who were commanded to kill.
  • Methodist preacher and followers accused of rejecting the Old and New Testaments.
  • Debate escalates into outright rejection of religious texts by some attendees.
  • Meeting ended in chaos, with attendees showing infidelity towards sacred texts.
  • Uncertainty over whether Mr. Sleep and his followers would form a new group.
  • Editorial remarks reflect on the unfortunate turn towards disbelief.

history.author: R., L. H.
history.citation: “Prevalence of Mormonism.” Christian Advocate and Journal (New York) 16, no. 17 (8 December 1841).
history.teaser:
An 1841 article discussing the surprising spread of Mormonism both in the United States and abroad, highlighting its growth and the public’s reaction.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon published in 1830
  • Mormonism spread to nearly every city and state in the US
  • Mormons number thousands in England, with missions worldwide
  • Joseph Smith unlikely anticipated such growth
  • Mormons rallied to build Nauvoo House and temple
  • Sect gained sympathy through persecution
  • Mormonism flourished despite opposition
  • Concerns raised about the potential spread of Mormonism

history.citation: “The Mormons.” Auburn Journal and Advertiser (22 December 1841).
history.teaser:
An article from the Auburn Journal and Advertiser discussing the surprising success and growing influence of the Mormon community in 1841.

Key Points:

  • Mormons’ success is astonishing and deeply interesting
  • Their numbers have reached around one hundred thousand
  • Many Mormons are intelligent and formerly high-standing Christians
  • Men of property are joining, adding wealth to the community
  • Illinois Legislature granted them the right to maintain a standing army
  • Smith and Rigdon ordained twelve Apostles
  • The Book of Mormon claimed as an additional revelation
  • The manuscript believed to be a stolen work of fiction

history.citation: “Mormons and Mormonism.” Christian Register and Boston Observer (Boston) 20,no. 52 (25 December 1841).
history.teaser:
An 1841 article offering a critical and detailed account of Joseph Smith and the early Mormon community in Nauvoo, Illinois.

Key Points:

  • Witness account from a gentleman in St. Louis about Mormons
  • Mormon community in Nauvoo numbers over 5,000
  • Many converts coming from England
  • Mormons exhibit a self-sacrificing spirit and endure for their faith
  • Leaders decry human knowledge, little provision for education
  • Mormons claim to be the only true Christians
  • Nauvoo viewed as the future dwelling of Christ on earth
  • Joseph Smith considered a good manager by himself

history.citation: Anti-Mormon Almanac for 1842, 4. New York, 1841.
history.teaser:
An Anti-Mormon publication from 1841 aiming to discredit the Book of Mormon and its followers by alleging it supports criminal behavior.

Key Points:

  • Claims to expose treasonable tendency and wicked imposture of Mormonism
  • Alleges Mormonism authorizes theft, robbery, high treason, and murder
  • Includes astronomical calculations and facts against the LDS Church
  • Cites Public Document No. 189 published by order of Congress
  • An old Indian criticizes the Book of Mormon
  • Comparison made between the Bible and the Book of Mormon
  • Claims the devil authored the Book of Mormon
  • Joseph Smith accused of publishing the Book of Mormon as divine revelation

history.author: Crawford, Robert P.
history.document: An Index or Reference to the Second and Third Editions of the Book of Mormon
history.citation: Crawford, Robert P. An Index or Reference to the Second and Third Editions of the Book of Mormon, Alphabetically Arranged, 4–21. Philadelphia: Brown, Bicking & Guilbert, 1842. PREFACE. INDEX, OR REFERENCE
history.teaser:
An index created by Robert P. Crawford to assist in navigating the second and third editions of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Designed for convenience of church members and others
  • Alphabetically arranged for easy reference
  • Includes significant events and concepts from the Book of Mormon
  • Examples include “Abridgment of Nephi,” “A great and marvellous work”
  • Mentions “A man in white robes” referring to John
  • References to “Angels become devils” and “A Bible a Bible”
  • Notable entries like “Alma believed Abinadi and repented”
  • Includes “Appointment of Judges,” “Amlici made king”

history.author: Clark, John A. (John Alonzo), 1801-1843
history.document: A Letter Written by Professor Anthon
history.citation: “A Letter Written by Professor Anthon.” Charles Anthon to Rev. Coit, New York, 3 April 1841. John A. Clark, Gleanings By the Way, 232–38. Philadelphia: W. J. & J. K. Simon, 1842.
history.teaser:
A letter from Charles Anthon, detailing his encounter with Martin Harris concerning characters from the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Anthon was asked about his alleged support for Mormonism.
  • Martin Harris sought Anthon’s help to decipher characters.
  • Anthon deemed the characters a hoax and clumsy.
  • Harris described a gold book with unknown characters.
  • Anthon refused a translated volume of the “Golden Bible”.
  • Harris eventually sold his farm for the book’s publication.
  • Anthon suspected Smith himself might have visited him.
  • Anthon aims to expose the delusions of Mormonism.

history.author: Kidder, Daniel P.
history.citation: Kidder, Daniel P. Mormonism and the Mormons: A Historical View of the Rise and Progress of the Sect Self-Styled Latter-day Saints, 3–19, 36, 49, 51–61, 253–311, 329–337. New York:Lane and Sandford, 1842.
history.teaser:
An early critical examination of Mormonism and its founder, Joseph Smith, by Daniel P. Kidder, detailing the origins, beliefs, and practices of the Latter-day Saints.

Key Points:

  • Introduction to the rise and progress of the Latter-day Saints
  • Addresses departures from traditional faiths to Mormonism
  • Kidder’s personal encounter with Joseph Smith and Mormons
  • Book aims to provide a historical view of Mormonism
  • Details the sect’s beliefs, practices, and controversies
  • Examines the Book of Mormon and its origins
  • Critical of Joseph Smith’s revelations and leadership
  • Discusses the establishment and growth of Mormon communities

history.source: The Eastern and Western States of America
history.author: Buckingham, J.S. (James Silk), 1786-1855
history.document: The Eastern and Western States of America
history.citation: Buckingham, J. S. The Eastern and Western States of America, vol. 3, 190–94. London:Fisher, Son, & Company, 1842.
history.teaser:
An account of J.S. Buckingham’s observations on the Mormon community and Joseph Smith during his travels in America, highlighting early Mormon settlement challenges and Smith’s leadership.

Key Points:

  • Mormons established at Keokuck near the Des Moines Rapids
  • Joe Smith claimed to find and translate the Book of Mormon
  • Mormons aimed to build a New Jerusalem in Missouri
  • Conflict with Missouri settlers led to Mormons’ expulsion
  • Mormons resettled in Commerce, Illinois, numbers exceeding 5,000
  • Described as averse to labor, believing in a Promised Land
  • Smith described as ignorant but sincere, failed to gain support from President Van Buren
  • Smith encouraged followers to vote against Van Buren

history.author: Turner, J. B. (Jonathan Baldwin), 1805-1898
history.citation: Turner, J. B. Mormonism in All Ages: Or the Rise, Progress, and Causes of Mormonism: with the Biography of Its Author and Founder, Joseph Smith Junior, 1–33, 65–206, 210–22,300–304. New York: Platt & Peters, 1842. A WORD TO JOSEPH SMITH, JUNIOR, AT NAUVOO, ILLINOIS.
history.teaser:
An early critical examination of Mormonism, including a biography of its founder, Joseph Smith Jr., by J.B. Turner.

Key Points:

  • Early critical overview of Mormonism and its origins
  • Includes a biography of Joseph Smith Jr.
  • Claims Mormonism had 100,000 adherents in the US, 10,000 in Great Britain
  • Argues that Mormonism’s absurdities need to be exposed
  • Describes Mormonism as dangerous to political and religious purity

history.citation: Doctrine of the Mormonites, 1–4. London: J. Wertheimer & Company, 1842.
history.teaser:
A critical 1842 pamphlet from London examining and disputing the doctrines of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

Key Points:

  • Claims LDS doctrines contradict and supplement the Bible
  • Asserts the Book of Mormon and Doctrine and Covenants as sources of LDS teachings
  • Questions the need for additional revelation beyond the Bible
  • Argues LDS teachings undermine the completeness of the Bible
  • Criticizes the LDS view of faith and salvation
  • Accuses LDS teachings of promoting works over grace
  • Suggests LDS teachings include disloyalty to government and acceptance of slavery
  • Challenges the authenticity and authority of LDS scriptures

history.author: Hardy, John
history.citation: Hardy, John. Hypocrisy Exposed, or J.V. Himes Weighed in the Balances of Truth, Honesty and Common Sense, and Found Wanting; Being a Reply to a Pamphlet put forth By Him Entitled Mormon Delusions and Monstrosities, 3–12. Boston: Albert Morgan, 1842. [*unreadable in copy*][*unreadable in copy*][*unreadable in copy*][?]
history.teaser:
A detailed rebuttal by John Hardy to J.V. Himes’ criticisms of the Latter Day Saint movement, focusing on accusations of hypocrisy and misrepresentation.

Key Points:

  • John Hardy responds to J.V. Himes’ anti-Mormon pamphlet.
  • Highlights the biased criticisms from religious opponents.
  • Refutes claims against the Book of Mormon and Joseph Smith.
  • Accuses Himes of hypocrisy and spreading falsehoods.
  • Defends the prophetic role and revelations in the Latter Day Saint movement.
  • Challenges the portrayal of the Book of Mormon’s origins.
  • Addresses the priesthood and gifts of the spirit.
  • Criticizes Himes for inconsistency and misquoting scriptures.

history.author: Adams, George J.
history.citation: George J. Adams to Parley P. Pratt, 14 December 1841. Latter-day Saints’ Millennial Star (Manchester, England) 2, no. 9 (January 1842): 141–43.
history.teaser:
A letter from George J. Adams to Parley P. Pratt describing Adams’ experiences defending the doctrines of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints in public discussions in England.

Key Points:

  • Adams had public discussions defending LDS doctrines in Liverpool.
  • Used the Bible to prove the Book of Mormon and LDS principles.
  • Opponents resorted to character attacks and false accusations.
  • A glass of poison was presented as a challenge to Adams.
  • Adams insisted on discussing doctrine, not personal attacks.
  • Over half of the audience supported LDS doctrines by show of hands.
  • Engaged in respectful discussions with a Socialist and a Wesleyan minister.
  • Adams’ farewell address in Liverpool was well received.

history.document: Evidences in Proof of the Book of Mormon
history.citation: “Evidences in Proof of the Book of Mormon.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 5 (1 January 1842): 640–44.
history.teaser:
An article from the Times and Seasons newspaper discussing the evidences supporting the truth of the Book of Mormon, particularly through archaeological findings and comparisons with American Antiquities.

Key Points:

  • Comparison of ancient American fortifications with Book of Mormon descriptions
  • Book of Mormon published before Josiah Priest’s American Antiquities
  • Descriptions of military defenses in both sources align closely
  • Evidence suggests Nephites built ancient American fortifications
  • Gadianton robbers’ strongholds described in both Book of Mormon and recent discoveries
  • Book of Mormon’s accuracy supported by archaeological findings
  • Claims of divine inspiration and authority for the LDS Church
  • Rapid spread and acceptance of the Book of Mormon as divine

history.author: Thompson, Charles Blancher, b. 1814
history.citation: “Extract.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 6 (15 January 1842): 657–59.
history.teaser:
A proclamation and warning published in the Times and Seasons that emphasizes the divine significance of America and its relation to biblical prophecy, the destiny of the Native American peoples, and the importance of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • America was given to the son of Jacob by God
  • Jesus Christ appeared to the ancestors of American Indians
  • Nations must serve God to possess the land
  • Columbus was inspired by God to discover America
  • The American Constitution was inspired to establish liberty
  • The Book of Mormon is true and divinely inspired
  • Warning to Gentiles to repent and accept the Book of Mormon
  • The mistreatment of Native Americans and call for justice

history.author: M., R. T.
history.citation: M., R. T. “The Mormons.” Religious Monitor and Evangelical Repository ( 18 January 1842): 345–46.
history.teaser:
An 1842 critique of Mormon beliefs and practices, raising concerns about their growing influence and political power.

Key Points:

  • Mormons have twelve stakes for building temples
  • Joseph Smith considered a prophet on par with Isaiah
  • Claims of exclusive truthfulness of the Mormon church
  • Baptism by immersion by an authorized person is mandatory
  • Direct revelation needed to preach or administer ordinances
  • Zion or New Jerusalem is located in Missouri
  • Indians considered lost tribes of Israel to be gathered
  • Joseph Smith’s translation of the Bible includes significant alterations

history.author: Nicklin, Levi O. C.
history.citation: Levi O. C. Nicklin to Walter Scott, Pittsburgh, 18 January 1841. “Mormonism inPittsburgh.” The Evangelist (Carthage, Ohio) 10, no. 2 (1 February 1842): 32–34.
history.teaser:
A letter describing a public challenge between a Mormon apostle, John E. Page, and a local religious figure, brother Church, over the authenticity of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Public interest was high for a Mormon preaching in Pittsburgh
  • John E. Page, a Mormon apostle, claimed Book of Mormon’s divinity
  • Page referenced discoveries in South America as evidence
  • Clergy initially avoided confrontation, believing Mormonism’s flaws would be self-evident
  • Brother Church accepted the challenge to discuss the Book of Mormon
  • Page shifted discussion to other topics; Church focused on Book of Mormon
  • Page struggled under scrutiny during the public debate
  • Local religious activities continue to thrive, with new baptisms reported

history.citation: “Ruins in Central America” Latter-day Saints’ Millennial Star (Manchester, England) 2,no. 11 (March 1842): 161–65.
history.teaser:
An article linking the ruins discovered in Central America by Mr. Stephens to the ancient Nephites described in the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Mr. Stephens’ explorations reveal remarkable ancient edifices in Central America.
  • Stephens concludes these cities were built by races present during the Spanish invasion.
  • Ruins suggest a highly advanced, indigenous civilization.
  • The article suggests the ruins are of Nephite cities mentioned in the Book of Mormon.
  • Link between modern discovery and ancient records claimed to be revealed by God.
  • The Book of Mormon provides history of a civilization unknown to the rest of the world.
  • Names of Nephite cities and leaders are claimed to match those found by Stephens.
  • The article asserts the Book of Mormon explains the “mystery” of these ancient ruins.

history.author: Smith, Joseph, 1805-1844
history.citation: Smith, Joseph. “Church History.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 9 (1 March 1842): 706–10.
history.teaser:
An account by Joseph Smith detailing the origins and beliefs of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, written for a non-member audience.

Key Points:

  • Written at the request of John Wentworth for a history project
  • Smith’s early life and the initial revelation in a grove
  • The visitation by an angel revealing the Book of Mormon
  • The translation of the Book of Mormon through Urim and Thummim
  • Persecutions faced by the early church and migrations
  • Foundation of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
  • Expulsion from Missouri under Governor Boggs’ extermination order
  • Establishment in Nauvoo, Illinois, and the growth of the church

history.citation: “History of Mormonism.” Southern Quarterly Review (New Orleans) 1, no. 2 (April 1842): 398–413.
history.teaser:
An early critical examination and denunciation of Mormonism and its founder, Joseph Smith, from a secular perspective.

Key Points:

  • Describes Mormonism as a form of mass delusion and imposture.
  • Joseph Smith criticized as a cunning and ambitious impostor.
  • Mormonism’s rapid growth and establishment of communities noted.
  • Mormon missionaries’ success in England highlighted.
  • Discusses the dangers of credulity and lack of critical thinking.
  • Compares Mormonism’s absurdities to historical superstitions and myths.
  • Expresses concern over the sophisticated use of press by Mormons.
  • Critiques the shallow nature of what is often termed “education”.

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 12 (15 April 1842):753–54.
history.teaser:
An account of Joseph Smith’s vision of the angel Nephi, detailing the calling and revelations pertaining to the translation of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith describes a vision of a messenger from God
  • Messenger identified as Nephi, later corrected to Moroni
  • Revelation of a book written on gold plates
  • Introduction to the Urim and Thummim for translation
  • Quotes prophecies and scriptures about the coming events
  • Commanded not to show the plates except to those commanded
  • Receives a vision of where the plates were deposited
  • Warned about Satan’s temptation and the importance of purity of intent

history.citation: “The Mormons.” Western Christian Advocate (Cincinnati, Ohio) 9, no. 1 (22 April 1842).
history.teaser:
A letter published in the Western Christian Advocate detailing Charles Anthon’s encounter with early Mormonism and his skepticism towards it.

Key Points:

  • Anthon denies being a proselyte to Mormonism
  • Anthon considered the characters shown to him a hoax
  • A countryman presented a transcript of characters for examination
  • The characters were a mix of various alphabetic symbols
  • A story of golden plates and spectacles with translation abilities
  • Anthon advised against selling property for publishing the book
  • Anthon refused to accept a copy of the “golden bible”
  • Anthon suspects the countryman was Joseph Smith himself

history.document: A Short and Easy Method with the Mormonites
history.citation: “A Short and Easy Method with the Mormonites.” Anti-Socialist Gazette (Chester) no. 8 (1 May 1842): 142.
history.teaser:
An 1842 critique in the Anti-Socialist Gazette of the Book of Mormon, accusing it of being a blasphemous parody of the Bible.

Key Points:

  • Accuses the Book of Mormon of copying the Bible’s translation word for word
  • Describes the Book of Mormon as a blasphemous parody
  • Points out that it includes even minor errors found in the Bible
  • Asserts that claimed divine origin of Book of Mormon is exposed as a deception
  • Recommends pressing the issue of identical translations to confound believers
  • Highlights the absurdity of the narrative found in the Book of Mormon
  • Compares the Book of Mormon’s account unfavorably to the Bible’s sublimity
  • Specifically criticizes the narrative of barges built by the brother of Jared

history.document: A Catacomb of Mummies Found in Kentucky
history.citation: “A Catacomb of Mummies Found in Kentucky.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo,Illinois) 3, no. 13 (2 May 1842): 781–82.
history.teaser:
An article from the LDS periodical Times and Seasons connecting the discovery of a catacomb of mummies in Kentucky to the Book of Mormon narrative.

Key Points:

  • Discovery of a catacomb in Lexington, Kentucky in 1775
  • Catacomb contained mummies preserved similarly to ancient Egyptians
  • Discovery linked to ancient town of great extent and magnificence
  • Speculation on the origin and preservation methods of the mummies
  • Article suggests Book of Mormon could solve the mystery
  • Book of Mormon links descendants of Israel to America
  • Embalming knowledge possibly transmitted from Jerusalem
  • Finding of mummies seen as evidence for the Book of Mormon

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 13 (2 May 1842): 771–73.
history.teaser:
An account from Joseph Smith about the early history of his life, including the discovery and translation of the Book of Mormon plates.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith recounts obeying a divine messenger’s command
  • Details the discovery of the plates in a stone box
  • Forbidden to take the plates until the appointed time
  • Describes annual visits to the plate’s location for instruction
  • Joseph’s early life involved laboring and moving due to persecution
  • Marriage to Emma Hale amidst family opposition
  • Received assistance from Martin Harris for the translation work
  • Account of Martin Harris’s consultation with scholars about the characters

history.citation: “Mormonism and Mesmerism.” New York Herald (New York) 7, no. 413 (10 May 1842).
history.teaser:
An 1842 New York Herald article discussing Mons. L. de Bonneville’s arrival in New York, who combined mesmerism with Mormon beliefs.

Key Points:

  • Mons. L. de Bonneville arrives in New York, associated with Mormons
  • Formerly a professor at Harvard, now a proponent of Mesmerism and Mormonism
  • Claims to have discovered the true Mormon mode of revelation through Mesmerism
  • Teaches multiple languages and can cure various disorders
  • Abandoned a lucrative position at Harvard for his beliefs
  • Advised to lecture on the connection between Mormonism and Mesmerism

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 14 (16 May 1842):785–86.
history.teaser:
A segment from the “History of Joseph Smith” published in the Times and Seasons detailing the loss of the first 116 pages of the Book of Mormon manuscript.

Key Points:

  • Martin Harris returned to assist Joseph Smith in translation
  • Harris wrote 116 pages of manuscript
  • Harris repeatedly asked to show the writings to others
  • Joseph Smith inquired of the Lord, eventually granted permission with conditions
  • Harris broke his covenant, showing the writings to others and losing them
  • The Urim and Thummim were temporarily taken from Smith
  • A revelation was received chastising Smith and Harris but reaffirming the work’s continuation
  • The revelation also emphasizes the importance and future of the work among the Lamanites

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 15 (1 June 1842):801–4.
history.teaser:
A publication detailing a revelation given to Joseph Smith, describing challenges faced during the translation of the Book of Mormon and assurances given by God regarding the continuation and protection of his work.

Key Points:

  • Revelation given after the loss of the initial manuscript
  • Joseph Smith warned against the consequences of trusting the wrong individuals
  • Satan’s influence on people to alter and discredit Joseph’s work highlighted
  • God assures protection against Satan’s attempts to thwart the work
  • Joseph Smith instructed not to retranslate the lost portion
  • Wisdom and commandments given to Joseph Smith for translation work
  • Christ’s intention to gather and protect his followers emphasized
  • Doctrine of the church defined by repentance and coming unto Christ

history.author: Tucker, J. N. T.
history.citation: Tucker, J. N. T. “Mormonism—Some Curious Facts.” Signs of the Times, An Expositor of Prophecy, 3, no. 10 (8 June 1842): 79–80.
history.teaser:
An article by J.N.T. Tucker detailing skepticism and accusations of deceit during the publication of the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Tucker was a printer during the Book of Mormon’s publication
  • Martin Harris funded the printing
  • Printers tested the translators by claiming to lose a sheet
  • A replacement sheet did not match the original
  • No workers at the printing office converted to Mormonism
  • Tucker claims to witness impostures and false miracles
  • Martin Harris’s wife refused to follow him due to his actions
  • Tucker warns of deception as a sign of the end times

history.citation: “Traits of the Mosaic History, Found Among the Azteca Nations.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 16 (15 June 1842): 8 18–20.
history.teaser:
An article discussing the parallels between Mosaic history and Aztec traditions, suggesting common spiritual and historical narratives.

Key Points:

  • Article starts with an Aztec account of the deluge.
  • Draws parallels between Aztec and Biblical stories of Noah.
  • Discusses the confusion of languages, similar to Babel.
  • References to animals and grains saved, paralleling Noah’s Ark.
  • Cites Baron Humboldt’s research on Mexican traditions.
  • Paintings depict the flood and confusion of languages.
  • Links between Aztec traditions and the Book of Mormon.
  • Discussion of the migration to America and the preservation of languages.

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 16 (15 June 1842):817– 18.
history.teaser:
An installment from the serialized “History of Joseph Smith” that appeared in the “Times and Seasons” newspaper, discussing revelations received by Joseph Smith.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith worked on a farm before continuing translation
  • Revelation received for Joseph Smith, Sr. in February 1829
  • Encouragement to serve God with all heart, might, mind, and strength
  • Qualities that qualify someone for the work of God
  • Revelation given in March 1829 concerning Martin Harris
  • Joseph Smith commanded to show the plates to select individuals
  • Testimony of three witnesses foretold
  • Warnings of consequences for unbelief and disobedience

history.author: Lee, John D., A. Young, and Samuel B. Frost
history.citation: Lee, John D., A. Young, and Samuel B. Frost. Letter from Tennessee. Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 16 (15 June 1842): 820–21.
history.teaser:
A letter detailing the efforts and challenges faced by LDS missionaries in Tennessee, including encounters with false teachings and spiritual manifestations.

Key Points:

  • Report of false teachings in Putnam County, Tennessee
  • False teachers claimed supernatural powers and distorted LDS teachings
  • Described bizarre and violent spiritual manifestations among converts
  • John D. Lee and companions work to correct false teachings
  • Encountered threats of violence and opposition
  • Lee and companions proclaimed against the false spirits and teachings
  • Reported success in restoring sick through faith and priesthood power
  • 28 baptisms in Rutherford, Smith, and Putnam counties

history.document: “A new edition of the Book of Mormon”
history.citation: “A New Edition of the Book of Mormon.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3,no. 16 (15 June 1842): 822.
history.teaser:
An announcement for the release of a new edition of the Book of Mormon in 1842.

Key Points:

  • New edition of the Book of Mormon has been printed
  • Will be bound and ready for sale in a few days

history.author: A Disciple
history.citation: A Disciple. [Question for John E. Page.] Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (17 June 1842).
history.teaser:
A public challenge in a newspaper to John E. Page, an LDS Elder, comparing teachings in LDS scriptures with the Bible.

Key Points:

  • Questioning the relevance of John E. Page’s self-promotion
  • Comparing LDS teachings to traditional Christian teachings
  • Doctrine and Covenants vs. Matthew: Treatment of enemies
  • Book of Mormon vs. Matthew: Response to evil and violence
  • Book of Mormon vs. Romans: Dealing with enemies
  • Seeking clarification on LDS teachings

history.author: Page, John E.
history.citation: Page, John E. [Reply to A Disciple.] Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (20 June 1842).
history.teaser:
John E. Page responds to misinterpretations of Mormon scripture in a Pittsburgh newspaper.

Key Points:

  • John E. Page confirms the accuracy of page references
  • Illustrates misinterpretation using out-of-context Bible quotes
  • Compares scripture misinterpretation to that of LDS texts
  • Highlights the short history of LDS scripture compared to the Bible
  • Notes difficulty in correcting misinterpretations without access to texts
  • Challenges the critic to reveal their real name
  • Defends the integrity of LDS scripture against distortion
  • Identifies himself as an Elder of the LDS Church

history.author: Page, John E.
history.citation: Page, John E. “Mormonism, alias Truth.” Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania)(28 June 1842).
history.teaser:
An article by John E. Page in defense of Mormonism against criticisms and misrepresentations in the press, specifically addressing misconceptions about the Book of Mormon and the Book of Doctrine and Covenants.

Key Points:

  • Defends Mormonism against falsehoods in “The Morning Chronicle”
  • Criticizes the low standards of critics compared to other skeptics
  • Addresses misconceptions about the New Jerusalem in Missouri
  • Clarifies Mormon teachings on acquiring land peacefully
  • Refutes claims that Mormons are commanded to take land by force
  • Highlights the importance of purchasing land to avoid conflict
  • Emphasizes commandments against killing and stealing
  • Condemns the misrepresentation of Mormon doctrines by critics

history.author: A Disciple
history.citation: A Disciple. [Reply to John E. Page.] Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (29 June 1842).
history.teaser:
A letter to the editor questioning the credibility of the Book of Mormon with specific references to its content.

Key Points:

  • Questions about the physical location of the city of Morourhah
  • Description of Jaredite ships likened to dishes and whales
  • Mentions Jaredites’ genealogy extending beyond Adam
  • Claims the Book of Mormon quotes Shakespeare 2000 years early
  • Notes use of a mariner’s compass 600 years before the Christian era
  • Points out contradiction: Jesus’s birthplace as Jerusalem, not Bethlehem
  • Discrepancy in duration of darkness during Crucifixion noted
  • Asserts irreconcilable contradictions between the Bible and the Book of Mormon

history.author: Page, John E.
history.citation: Page, John E. “Mormonism alias, Truth.” Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania)(30 June 1842).
history.teaser:
An article by John E. Page defending Mormonism against criticisms, emphasizing divine revelations and the uniqueness of the Latter-day Saint church.

Key Points:

  • Mormons have interactions with angels as biblical figures did
  • Mormonism claims to be the only true church
  • Comparison of the LDS church to ancient Christian church
  • Scriptural basis for the existence of a true church in the last days
  • Misinterpretation and criticism of LDS beliefs addressed
  • Book of Mormon claimed to be written by divine inspiration
  • Assertion that truth will prevail despite persecution
  • John E. Page emphasizes the eternal principle of truth

history.author: Pratt Parley P. (Parley Parker), 1807-1857
history.document: “When we reflect on the great purposes of God”
history.citation: Pratt, Parley P. Editorial Remarks. Latter-day Saints’ Millennial Star (Liverpool,England) 3, no. 3 (July 1842): 44–47.
history.teaser:
Parley P. Pratt’s editorial in the Millennial Star advocates for the divine origins and purposes of the Latter-Day Saint movement, critiquing contemporary religious practices and emphasizing the need for direct revelation and divine authority.

Key Points:

  • Editorial reflects on God’s purposes and criticizes current religious creeds.
  • Questions the acceptance of Jesus by the present generation.
  • Highlights opposition between God’s ways and human wisdom.
  • Discusses conflicts among religious societies and their impact.
  • Prophesies a “marvellous work and a wonder” through Joseph Smith.
  • Details the providential discovery of the Book of Abraham.
  • Asserts the Book of Abraham’s translation through divine means.
  • Encourages Saints to be receptive to ongoing revelation.

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 17 (1 July 1842):832–33.
history.teaser:
An account detailing the arrival of Oliver Cowdery at Joseph Smith’s home and the beginning of their collaboration on translating the Book of Mormon, including a revelation encouraging their work.

Key Points:

  • Oliver Cowdery came to inquire about the plates in April 1829
  • Translation of the Book of Mormon began on April 17, 1829
  • A revelation was received encouraging the translation work
  • God’s word described as quick, powerful, and capable of enlightenment
  • Commanded to seek not riches but wisdom and to bring forth Zion
  • Oliver Cowdery is encouraged to use his gift for God’s work
  • The importance of being faithful and diligent in keeping commandments
  • Promise of Jesus Christ’s presence in the midst of their work

history.author: Page, John E.
history.citation: Page, John E. To a Disciple. Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (1 July 1842).
history.teaser:
An article by John E. Page in the Morning Chronicle addressing criticisms of the Book of Mormon and affirming its authenticity through scriptural and archaeological references.

Key Points:

  • Refers to Isaiah to defend the Book of Mormon
  • Discusses the Book of Mormon’s prediction of ancient American cities
  • Mentions Mr. Anthon’s encounter with characters from the plates
  • Addresses the location of the city of Moronihah
  • Claims the Book of Mormon will be ranked with the Bible
  • Counters accusations of inaccuracies in the Book of Mormon
  • Defends the Book of Mormon’s account of Christ’s birth
  • Challenges critics and defends the truth of the Book of Mormon

history.author: Serrine, Mephibosheth
history.citation: Serrine, Mephibosheth. Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 17 (1 July 1842):838–39.
history.teaser:
A letter published in the “Times and Seasons” describing the missionary efforts and public debate in Michigan that resulted in support for the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Mephibosheth Serrine reports on spreading the truth in Michigan
  • Visited different churches; found them generally prosperous
  • Held two-day meetings, leading to baptisms and interest
  • Faced opposition from various religious leaders
  • Engaged in a public debate on the Book of Mormon’s divinity
  • Debate resulted in a decision favoring the Book of Mormon
  • Some attendees lost faith in Methodism after the debate
  • Serrine sees this as part of the Book of Mormon’s prophecy fulfillment

history.author: A Disciple
history.document: “Not feeling that I have any personal difference”
history.citation: A Disciple. [Reply to John E. Page.] Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (2 July 1842).
history.teaser:
A critical letter in the Morning Chronicle addressing discrepancies between the Book of Mormon and the Bible.

Key Points:

  • Author challenges Elder Page without personal animosity
  • Points out anachronisms and inconsistencies in the Book of Mormon
  • Highlights differences between the 1st and 3rd editions of the Book of Mormon
  • Claims the Book of Mormon contradicts the Bible on Jesus’s birthplace and the duration of darkness at his crucifixion
  • Asserts that both records cannot be true; one must be false
  • Concludes the Bible is true, thus the Book of Mormon must be false
  • Uses the metaphor “Dagon has fallen before the ark of the Lord” to illustrate his point

history.author: Page, John E.
history.citation: Page, John E. “Mormonism Defended.” Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (2 July 1842).
history.teaser:
An article by John E. Page defending Mormonism against claims made in “Mormonism Unveiled,” specifically addressing the theory that Sidney Rigdon created the Book of Mormon from a manuscript by Solomon Spaulding.

Key Points:

  • Page refutes the claim that Rigdon authored the Book of Mormon.
  • Benjamin Winchester’s testimony is used to discredit “Mormonism Unveiled.”
  • “Mormonism Unveiled” suggests Rigdon used a Spaulding manuscript.
  • Rigdon’s timeline disputes his ability to have used the manuscript.
  • Mrs. Davidson (Spaulding’s widow) had the manuscript, not Rigdon.
  • Page argues against the credibility of “Mormonism Unveiled.”
  • The article illustrates the lengths to which enemies of Mormonism will go.
  • Compares persecution of Mormons to that of early Christians.

history.author: A Disciple
history.document: “I have a few questions to ask Elder John E. Page:”
history.citation: A Disciple. [Reply to John E. Page.] Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (7 July 1842).
history.teaser:
A critical editorial questioning the teachings and intentions of Mormonism, as addressed to Elder John E. Page.

Key Points:

  • Questions if Mormonism intends to supersede Christianity
  • Compares Joseph Smith to Moses and Jesus as a religious author
  • Asks if the Book of Mormon sets aside the Old and New Testaments
  • Questions why Mormons don’t baptize into Joseph Smith
  • Inquires about divine confirmation of Joseph Smith’s authority
  • Contrasts peaceful prophetic visions with Joseph Smith’s military actions
  • Claims Mormons consider America their promised land
  • Questions if Mormons will attempt to expel non-believers from America
  • Accuses Mormonism of promoting conversion through force
  • Alleges Joseph Smith required a bodyguard for suspicion of assassination involvement
  • Claims assassination is commanded for dissenters within Mormonism
  • Asserts Mormonism aims to establish a Western Empire

history.author: Page, John E.
history.citation: Page, John E. “Mormonism, alias Truth.” Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (8 July 1842).
history.teaser:
An article by John E. Page in the Pittsburgh Morning Chronicle defending Mormonism against accusations and explaining the Spaulding theory origins.

Key Points:

  • Defends Mormonism against falsehoods and misrepresentations
  • Addresses accusations published in “The Morning Chronicle” and “New York Watchman”
  • Proceeds to detail the Spaulding story origin
  • Cites Benjamin Winchester’s work on the Spaulding theory

history.author: A Disciple
history.citation: A Disciple. [Reply to John E. Page.] Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (9 July 1842).
history.teaser:
A critical letter in a Pittsburgh newspaper challenging the claims and integrity of the Book of Mormon and its proponents, particularly targeting Elder John E. Page’s defenses.

Key Points:

  • Accuses Elder Page of avoiding criticisms of Mormonism
  • Claims Mormonism has been exposed to public indignation
  • Doubts the credibility of Mormon witnesses compared to biblical apostles
  • Equates belief in the Book of Mormon with credulity
  • Compares the moral and dignified essence of Christianity with Mormonism negatively
  • Lists negative qualities associated with Mormonism
  • Challenges the authenticity of the Book of Mormon and its witnesses
  • Questions specific claims made in the Book of Mormon about Jesus

history.author: Piccoola
history.citation: Piccoola. [Letter to the Editors.] Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (11 July 1842).
history.teaser:
A letter to the editors of the Morning Chronicle mocking the Book of Mormon and its followers.

Key Points:

  • Compares a Book of Mormon story to the Kilkenny cats tale
  • Mentions a great battle where only two generals survive
  • Describes an impossible recovery of General Shiz after decapitation
  • Jokes about a Mormon captain’s exhortation to his soldiers
  • Mentions a miraculous survival story of Peter Wimmer’s son-in-law
  • Compares Mormons to cats, suggesting they have many lives

history.author: A Disciple
history.citation: A Disciple. [Reply to John E. Page.] Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (14 July 1842).
history.teaser:
An editorial challenging the divine origin of the Book of Mormon and questioning Joseph Smith’s claim to be its author and proprietor.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith swore he was the author and proprietor of the Book of Mormon
  • The book claims divine origin yet Smith claims authorship
  • If God wrote and translated it, Smith can’t be the author
  • Smith’s claim challenges the book’s divine inspiration
  • Claiming authorship contradicts divine authorship
  • If the book is divine, Smith has perjured himself
  • Questioning the propriety of profiting from a divine book
  • Asks why original texts are not presented like the Bible

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Time and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 18 (15 July 1842):853–54.
history.teaser:
An account of Joseph Smith’s and Oliver Cowdery’s experiences in receiving revelations, including their inquiry about John the Apostle and Cowdery’s desire to translate.

Key Points:

  • Oliver Cowdery received confirmation of the Book of Mormon’s truth
  • Several revelations received during translation in April
  • Revelation on whether John the Apostle remained on earth
  • John desired to bring souls to Christ and was granted to tarry
  • Oliver Cowdery desired the power to translate ancient records
  • Revelation given to Cowdery concerning his gift and limitations
  • Importance of faith and proper intent in asking God
  • Cowdery counseled to be patient and continue writing for Smith

history.citation: “American Antiquities.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 18 (15 July 1842): 858–60.
history.teaser:
An article in the LDS periodical “Times and Seasons” discussing ancient American civilizations, their cultures, and technologies, and suggesting a connection with the peoples described in the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Questioning if current Native Americans built ancient mounds and used metals
  • Artifacts found that suggest advanced ancient civilizations
  • Comparison of ancient American artifacts with those of ancient Asia
  • Discussion on the knowledge of metals and craftsmanship
  • Artifacts include idols, vessels, and metal ornaments
  • Evidence of large, civilized nations existing in America before Europeans
  • Book of Mormon as a historical document detailing ancient American civilizations
  • Call for researchers to consider the Book of Mormon in their studies

history.author: Page, John E.
history.citation: Page, John E. “To ‘A Disciple.’” Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) (19 July 1842).
history.teaser:
John E. Page defends the legitimacy of the Book of Mormon and its compatibility with the Bible.

Key Points:

  • Page challenges the credibility of skeptics’ testimonies
  • Compares the apostles’ testimonies to those of Mormons
  • Asserts knowledge of scriptures through the Holy Ghost
  • Addresses perceived contradictions between Bible and Book of Mormon
  • Argues against the dismissal of Book of Mormon based on bias
  • References skepticism towards scriptures by citing specific works
  • Highlights the importance of understanding historical context
  • Emphasizes the Book of Mormon’s account as historical fact

history.author: Page, John E.
history.citation: Page, John E. “Mormonism Concluded: To ‘A Disciple.’” Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh,Pennsylvania) (20 July 1842).
history.teaser:
An article by John E. Page defending the actions and intentions of Mormons in Nauvoo, Illinois, and correcting misconceptions about the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Nauvoo Legion organized by Illinois Legislature, not Mormons
  • Legion intended for country’s safety against threats
  • Mormons love their country and its free institutions
  • No fortification of Nauvoo, only construction of buildings
  • Corrects misrepresentation of Jesus Christ’s birthplace in Book of Mormon
  • Book of Mormon says “at Jerusalem,” not “in Jerusalem”
  • Accuses critic of dishonesty in misrepresenting Book of Mormon
  • Defends Prophet Alma’s prophecy regarding Christ’s birth

history.author: A Disciple
history.citation: A Disciple. [Concluding Remarks.] Morning Chronicle (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania)(22 July 1842).
history.teaser:
An article from the Morning Chronicle expressing criticism towards Joseph Smith, Jr., the Book of Mormon, and Mormon practices.

Key Points:

  • Author criticizes the character and actions of Joseph Smith, Jr.
  • Claims the Book of Mormon contradicts the Bible regarding Christ’s birthplace and the duration of darkness at crucifixion
  • Joseph Smith, Jr. swore he was the author of the Book of Mormon
  • Mention of a military organization within the Mormon Church called the Danite band
  • Accusations against Joseph Smith of swearing, blasphemy, and adultery
  • Questioning the authenticity of Mormons speaking in tongues
  • Joseph Smith instructed to learn languages by study
  • Invites Elder Page to a public discussion on Mormonism

history.citation: “Extracts from the Weekly Bostonian.” Latter-day Saints’ Millennial Star (Liverpool,England) 3, no. 4 (August 1842): 65–67.
history.teaser:
An article detailing the activities and growth of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church) in Boston and surrounding areas, including commentary on Joseph Smith.

Key Points:

  • LDS meetings held at 82 Commercial Street, Boston
  • Church formed in March with over thirty members
  • Approximately seventy baptized in Salem and vicinity
  • High demand for LDS preachers
  • Joseph Smith described as a significant and successful leader
  • LDS Church activities include healing and preaching
  • Elder Nickerson reports significant growth and baptisms
  • Invitation to investigate LDS teachings and witness miracles

history.document: Great Discussion between Dr. West and Elder Adams
history.citation: “Great Discussion on Mormonism Between Dr. West and Elder Adams, at theMarlboro’ Chapel.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 19 (1 August 1842):863–64. Reprinted The Bostonian (25 June 1842).

  • Elder Adams defended Mormonism using biblical references.

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 19 (1 August 1842):865–67.
history.teaser:
An account of Joseph Smith’s history focusing on the reception of the Aaronic priesthood and early missionary efforts in the LDS Church.

Key Points:

  • Joseph and Oliver prayed about baptism and received a heavenly messenger
  • John the Baptist ordained them with the Aaronic Priesthood
  • Commanded to baptize each other and did so
  • Experienced blessings and the spirit of prophecy after baptism
  • Kept their baptism and priesthood reception secret due to persecution
  • Joseph’s brother Samuel H. Smith was baptized after seeking revelation
  • Revelation given to Hyrum Smith emphasizing the importance of God’s word
  • Encouragement to focus on obtaining and keeping God’s commandments

history.citation: From the Bostonian, July 2nd. Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 19 (1 August 1842): 865. Reprinted from The Bostonian (2 July 1842).
history.teaser:
A report from The Bostonian detailing a public discussion on the validity of the Book of Mormon and the claims of the Latter Day Saint movement.

  • Dr. West criticized the Book of Mormon as a humbug.
  • West accused Mormonism of lying, fraud, and blasphemy.
  • Elder Adams defended the Book of Mormon and its witnesses.

  • Controversy over the credibility of interested witnesses.
  • Adams referenced Biblical prophecies supporting the Book of Mormon.
  • Debate included audience and chairman’s reactions.
  • Discussion ended with plans for further debate.

history.document: Great Discussion between Dr. West and Elder Adams

A summary of a public debate on Mormonism between Dr. West and Elder Adams, highlighting challenges to the credibility of Joseph Smith and the Book of Mormon, and the defense of its truthfulness.

  • Dr. West attempted to impeach Joseph Smith and Mormon witnesses’ characters
  • Accusations included being money diggers and superstitious
  • Dr. West cited a letter claiming the Book of Mormon was not believed by its printer
  • Elder Adams compared the accusations to those faced by Christ and His apostles

  • Adams offered to finance verification of the accusers’ claims
  • The discussion ended with a note claiming a triumph of truth over error

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 3, no. 20 (15 August 1842): 884–85.
history.teaser:
An article detailing Joseph Smith’s early experiences translating the Book of Mormon and receiving revelations for his early supporters.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Knight Sr. provided provisions for Smith’s translation work
  • Revelation given to Joseph Knight Sr. about a great work
  • Peter Whitmer and family offered support and accommodations
  • David, John, and Peter Whitmer Jr. became zealous assistants
  • Revelations given to David, John, and Peter Whitmer Jr.

history.author: Kimball, Heber C., Orson Hyde, and Willard Richards
history.citation: Kimball, Heber C., Orson Hyde, and Willard Richards. “Mission to England, or theFirst Foreign Mission of the Latter-day Saints.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo,Illinois) 3, no. 20 (15 August 1842): 879–84.

An account of the first foreign mission of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints to England, detailing the experiences and challenges faced by the missionaries.

  • Without financial means, missionaries relied on Providence and kindness
