  • Plates appeared to be brass, covered in unknown characters
  • Plates cleaned with soap and dilute sulphuric acid
  • Discovery has generated interest in the translation of the hieroglyphics
  • Plates were found more than twelve feet below the mound’s surface
  • Certificate by Kinderhook citizens confirms the discovery

history.citation: “Ancient Records.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 4, no. 12 (1 May 1843): 185–86.
history.teaser:
An article discussing the increasing evidence supporting the authenticity of the Book of Mormon, paralleling its initial skepticism to that faced by Columbus.

Key Points:

  • New evidence supports the Book of Mormon’s authenticity
  • Initial skepticism compared to Columbus’s voyage
  • Early objections based on perceived danger to religious interest
  • Recent discoveries suggest an advanced ancient civilization in America
  • Letter and certificate may convince skeptics of the existence of ancient plates
  • Discovery of plates could validate the Book of Mormon
  • Editor suggests Joseph Smith’s translation could enlighten early American history
  • Encouragement to read the Book of Mormon for personal understanding

history.author: Smith, Joseph, 1805-1844
history.document: “To the Editor of the Times & Seasons”
history.citation: Smith, Joseph. “To the Editor of the Times & Seasons.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo,Illinois) 4, no. 13 (15 May 1843): 194.
history.teaser:
Joseph Smith addresses misconceptions about the word “Mormon” and clarifies its origin and meaning in a letter to the editor.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith corrects an error about the word “Mormon.”
  • “Mormon” is not derived from the Greek word “mormo.”
  • The Book of Mormon was translated from “Reformed Egyptian,” not Greek or Latin.
  • Only God could interpret the Book of Mormon’s language after its people died.
  • The word “Mormon” stands independent of contemporary learning and wisdom.
  • The Bible’s meaning of “good” aligns with various languages’ interpretations.
  • “Mormon” means “more good” according to Joseph Smith.

history.author: Stewart, G. C.
history.citation: Stewart, G. C. “The Book of Mormon.” The Perfectionist (Putney, Vermont) 3, no. 7 (15 May 1843): 28. The Book of Mormon.
history.teaser:
A critical examination of the Book of Mormon, highlighting perceived inconsistencies and absurdities.

Key Points:

  • Book contains grammatical blunders and contradictions
  • Errors persist despite revisions by Joseph Smith
  • Modern phrases suggest it’s a modern work
  • Describes an impossible scenario of total darkness
  • Claims of a race annihilating itself are absurd
  • Description of barges is considered illogical
  • Book attempts to settle theological questions
  • Author criticizes the practicality of the barges’ design

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 4, no. 13 (15 May 1843): 193–94.
history.teaser:
An article detailing Joseph Smith’s journey and experiences leading to his distancing from traditional religious groups, focusing on integrity and the search for truth.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith chose truth over wealth, popularity, and ease
  • Announced departure from his church in 1824, causing shock
  • Alexander Campbell and Walter Scott also left their churches
  • Smith, Campbell, and Scott engaged in religious discussions
  • Smith worked as a tanner after leaving ministry
  • Removal to Bainbridge, Ohio, where Smith resumed preaching
  • Preached doctrines of repentance, baptism for remission of sins
  • Urged hearers to use the Bible as the rule of faith

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 4, no. 14 (1 June 1843): 209–10.
history.teaser:
An account from the “Times and Seasons” detailing Elder Sidney Rigdon’s early ministry efforts, challenges, and eventual success in spreading religious teachings.

Key Points:

  • Moved to Mentor, Ohio, upon invitation from a Baptist Church remnant
  • Faced initial skepticism and slander from locals
  • Overcame opposition through consistent behavior and eloquence
  • Preached new doctrines that resonated with many, expanding his ministry
  • Challenged traditional religious interpretations, offering new insights
  • Highlighted prophesies relevant to the present and future
  • Conducted baptisms, drawing people from all societal ranks
  • Gained respect from the learned and intelligent for his biblical knowledge

history.author: Campbell, Alexander, 1788-1866
history.citation: Campbell, Alexander. “Remarks on the Mormon Expose.” Millennial Harbinger 7,no. 13 (August 1843): 351.
history.teaser:
A critical commentary by Alexander Campbell, dismissing the Book of Mormon as a fraudulent and wicked delusion.

Key Points:

  • Campbell criticizes the Book of Mormon as a significant humbug
  • Describes it as a mix of ignorance, impudence, and impiety
  • Claims to have published an expose for the benefit of the community
  • Compares Mormonism’s wickedness unfavorably with other delusions
  • Views it as worse than the Koran but limited by the era’s enlightenment
  • Deplores the ignorance and gullibility of religious masses
  • Expresses embarrassment over its spread in America and elsewhere
  • Refers readers to previous documents for further evidence of its impiety

history.citation: Daily National Intelligencer 31, no. 9509 (10 August 1843).
history.teaser:
A newspaper commentary expressing skepticism about newly “discovered” works, comparing them to potential claims by Joseph Smith about finding more Mormon scripture.

Key Points:

  • Comparison made between alleged Byron works and Mormon scripture
  • Statement viewed as an attempt to deceive the public
  • Byron left no such manuscripts, according to the commentary
  • Any genuine manuscripts would have been published much earlier

history.citation: “History of Joseph Smith.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 4, no. 19 (15 August 1843): 289–90.
history.teaser:
An account detailing the early history of Joseph Smith and the spread of the Book of Mormon, highlighting his humble circumstances and the arrival of key figures sharing the Book of Mormon in Nauvoo, Illinois.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith’s indifferent view towards wealth for promoting principles
  • Community support for providing Smith a suitable residence
  • Joseph Smith’s temporal prospects improved significantly
  • Visits by Parley P. Pratt, Ziba Peterson, Oliver Cowdery, and Peter Whitmer to testify about the Book of Mormon
  • Introduces the Book of Mormon to Sidney Rigdon, who was initially skeptical
  • Rigdon agrees to investigate the Book of Mormon’s claims
  • Many in Kirtland, including Rigdon, eventually accept the Book of Mormon
  • Rigdon convinced of the Book of Mormon’s truth through personal revelation

history.citation: “Stephens’ Works on Central America.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 4, no. 22 (1 October 1843): 346–47.
history.teaser:
An article from a Latter-day Saint publication discussing the significance of Stephens’ explorations in Central America to the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Stephens’ work details ancient, sophisticated civilizations in America
  • Work has passed through twelve editions, indicating widespread interest
  • Stephens made further explorations with the Daguerreotype
  • His findings are seen as supporting the Book of Mormon
  • Stephens visited ancient cities, aligning with Book of Mormon accounts
  • Describes ruins as evidence of a once mighty people
  • Book of Mormon published years before these discoveries
  • Explorations considered strong circumstantial evidence for the Book of Mormon

history.author: Johnson, T. C.
history.citation: “Methodistic Candor And Consistency.” T. C. Johnson to Alexander Campbell. Millennial Harbinger 7, no. 12 (December 1843): 553–57.
history.teaser:
A letter by T. C. Johnson to Alexander Campbell discussing the misconceptions and misrepresentations of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church) and its doctrines as compared to those of Alexander Campbell and his followers.

Key Points:

  • Johnson critiques a book that conflates Mormonism with Campbellism.
  • The book claims early Mormons were influenced by Alexander Campbell.
  • Johnson argues the book falsely associates Campbell’s teachings with Mormonism.
  • Johnson points out the absurdity of linking Mormon baptism practices to Campbellism.
  • Methodism, by the author’s logic, could also be linked to Mormonism.
  • Johnson defends the original teachings of Campbell against accusations of similarity to Mormon doctrine.
  • He criticizes the Methodist Episcopal Church for endorsing the book’s misrepresentations.
  • Johnson calls for fairness, truth, and preparation for divine judgment.

history.author: Brown, Henry, 1789-1849
history.citation: Brown, Henry. The History of Illinois, from its first discovery and settlement, to the present time, 394. New York: J. Winchester, New World Press, 1844.
history.teaser:
An 1844 critique of the Book of Mormon and the Latter Day Saints, comparing their beliefs and practices unfavorably with traditional Christianity.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon held in same veneration as New Testament
  • Author skeptical of the Book of Mormon’s authenticity
  • Mormons’ story seen as implausible by the author
  • Comparison with other contemporary “impostures”
  • Age described as “an age of humbugs”
  • Gold plates no longer exist, arousing suspicion
  • Law of Moses on stone vs. Mormon law on gold plates
  • Contrast between Christ’s actions and Mormon prophet’s goals

history.author: Hunt, James H.
history.citation: Hunt, James H. Mormonism: Embracing the Origin, Rise and Progress of the Sect, with an Examination of the Book of Mormon; Also, Their Troubles in Missouri, and Final Expulsion from the State, St. Louis: Ustick & Davies, 1844.
history.teaser:
A critical examination of the origins, beliefs, and historical conflicts of Mormonism, focusing on its development and the controversies surrounding the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Objective to provide a factual account of conflicts in Missouri
  • Focuses on denouncing wrongdoings by both Mormons and Missourians
  • Includes an examination of the Book of Mormon
  • Covers the rise and progress of the Mormon sect
  • Discusses the expulsion of Mormons from Missouri
  • Appendix details disturbances in Illinois leading to the Smiths’ deaths
  • Intends to correct falsehoods spread by Mormons
  • Published shortly after the death of Joseph and Hyrum Smith

history.author: Baird, Robert
history.document: Religion in the United States of America
history.citation: Baird, Robert. Religion in the United States of America: Or, An account of the origin, progress, relations to the state, and present condition of the evangelical churches in the United States, with notices of unevangelical denominations, 647–49. Glasgow: Blackieand Son, 1844.
history.teaser:
A critical examination of the origins and development of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons) by Robert Baird, highlighting perceived fraudulence and delusion.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism seen as an example of cunning leadership and deluded followers
  • Joseph Smith claimed to receive golden plates from an angel in 1827
  • Book of Mormon published as a result of these revelations
  • Book of Mormon is not considered a substitute but a supplement to the Bible
  • Joseph Smith also attempted a new translation of the Bible
  • Origins of Mormonism traced to the publication of the Book of Mormon in 1830
  • Mormons moved to several locations, facing opposition, before settling in Nauvoo, Illinois
  • Leaders criticized for ambition and character, leading to predictions of the sect’s demise

history.author: Lewis, R. B. (Robert Benjamin)
history.citation: Lewis, R. B. Light and Truth; Collected from the Bible and Ancient and Modern History, Containing the Universal History of the Colored and the Indian Race, from the Creation of the World to the Present Time, 34. Boston: A Committee of ColoredGentlemen, 1844.
history.teaser:
A historical account linking the genealogy of Joseph from the Bible to the peoples described in the Book of Mormon, emphasizing connections to Egyptian and Ethiopian heritage.

Key Points:

  • Joseph’s sons Manasseh and Ephraim lead to Manassehites and Ephraimites
  • Descendants include various tribes such as Machirites and Gileadites
  • Zelophehad’s daughters listed, showing female lineage importance
  • Claims Manasseh’s descendants were Egyptians or Ethiopians
  • Book of Mormon peoples are descendants of Joseph and Ishmael
  • Lehi’s sons were Laman, Lemuel, Sam, and Nephi
  • Lehi’s sons married daughters of Ishmael, described as “dark red people”
  • Emphasizes a genealogical link between biblical figures and Book of Mormon peoples

history.author: Evans, John, 1767-1827
history.document: History of All Christian Sects and Denominations
history.citation: Evans, John. L. L. D. History of all Christian Sects and Denominations; Their Origin, Peculiar Tenets, and Present Condition. With an Introductory Account of Atheists, Deists, Jews, Mahometans, Pagans, &c. , from the fifteenth London edition. Revisedand Enlarged. 2nd ed., 232–33. New-York: James Mowatt & Co., 1844.
history.teaser:
An early and critical overview of the origins, beliefs, and spread of the Latter-Day Saint movement, focusing on the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Book of Mormon published in 1830
  • Doctrines zealously propagated throughout the United States and Canada
  • Thousands of converts in England, missionaries sent to Palestine
  • Book of Mormon claims history of a pre-Columbian American people
  • Records engraved on plates, deposited in Hill Cumorah, New York
  • Joseph Smith Jr. found the plates in 1825, translated them
  • Translation claimed to be by divine inspiration
  • Smith’s account of obtaining the plates included in a 1842 letter

history.author: Adams, George J. (George Jones), 1811-1880
history.document: A Lecture on the Authenticity & Scriptural Character of the Book of Mormon
history.citation: Adams, George J. A Lecture on the Authenticity & Scriptural Character of the Book of Mormon, 1–24. Boston: J. E. Farwell, 1844.
history.teaser:
A lecture by George J. Adams advocating for the authenticity and scriptural alignment of the Book of Mormon, delivered in Charlestown, Massachusetts, in 1844.

Key Points:

  • Addressed misconceptions about the Latter Day Saints’ beliefs.
  • Argued that the Book of Mormon is foretold by biblical prophecy.
  • Presented the Book of Mormon as a continuation of biblical revelation.
  • Emphasized unity between the Book of Mormon and the Bible.
  • Highlighted scriptural references indicating the coming of an additional book.
  • Discussed the prophecy of a sealed book understood by the unlearned.
  • Connected the coming forth of the Book of Mormon to the gathering of Israel.
  • Encouraged scrutiny of scriptures to find truth and understanding.

history.author: Merrill, Joseph W.
history.citation: Merrill, Joseph W. The People’s Cabinet: Containing A Compendium Upon the Subjects of Natural History; Natural Philosophy; Astronomy; Constitution, Organization, and Functions of the Human Body; and the Mind and Its Faculties; History of the United States: Government and Law, Particularly of the United States; Also, The Beliefs of Various Religious Denominations; And Biographical Sketches of Distinguished Characters in all Ages of the World, 279–80. Boston: Joseph W. Merrill, 1844.
history.teaser:
A comprehensive overview of the beliefs of the Latter Day Saints as presented in The People’s Cabinet, highlighting the foundational role of the Book of Mormon in Mormonism.

Key Points:

  • The Book of Mormon was first published in 1830
  • It records the history of people in America before Columbus
  • Joseph Smith, Jr. found and translated the plates by God’s direction
  • Belief in God, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost
  • Salvation through Christ and obedience to gospel ordinances
  • Ordinances include faith, repentance, baptism, and laying on of hands
  • Belief in the organization of the primitive church
  • Belief in the Bible and Book of Mormon as God’s word

history.author: Raumer, Fredrich von (1781-1873)
history.citation: Raumer, Fredrich von. America and the American People, 334–36. 1844.
history.teaser:
A historical account by Fredrich von Raumer regarding Joseph Smith, the founding of Mormonism, and early conflicts involving Mormons.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith characterized as lively and cunning
  • Smith announced a new revelation in 1827
  • Smith refused to produce the original tablets
  • Smith gained numerous followers despite skepticism
  • Mormons faced opposition and settled in Mississippi
  • Governor Dunklin advocated for religious freedom
  • Mormons’ views conflicted with democratic institutions
  • Smith’s death did not change the course of opposition

history.document: Book of Mormon Broadside–Notice of Publication
history.citation: Book of Mormon Broadside (Palmyra, N. Y.) ( 1844).
history.teaser:
A broadside promoting the Book of Mormon in 1844, linking it to biblical prophecies and the narrative of a sacred text lost and found.

Key Points:

  • Title refers to the Stick of Joseph, from Ephraim
  • Contains a copy of characters from the Book of Mormon plates
  • Characters were shown to Professor Anthon by Martin Harris in 1827
  • Links the story to Isaiah 28. 11, 12 about a sealed book
  • Quotes Psalm 85:11 about truth springing from the earth
  • References Hosea 8:12 about God’s laws given to Ephraim
  • Ezekiel 37:19 prophecy about joining the sticks of Joseph and Judah
  • Mentions an aged Indian’s lament about a lost sacred book

history.author: Gregg, Josiah, 1806-1850
history.citation: Gregg, Josiah. Commerce of the Prairies: or the Journal of a Santa Fé Trader, during Eight Expeditions across The Great Western Prairies, and a Residence of Nearly Nine Years in Northern Mexico, vol. 1, 312–20. New York: Langley & Astor, 1844.
history.teaser:
An account by Josiah Gregg detailing the conflicts between early Mormons and their Missouri neighbors, leading to the Mormons’ expulsion.

Key Points:

  • Mormons originally selected Independence, Missouri, for their New Jerusalem.
  • Conflicts arose due to alleged Mormon thefts and immorality.
  • Increasing Mormon population threatened local control, leading to violence.
  • A mob destroyed a Mormon printing establishment and punished leaders.
  • Joseph Smith, the Mormon leader, was not present during conflicts.
  • Mormons eventually surrendered and were forced to leave the area.
  • After moving to Clay County, Mormons faced further conflicts and moved again.
  • Mormons refused to sell Missouri property, aiming to reconquer it.

history.author: Appleby, W. I. (William Ivins), 1811-1870
history.citation: Appleby, W. I. A Dissertation of Nebuchadnezzar’s Dream: Showing that the Kingdom Spoken of by Daniel the Prophet was not set up in the Days of the Apostles; and the Order of the Kingdom set up then Explained. Also: The Rise and Faith of the most Notable Orthodox Societies of the Present Day, Together with a Synopsis of the Origin and Faith of the Church of “Latter-Day Saints,” Comparing their Faith with the Faith of Other Societies, 1–24. Philadelphia: Brown, Bicking & Guilbert, 1844.
history.teaser:
A summary of an 1844 document by W. I. Appleby providing a detailed account of the early history, beliefs, and experiences of Joseph Smith, founder of the Latter Day Saint movement, including his first visions, the reception of the Book of Mormon, and the establishment of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith’s early visions and visitations by angels
  • Reception and translation of the Book of Mormon
  • Establishment of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints in 1830
  • Belief in living prophets and continuous revelation
  • Emphasis on obedience to God’s commandments and ordinances
  • Persecutions faced by early Latter-Day Saints
  • Rapid growth and missionary work of the Church globally
  • Assertion of the Church’s divine origin and destiny to prevail

history.author: Campbell, Alexander, 1788-1866
history.document: Mistakes Touching the Book of Mormon
history.citation: C., A. (Alexander Campbell). “Mistakes Touching the Book of Mormon.” Millennial Harbinger 1, no. 1 (January 1844): 38–42.
history.teaser:
A critique by Alexander Campbell on misconceptions regarding the Book of Mormon’s origins and teachings, specifically addressing the concept of baptism for the remission of sins.

Key Points:

  • Mormonism accused of stealing the true gospel
  • Rigdon said to have learned gospel elements before meeting Smith
  • Baptism for remission of sins is indeed found in the Book of Mormon
  • Misconceptions about the origin and teachings of the Book of Mormon addressed
  • Campbell refutes claims baptism for remission wasn’t initially part of Mormon doctrine
  • Discussion on the public and internal Christian debate regarding baptism
  • Campbell advocates for correct understanding and practice of baptism
  • Emphasizes importance of addressing misconceptions for unity and clarity within Christian beliefs

history.citation: “Ancient Ruins.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 5, no. 1 (1 January 1844):390–91.
history.teaser:
An article discussing the discovery of ancient ruins in America, supporting the authenticity of the Book of Mormon’s account of advanced ancient civilizations on the continent.

Key Points:

  • Fresh testimony supports the Book of Mormon’s authenticity
  • Discovery of ancient cities challenges previous beliefs
  • Stephens’ travels add evidence of advanced ancient civilizations
  • Ruins found in Northern Texas and between Santa Fe and the Pacific
  • Immense ruins of an ancient temple described
  • Architecture not attributed to Spaniards or Europeans
  • Ruins believed to resemble Palenque or Otulum
  • Speculation about connections to the Aztic or Toltec races

history.citation: “The Gathering.” Times and Seasons 5, no. 2 (15 January 1844): 407–10.
history.teaser:
An article from the “Times and Seasons” discussing the concept of the gathering of the saints, its biblical precedents, and its theological significance.

Key Points:

  • Gathering of saints seen as strange by the religious world.
  • Gathering is a principle Jehovah has acted upon throughout history.
  • All nations shall flock to Zion, established in righteousness.
  • God’s plans for humanity are comprehensive and wise.
  • Everything created by God was for a purpose and His glory.
  • Different glories for different beings in the afterlife.
  • The earth will be purified and become celestial.
  • Prophets and apostles sought a celestial inheritance through faith.

history.document: The Bible and the Book of Mormon.–A Prophecy!
history.citation: “The Bible and the Book of Mormon.—A Prophecy.” Boston Investigator (17 January 1844).
history.teaser:
An article from the Boston Investigator proposing the idea that the Bible and the Book of Mormon originated in similar manners and predicting the eventual incorporation of the Book of Mormon into the Bible and the LDS Church becoming a major religious force.

Key Points:

  • Proposes similarity in origin between the Bible and the Book of Mormon
  • Predicts Mormonism will become the predominant religious sect
  • Book of Mormon will be incorporated into the Bible
  • Old and New Testaments and the Book of Mormon were “found”
  • Councils confirmed the canonical status of Biblical books
  • Mormonism’s growth attributed to its adaptation to the times
  • Persecution predicted to increase Mormonism’s followers
  • Asserts the inevitability of Mormonism’s predominance based on current trends

history.citation: “The Gathering (continued).” Times and Seasons 5, no. 3 (1 February 1844): 423–27.
history.teaser:
An article discussing the biblical and Book of Mormon teachings on the scattering and gathering of Israel, emphasizing God’s continuous care and plan for all branches of the house of Israel.

Key Points:

  • Jared, his brother, and their descendants blessed but eventually swept away
  • Abraham chosen to preserve God’s laws and ordinances through his seed
  • Provisions made for preserving a remnant of Israel in various lands
  • Lehi and Ishmael’s families directed to the Americas
  • Ten Tribes taken to a distant land to be gathered in the latter days
  • Parable of the olive tree in the Book of Mormon explained
  • Some branches of Israel hidden, explaining why not all were known historically
  • Jesus Christ’s teachings in the Book of Mormon about other sheep not of the Jerusalem fold

history.author: M., G. W.
history.citation: [G. W. M. to Br. Whittemore January 1844] “Mormonism,” Trumpet and Universalist Magazine (Boston) 16, no. 37 (2 March 1844): 1. Mormonism.
history.teaser:
An article challenging the association between Mormonism and the doctrine of Universal Salvation, using the Book of Mormon.

Key Points:

  • Elder E. J. Adams delivers lectures on Mormonism in Boston
  • Article questions whether Mormonism teaches Universal Salvation
  • Book of Mormon teaches the Trinity and a personal Devil
  • Adam’s immortality and a state of probation discussed
  • Book of Mormon supports the concept of an infinite atonement
  • Endless misery for the wicked endorsed, against Universal Salvation
  • Preaching Universal Salvation as Mormon belief seen as dishonest
  • Mormons urged to preach their own faith accurately

history.citation: “The Mormons.” Boston Investigator (22 May 1844).
history.teaser:
An 1844 newspaper article from the Boston Investigator discussing the growth and normalization of the Mormon community in Nauvoo, including their engagement in theatrical productions.

Key Points:

  • New York Aurora reports on a theatre in Nauvoo
  • The play Pizarro performed to a large audience
  • Prediction that Mormons will become a significant sect
  • Comparison of Mormon leaders to founders of other sects
  • Joseph Smith’s claims of divine inspiration not unique
  • Reference to other religious founders claiming divine inspiration
  • Future acceptance of Mormons predicted

history.document: Some of the Remarks of John S. Reed
history.citation: Reed, John S. “Some of the Remarks of John S. Reed, Esq., As Delivered Before theState Convention.” Times and Seasons 5, no. 11 (1 June 1844): 549–52.
history.teaser:
John S. Reed’s account of early persecutions faced by Joseph Smith, emphasizing his innocence and integrity.

Key Points:

  • John S. Reed defends Joseph Smith’s character and early history
  • Joseph Smith faced persecution from professed Christians
  • Smith’s character described as irreproachable and intelligent
  • Smith had revelations about finding golden plates
  • Smith was arrested and tried multiple times but found not guilty
  • Reed viewed Smith as predestined by God for a great work
  • Smith’s religious opinions were the main cause of persecution
  • Reed believed God assisted in Smith’s protection and success

history.author: [Pratt, Parley P.]
history.citation: [Pratt, Parley P.] “Joe Smith and the Devil: A Dialogue.” The New York Herald (New York)10, no. 236 (25 August 1844). [undecipherable]
history.teaser:
A satirical piece by Parley P. Pratt presenting a fictional dialogue between Joseph Smith and the Devil, published in The New York Herald.

Key Points:

  • Devil seeking to recruit against Joseph Smith and the Mormons
  • Devil claims Joseph Smith caused him more trouble than others
  • Joseph Smith denies causing trouble, adheres to Mormon creed
  • Devil admits respect for all forms of Christianity except direct revelation
  • Joseph Smith challenges the Devil’s opposition to new revelation
  • Devil acknowledges inability to counter Smith’s arguments
  • Devil admits to spreading falsehoods but blames clergy and editors
  • Ending with a humorous reconciliation and a toast between Smith and the Devil

history.document: The Rise and Ruin of the Sect of Mormon
history.citation: “The Rise and Ruin of the Sect of Mormon.” The Congregational Magazine (September 1844): 641–649.
history.teaser:
An article from The Congregational Magazine providing a critical overview of the rise of Mormonism and the violent death of its founder, Joseph Smith.

Key Points:

  • Joseph Smith’s tragic death announced
  • Smith’s history and claimed revelations discussed
  • Accusations of fraud and the Spaulding manuscript theory mentioned
  • Smith’s narrative of angelic visitations and finding golden plates
  • Critique of the Book of Mormon’s content and claims
  • Persecution and migration of Mormons to Missouri and Illinois
  • Narrative of Smith’s downfall, including charges and mob violence
  • Smith and his brother Hyrum’s deaths in jail by an armed mob

history.author: D., E.
history.document: The Rise and Progress of the Mormon Faith and People
history.citation: D., E. “The Rise and Progress of the Mormon Faith and People.” Southern Literary Messenger 10 (September 1844): 526–38.
history.teaser:
An article from the “Southern Literary Messenger” detailing the history, beliefs, and practices of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons) and their founder, Joseph Smith.

Key Points:

  • Article explores the rise and doctrines of the Mormon church.
  • Joseph Smith’s revelations and translations form the basis of Mormonism.
  • The Book of Mormon is considered a historical and religious record.
  • Mormons believe in modern-day revelation and prophecy.
  • Nauvoo, Illinois, serves as a central gathering place for Mormons.
  • The article critiques the logic and consistency of Mormon beliefs.
  • Mormon missionaries extend their reach globally, even to Jerusalem and India.
  • The rapid growth of Mormonism reflects a deep human yearning for spiritual guidance.

history.citation: “Ancient Ruins.” Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, Illinois) 5, no. 23 (15 December 1844): 744–48.
history.teaser:
An article from the Times and Seasons discussing the significance of ancient ruins in relation to scriptural prophecy and the divine history of the earth as understood by the Latter-Day Saints.

Key Points:

  • Discussion on civilizations before and after Noah’s flood
  • Prophecy fulfillment seen in discovery of ancient ruins
  • Contemporary speculations on ruins compared to scriptural accounts
  • Ruins as evidence of God’s actions on earth
  • Scriptural references to the scattering of people at Babel
  • Comparisons between ancient and modern acts of greatness and folly
  • Book of Mormon as a source for understanding ancient American civilizations
  • Calls for recognition of revelation in understanding ruins and divine history
